speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. On December 1, David McTaggert, Canadian skipper of the Greenpeace III, a vessel of Canadian registry, was boarded in international waters by officers of a French warship as McTaggert was protesting further nuclear testing in the South Pacific. A similar incident occurred in 1973 at which time Mr. McTaggert was injured, removed from his vessel, and incarcerated by French authorities. The Government of Canada later offered Mr. McTaggert an ex gratia payment to espouse his cause.
I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell):
That once the allegation of boarding is confirmed, our government protest in the strongest possible terms this act of piracy on the high seas, condemn further nuclear testing by France in the South Pacific, and urge that that country become a signatory to a treaty banning further nuclear weapons testing, both atmospheric and underground.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I trust that the gathering of the clans in Scotland was more pleasant than the reception he received on his return to Canada. Governor Bouey of the Bank of Canada has for some time been pressing to have the government adopt a tougher fiscal policy. We have a classic example of bad timing in this latest budget because the government is now increasing tax revenues by 31 per cent and Mr. Bouey is saying he is going to continue the high interest rate policy just as we are going into the deepest recession we have had in 30 years. I would ask the President of the Privy Council to indicate where this matter stands on the parliamentary timetable.

Madam Speaker, I am a member of a minority group that remembers very well the way we were treated in World War II. That is why I am concerned about the cabinet document published on June 10 regarding civilian internment camps. It is for that reason that I put down a motion for the production of papers regarding that document. I am now told by one of the officials of the House that it will be months before the papers that will be necessary to debate that document will be translated. It was my impression that the facilities of this chamber are supposed to be bilingual. This is an emergency security document. I was under the impression that the document would be translated relatively simultaneously to its production and that we would therefore be able to debate the matter in the House.

I am very concerned about the issue and I know that other hon. members are also concerned about the matter of civilian internment camps, in spite of the fact that we now have a so-called Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

subsubtopic: MR. FRIESEN-CIVILIAN INTERNMENT CAMPS-AVAILABILITY OF TRANSLATED DOCUMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not know what documents the hon. member is referring to when he says that certain documents have yet to be translated, but as minister responsible for emergency measures planning, I can confirm that there is an order in council which has been published and which only contains instructions for departments, on how to plan for and cope with emergency situations, and these instructions cannot be implemented without an act of Parliament, which would be subject to a complete debate. So, if the hon. member is referring to an order in council, it has been published, and if he is afraid the order in council goes against civil rights and liberties, in that case it is a little early for him to entertain this fear, because the provisions will not become effective until a bill is debated in the House and receives complete and final approval. However, I can confirm that there are no plans to do so in the short term. So if that is what is causing his concern, there is absolutely nothing, to my knowledge, that justifies the anxieties of the hon. member. But in any case, I shall find out exactly to what document he is referring, and if there is a case for speeding up its translation, I shall be glad to take appropriate action.

Such plans will become effective only if an act of Parliament is debated, and the hon. member will then have the debate he desires in the House, but he will have it only if we agree to introduce a bill. For the time being, we have no intention, in the short term, of introducing a bill to implement the plans contained in the order in council. If the hon. member wants to have a debate on emergency planning before the government decides to introduce a bill, I must remind him that there are opposition days when he may enter a private member's bill in his name on the Order Paper, and it will be debated in due course. But as far as the government is concerned, we do not intend to introduce a bill on emergency planning during this session. Furthermore, the order in council to which the hon. member is referring has no enabling authority. These are only instructions to ministers and respective departments, on planning in the event of a national emergency, whether it concerns the Solicitor General, public health, energy or any other area. This is what is known as sound planning. So I really wonder what the hon. member is complaining about. If there are other papers to which he is referring that have not been translated, I should appreciate it if he would give me a more specific reference, and I shall make arrangements to have them translated.

Madam Speaker, just on the same point of order, there is quite a high degree of concern on the issue of Privy Council Order 1305 which was gazetted, I think, on May 21 of this year. It comes under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, I believe. I am wondering why that vehicle has been used to put the nation on notice that the RCMP have been removed as the operators of civilian internment camps. There is a high degree of concern about this in the country at large. Also, why has the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) been given new powers to rearrange prison populations to make room for civilian internees?
Also, I have not been able to get to the bottom of the confusion regarding this order in that outside the body of the text for the Solicitor General, "in the event of war" is contained in the heading. There is, again, some confusion in that under the new charter of rights, the War Measures Act and emergency planning powers are broadened, and a court, on black and white definition, could say, "Yes, you may invoke your existing emergency planning orders", and away you would go.
On the other hand, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) has given a very deliberate and solid address on this issue that we have in our files. He has pointed out that even in the event of an emergency, without the legislation he is talking about, these planning orders would be invoked. Therefore, it would be of great assistance to many people in Canada at large and to some of us in the House if he could clarify just where this Privy Council Order 1305 stands.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the few minutes I have left to speak on the bill, having started my remarks yesterday, I would like to say that we are fortunate in the sense that the bill was delayed, as a result of the constitutional debate, for two reasons. First of all, it gave us the opportunity to measure some of the serious aspects of the bill against the new Constitution. We find after examination that there are some very serious flaws in the document with regard to the right to own property and the way native peoples in Canada lands will be treated when the decision is made to begin serious exploration and development in these Canada lands or in the north.
It is always interesting to speculate what people outside this chamber who are watching every move we make think about some of the matters we are discussing here. I cannot help but briefly review the discussions that took place just before 1 rose.
There is not anyone in the whole country who has followed with interest the debate leading to changes in our Constitution who did not hear someone say that never again will any
member of any ethnic group-and the reference was always made to Japanese Canadians who were incarcerated or interned in 1943 or periods during the Second World War-be subjected to that kind of treatment in our country once we have a Charter of Rights and Freedoms and a new Constitution.
I am sure there are probably thousands of people out there who must be confused, having heard the discussions that just went on here, to learn with alarm that we have a government which has passed an emergency planning order whereby the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan) is compelled and ordered to establish civilian internment camps.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
As you well know, Mr. Speaker, I am usually the last one in the House to abuse the rules of the House, but I would have been remiss had I not made the reference.
There are certain aspects of Bill C-48 which are not at all unrelated to that kind of autocratic and Draconian measure. As I said in my remarks yesterday in leading up to this point, one of those aspects is the fact that this government-this again is a totally unprecedented act on behalf of any government in western democracies-under the powers which we are about to grant it under Bill C-48, will confiscate private property and private assets, either the intellectual type of
December 3, 1981

capital or actual physical assets which are associated with leases in the north.
With Bill C-48, the government will receive the power to go to Canada lands in the north or offshore and confiscate up to 25 per cent of the assets of any company that have not yet been developed in the sense of the issuance of a production certificate. If this is not an area in which we should be seriously concerned, I do not know whether we should ever concern ourselves with anything again.
We have had time to learn of the serious flaws in the bill as they affect domestic companies, the economy in general, and certainly as they affect the potential of becoming energy self-sufficient by the year 1990. We have also had time to reflect on and come to grips with some of the serious condemnation and concerns voiced to us from outside our country. This matter interests me particularly because, as I have said in committee and in the earlier part of the debate, I am very much concerned about the reaction that we are to expect from the United States as well as other countries as a result of what is now clearly causing serious damage to certain treaty obligations that we have with the OECD countries, with the government moving against companies and giving preferential treatment to its agents over foreign companies which may have been or are presently operating in Canada lands in the field of energy exploration and development.
It is a fact that the government has brought about this condemnation and we had better brace ourselves for some very serious action that some of these countries will feel obliged to take against us. I shudder to think what would happen if the United States government, in its wisdom, said that if that is the way Canada treats U.S. companies in Canada then it should reciprocate in kind and treat Canadian companies likewise in the United States. If this reciprocal action resulted in certain trade restrictions in the free flow of goods between our countries, I shudder to think of the prospect of restrictions on our lumber and wood fibre industries, for example, because the consequences would be very serious and the effect on our economy would be incalculable.
Bill C-48 has already had very serious effects on our domestic economy. The Petroleum Services Association of Canada recently appeared before a Senate committee and in graphic terms showed the senators the effect Bill C-48 has had on their businesses even before being passed through the House of Commons. The Petroleum Services Association consists of roughly 150 companies which represent a wide variety of activities generally servicing the oil patch and the oil fields. The association employs roughly 15,000 Canadians and is not at all an insignificant sector of our economy.
This particular service association recently conducted a survey and found that the number of employees on staff fell from 7,998 to 6,743. These particular companies which responded to the questionnaire, some 77 out of 150, registered a loss of employment of 1,255 people. The total number which left the industry had between them 4,914 years of experience.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
The value of capital expenditures was cut back in Canada to the tune of $97,239,000. The gross sales over the period dropped by $131,639,000.
Bill C-48 was designed to bring about energy self-sufficiency by 1990. We all know that this would require a massive influx of capital, technology, people and a massive effort, almost an emergency and warlike effort, to move to the north and bring about new development and exploration to recapture what we once had, energy self-sufficiency.
I cannot believe at all that the minister should be so stubborn as not to realize what he is doing. Instead of increasing the activities in the north he is, of course, very seriously crippling the oil economy in the north. Also, he is not chasing the multinationals, they are already in the United States and all over the world; he is not chasing them out, he is chasing out Canadian companies.
I come from an area of British Columbia which is the only producing part of that province. The major share of fossil resources are located in the northeastern area of British Columbia. The oil exploration and development industry has been a very significant part of the economy of that part of the province. I would like the minister to share the picture we all had when he announced the great potential to regain energy self-sufficiency in Canada. We all shared in the excitement of that proposition. He set in motion events which he could not control because he did not believe that there were still people in this country who would respond to a challenge in the way that people in my part of the country would. He set in motion a massive effort for people to come to grips with this challenge and respond in a positive way so that British Columbia could participate in supplying its share of energy resources to meet the needs of Canadians.
The city of Fort St. George had roughly 20,000 people at that time. There were approximately 300 hotel and motel rooms in the city. Over a two-year period, in response to this great challenge, everyone got out and said that this is where the action is. There were roughly 23 drilling rigs; the number was increased to about 100 operating in the area. Private entrepreneurs responded by building hotels and within a two-year period, 1,000 hotel rooms were available. The capacity to accommodate people in hotels and motels increased from 300 to 1,000.
Likewise, young companies enticed to service the oil patch responded. They took incredible chances. They went to banks everywhere and borrowed, increased their capacity, bought trucks and equipment and machines shops, hired new people, built on to their shops and bought new tools and machinery to respond to this incredible challenge.
Then came Bill C-48 and the minister pulled the rug out from under this exciting venture. Today three major hotels, including a Holiday Inn in Fort St. John, are in receivership, and two of the major machine shops are shut down. In the area with the greatest potential in our country there is above average unemployment today.

December 3, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
I just wanted to take these few minutes to serve notice on the minister that people who walk away from their businesses on which they have worked all their lives do not behave rationally. People have been fooled by the government which held out a great promise. These people believed in it for a short period of time. They made commitments on the basis of that promise. They do not act rationally when they feel the rug being pulled out from under them. I dare say the minister had better be careful, because if that situation exists in many other parts of this country-and I think it does-people will take measures which are not ordinary or rational. When I go home I get a feeling of anger and frustration which frightens me because I am called in by some of those oil businessmen who are now forced to dig up their roots, move down to the United States and take with them their equipment and their technology. Of course, they cannot take with them their people because the people would have difficulty getting immigration visas.
I just wanted to spill my heart out to my hon. colleagues. This is a serious situation. I am deeply troubled by it, and I plead with the government at this late date to come to its senses and to make whatever changes can still be made to this bill so that it is at least in some way conducive to the laudable goals and objectives we have set for ourselves, namely, to recapture energy self-sufficiency and to bring about a greater degree of Canadian ownership by 1990.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 participated at the report stage of Bill C-48, and I am now taking the opportunity to address a few more remarks in perhaps a broader context. I will stay within the confines of the bill. I might wander a little, but I will rely on Your Honour to bring me back to reality.
Since becoming a member of the House of Commons I have had great opportunities to travel the Arctic quite widely. I took one very valuable trip up there with a group of colleagues. It was a formal trip. The hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) was the member in charge of that group. We travelled widely. We looked at the infrastructure of the transportation system the federal government had financed. I am speaking now of a trip back in 1974 or 1975. We had extensive meetings with the native peoples. We sat in their houses and talked out the communication problems and the other problems they had. We talked about federal government programs which had been delivered into the north for these people, and one of the things I found quite heart-rending was that a program would be in place, and two or three years later, just as the people were understanding the program, getting comfortable with it, starting to benefit from it or understanding what the original thrust of the government was, the program would be withdrawn and something new put in its place. I have never forgotten the frustration of the native people. They were wondering why there could not be a little continuity with some of the federal programs which were delivered into the north.
Back in the first half of the 1970s the federal government put millions of dollars into the infrastructure of the transportation system starting from Hay River and up through the Mackenzie Valley. It was all predicated on the explosion which
was going to start to take place in the Canada lands. At that time there were about 5 trillion cubic feet of gas locked in in the Mackenzie Delta. There was oil up in the Mackenzie Delta. Massive rigs and land fills were being constructed in the Beaufort. Tuktoyaktuk was starting to expand to get ready for Dome. It looked as though things were pretty bright indeed. There was also the Mackenzie Valley pipeline consortium. That pipeline was to move gas from the Prudhoe Bay fields. The consortium was seeking permission to run that transportation system across the north slope and down the Mackenzie Valley. The federal government had been putting in the transportation infrastructure with some foresight and some wisdom. It was quite impressive.
Also with foresight and wisdom the federal government put in vocational training schools in that area so that native people could be taught to repair diesel engines, to handle heavy equipment, and taught the semiskills and the skills that would be necessary.
One of the things the native people said repeatedly was that their only fear in all that was of hobnail boots trampling over their culture and through their villages. I think all the members who went up there-and I think three parties were represented on that trip-recognized it as being of paramount importance that the construction crews which would be going through the north should be kept isolated and that we would have to protect the culture and the families and the homes and townships in which the northern people lived. That does not mean to say that a highway had not been built. Inuvik attracted entrepreneurs. It was getting ready to be the hub and the distribution base for much of this activity, as were other centres down the Mackenzie Valley.
Then all of a sudden came the Berger report, and overnight all that planning, spending and infrastructure was stopped dead in the water.
Then I had the opportunity to return and travel up through the Mackenzie Valley and again over the high Arctic to meet the people and re-meet many of those I had the opportunity of meeting on the first trip. The devastation in Hay River was really heart-rending. Young native people who had been in the schools learning trades all of a sudden had their futures pulled out from under them. We keep hearing the words "We need an industrial strategy" and that only with forward planning will there be a future for a young person who wants to get out, get working and acquire a piece of property, a home or a van or truck. People with goals and people with jobs are, as a rule, very happy people.
I have said several times in the past-and I do not want to bore hon. members-that one of the tragedies of the Thirtieth Parliament was that we stopped dead the move toward the settlement of Indian land claims in the north by losing that $7.5 billion to $8 billion transportation project. We are now starting to see some rethinking on the part of the New Democratic Party. We have had our look, but we lost the opportunity to build that transportation system. Because it was not built, energy in the Prudhoe Bay field is being wasted because, through four stage pumps, gas coming up with the oil
December 3, 1981

is reversed back into the ground. That has been going on for years and years now, and that is a total waste of energy. It is really a crime, and not just against the United States; it is a crime against the world, which is becoming increasingly short of traditional fuels.
Had we proceeded with the Mackenzie Valley line at that time-for minimum megadollars-the United States could have been given a transportation system across Canada which would have left a taxation base behind in Canada and used our steel-making and pipe-making capacity to the full. It would have given us a new and vital transportation system. It would have created work again in the machine shops of Ontario and Quebec. We would have had almost a fully employed people from that period on. Politics interfered with that. Now that pipeline is something in a $24 billion to $30 billion package. The pre-build is going on in the west. The expense of the transportation system alone to get that Prudhoe Bay gas to the United States is horrendous. It has a tremendous inflationary impact. I am one who favoured the Mackenzie Valley line. I was very sorry and regretful to see what our failure to proceed with that project did to the native people and to the dreams and hopes of the people in the Mackenzie Valley.
I would like to come to the combination of the delay we have had to this period and the importation of foreign oil at world prices, getting into the struggle of the national energy policy through Bill C-48 which we are still debating in this House and which was interrupted by the constitutional debate and the constitutional accord with the first ministers.
We have been importing oil from abroad at a terrible cost to this country. There has been a great regional distortion in that the west, primarily the producing province of Alberta, in a two-year period delivered some $9.6 billion in compensation payments back into the system.
The last time I was up I was not allowed to place some statistics on the record. However, there was a feeling that there was a justification for drawing on money from the province of Alberta because the provinces of central Canada had paid more than world price for the early delivery of oil as the pipeline was being built from the western-producing areas. I now have the opportunity to finish that comment. In the years 1962 to 1972, the difference between imported world prices and the prices paid by Ontario consumers for western oil was $639 million. That was over ten years. In the short period of time that we got into these compensation payments after OPEC moved up, the province of Alberta delivered back $9.6 billion in compensation payments for our friends on the east coast.
One of the mistakes we made in the Thirtieth Parliament, and I do not know whether it was a mistake or political, was that we said we would tax oil because the generators in the Atlantic provinces were oil-fired. What we should have done, if we were going to be totally fair as a nation, is we should have taxed energy so that all provinces using hydroelectric energy, oil, gas, any form of energy, somehow or other par-
Canada Oil and Gas Act
ticipated in this equalization payment and this need to help the people of the Atlantic provinces who had entered heavily into oil-fired generation.
I have said, and I think with complete justification, that Bill C-48 and much of the constitutional debate has been a massive revenue grab of western and east coast resources. We have been very slow in this country moving to world oil prices. As a result, we have been very slow in moving to energy conservation. We have been very slow in moving to energy self-sufficiency.
Ottawa was addressing this problem in 1973. It established a national goal to be achieved before 1980. This is our ability to plan. In 1976 Ottawa scrapped the objective and replaced it with oil self-reliance, another study. In 1980 oil self-sufficiency was reinstated.
Our government saw the feasibility of achieving energy self-sufficiency by the year 1990, but it required an agreement with the producing provinces. That was almost in the palm of our hands. Now energy self-sufficiency has given way and is the third priority after Canadianization and revenue-sharing. That seems to be about the extent of Ottawa's ability to bring this nation to energy self-sufficiency.
In the five years between 1975 and 1980 the industry in the west contributed approximately $23 billion to federal and provincial treasuries in royalties and taxes. In addition, the oil industry contributed $24 billion to Canada's merchandise trade balance through exports of oil and gas. Then a mystery comes along. The poor people of Canada wonder whether there is a gas shortage.
Some years ago I started to read the bunk and propaganda that was beginning to come out. I felt I should reconsider the fact that I had a gas-heat installation in my business and a gas furnace in my house. I wondered whether I should start studying something that would give me continuity of energy. Lo and behold, just a couple of years later we found that we had more doggone gas locked in the ground, capped wells everywhere and cash flow pressures on the entrepreneurs and explorers.
With our energy nationalization and rush to corporate concentration in advance of the November 12 budget, we created some $17 billion of call-and-demand on our international reserves. It has put tremendous pressure on the Canadian dollar and thus is affecting the interest rates that are causing tragedies. It could trigger a domino effect across Canada and the United States if we do not get some discipline and order into our lives.
Unfortunately it has been a grab for revenue. Unfortunately, a political regime, a new economic order, has moved in and interfered with the opportunity we were given in the mid-seventies to be fully employed, to have that gift and heritage at large in Canada working so that we could make a positive donation to the world by withdrawing our demand for foreign energy resources. That is the tragedy.
There has been no excuse for this country not to have been fully employed and fully at work since the early mid-1970s.

We had a pipeline to build from the north to south of the 49th. We had a Syncrude plant which was an engineering marvel. We had an engineering body in place composed of Canadian and foreign engineers who should have been phased into another tar sands plant so that we would not lose that tremendous ability we have in engineering design, management, trade skills, engineering skills and our transportation infrastructure. All of that could have been gently and easily rolled over and phased into a second tar sands plant. Did that happen? No.
I remember when Sun Life nearly went bankrupt because of early pioneering work in the great Canadian tar sands. I remember the engineering tragedies it had, the metallurgical and other problems such as temperature and breaking up the tar sands. I remember the diggers breaking down and the belts breaking. I remember the struggles they had with the technology for separating the oil from the sand and then having to rebuild and redress the land as these great mining operations took place. I remember the negative cash flows they kept reporting. I remember years ago the seriousness of all this pioneering, this front-end entrepreneurial and innovative investment in rather large dollars. What does the national energy policy do, Mr. Speaker? It penalizes this company for that forward-looking investment into the future that was so necessary for us to become energy self-sufficient as a nation.
Why do we do these things, Mr. Speaker? We should be looking for national revenue as a good, solid taxation base where the decision-making process is at large in the country, using all of the talents that the magic of creation can give us. There is no decision-making base in Ottawa. The bureaucrats prepare laborious papers on the various options available to ministers to make decisions.
Today small companies throughout western Canada have to receive permission from some desk in IT&C in order to have an assessment for duty and tax and conform to all the other regulations to proceed with something that yesterday they used to be able to proceed with by picking up the telephone, having an expert assess the rules & regulations and then have a customs broker say that their interpretation is correct. If there was some doubt, the customs broker would telephone them in Ottawa so as to receive a ruling from the department. In a matter of hours, days, or weeks at the most, one could start the project; thereby the cash flow that small business always loses would turn around. That is the way it used to work.
I know of one company that last April needed about five or six items assessed for the duty rate or to see whether duty was applicable. It is a simple matter. They could then give that assessment, the professionals in the brokerage industry could assess it, and the company could start to move into the market again, in an area where it is all imports anyway-no Canadian manufacturing. The original request was made in April, and as of December 3, 1981, that single desk in IT & C has not been able to deliver its decision to the company in Vancouver. One thing after another is slowly coming to a halt as we force more
and move structuring on the economy and force the private sector to come back here for permission to blow its nose.
That is the cause of almost one million unemployed in the country. The government has taken all of the ability to make decisions away from the private sector.
Aside from Bill C-48, the national energy policy, we come to the day of the budget, November 12, 1981. When one considers what the government has done with the budget, coupled with the national energy policy of this government, things will grind to a complete halt. On November 12, the government pulled the cornerstone from under fair taxation policy. The first indication of retroactivity applied to the Canadian people was in Bill C-48. On November 12 the budget imposed retroactivity as a Liberal government policy upon the industrial, the job-creating and wealth-creating sector of Canada. When one has retroactivity in taxation policy, coupled with government policies that remove the ability to pay the tax, what one has done, in fact, is pulled out from under the private sector their decision-making base.
In 1971 a new taxation policy, the Carter principles, were introduced to this country-a buck was a buck. The market sector has been adjusting to that taxation philosophy for ten years. Most people were just becoming comfortable with the new rules. A decision-making base was in place. The game was starting to work. All it needed was some fiscal policy to lighten it up and some common sense planning in energy for it to proceed.
What happened? On November 12, the most infamous budget ever was introduced to the House. It applies retroactivity as a policy of this government, and at the same time it taxes wealth, leaving the taxpayer without ability to pay. That just furthers the confiscation aspect that is so evident in the national energy policy under Bill C-48.
There have been some wonderful speeches made by prominent industrialists. In a meeting some time ago I learned-and it had not occurred to me-that the major oil finds in Canada had been discovered by one company. It is interesting to note-and I am speaking of the new deep field under Pembina, as well as the Hibernia field out on the ocean bottom-that one company with its scientists and its expertise was able to put together software programs in seismology that allowed a new sensitivity and a new reading from that data. That is what enabled the discovery of a new, big find in Alberta, under traditional fields, and that is what gave us Hibernia.
That is a foreign company that has been a good corporate citizen of Canada for many years. That was a technology that was not developed in Canada but was developed offshore. They just happened to put the combination of minds together so as to provide this technology to enable these new, big finds to be made.
It is interesting to note that they are still at work. They still seem to be interested in new properties as a result of this lead they have in seismic technology. They are interested in starting exploration and drilling off British Columbia. However, there is a moratorium in place, further evidence of the federal
December 3, 1981

government and provincial government being unable to resolve problems that would provide jobs.
Exploration activity is important to the north coast of British Columbia. There are towns waiting to be the service and distribution outlets for the boats that service these offshore rigs. All of that is in place; the play is starting to take place; the land is under option. Everything is waiting for the federal and provincial government to get together and stop the moratorium so as to allow some of this west coast exploration to proceed.
The point I am making is that the official policy of this government is totally negative with regard to implementing forces that will allow us to achieve energy self-sufficiency. We shake our heads and wonder why we have the government wanting to move in and do everything; we have the government moving in and wanting to take over retroactively; we have the government not wanting to put up the front-end risk money within the Canada lands for gas and oil finds. But when there is a positive find, it moves in and takes 25 per cent.
With regard to that issue, I should like to discuss the problem that the industry is still encountering as a result of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) dealing with the producing provinces of Alberta, B.C. and Saskatchewan. We have read quite a bit about the success of finally reaching agreement with the province of Alberta, with the province of British Columbia and with the province of Saskatchewan. Politicians came to these agreements in spite of the fact that industry representatives kept saying, "Look, guys, you are taking too much in this money grab; you are not leaving us enough to operate or to risk a dime".
May I call it five o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order which I brought forward on a couple of previous occasions. If all goes as projected one of my bills may be called; if the opposition is concerned, I will be using my own time. The point I have raised before is that presently a lot of bills are listed on the Order Paper and marked as "Text received". In other words, these bills have not been printed.
Earlier in this session, as well as in previous sessions of Parliament, I have raised the point that when bills are listed but not printed, it is very difficult for the hon. member to do his work. If he is questioned on listed bills by the public, he is unable to respond, not having seen the bills in question. I pursued this matter again in the present session, and it was agreed that hon. members would be allowed a certain time in which to put their houses in order. After a certain period of time those members who had not produced any text saw their bills dropped from the Order Paper. However, those bills of hon. members who had produced texts within the time limit specified by the Chair remained on the Order Paper.
The problem we are facing now is that since the listing nothing further has happened. The bills still remain on the Order Paper, and beneath them it reads "Text received". This may be because the text received was not in good order for printing or the legal advisers of the Chair have been unable to put the material into proper form for printing. But for a multitude of reasons, the bills themselves are not available to hon. members at large.
When I brought forward this matter before, I followed it up with a letter to the Speaker. I received a response from Madam Speaker-I do not have the letter in front of me but I will try to state fairly her decision-in which she essentially decided that the matter rested with hon. members. If we do not regulate the problem, we could see considerable abuse in the next session; this is what really bothers me. Originally I suggested that I have perhaps 100 or so subjects which I

December 3, 1981
Point of Order-Mr. Herbert
should like to pursue. I could do so very easily by having them listed as bills, and the titles would convey a certain representation in themselves.
Under the new arrangements of this session, presumably within a limited period of time I would have to produce some sort of text. Nevertheless, this would not be particularly difficult. However, I suggest that the text I would produce would not necessarily result in the law officers who advise the Chair being able to produce a printed version. Although the Chair may have made some attempt to throw this matter back to hon. members to regulate, surely the good order of the House is that it is the responsibility of the Chair. Unless something is done about this item, I see the possibility of considerable misuse in the next session.
Probably Mr. Speaker is not willing to make any further comments this afternoon. I know another Speaker occupied the chair when I brought forward the matter previously. I felt it was appropriate to bring it up today because, in my opinion, it has not been satisfactorily attended to. Furthermore, if it is to be my time which is used up, obviously it is better to bring it forward today than on another occasion.
I suggest Mr. Speaker give further consideration to the matter. There has been no ruling so far by the Chair on this item. Despite Madam Speaker's letter, Mr. Speaker might think of some manner in which the problem could be resolved to prevent the abuse which could result if no further ruling comes from the Chair.

I thank the hon. member for bringing the matter to the attention of this particular occupant of the Chair. It was I who, approximately a year ago, undertook to assist the hon. member in this regard. I do not want to turn it into a question of privilege, but I think the hon. member for Vau-dreuil (Mr. Herbert) has a valid point. been denied to the member, as well as to other members who may appreciate the points made in the bill.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am not too sure what gets printed for the heading of the remarks I am about to make so I shall read from the bill. Clause 1 reads as follows:
Notwithstanding any other act, the Crown corporations specified in Schedule D of the Financial Administration Act are not agents of Her Majesty.
The explanatory note which accompanies the bill reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to put Crown corporations on the same level as private companies, to render Crown corporations subject to private law and to take away their privileges under public law.
Crown agencies are distinct entities established as instruments of public policy that have been directly delegated by Parliament, the government or another Crown agency, to specify continuing responsibilities and the decision-making powers that assure them a degree of autonomy from Parliament and the government in pursuit of their tasks.
The responsibilities are assigned to the agencies, not to ministers. Ministers must account to Parliament for the exercise of continuing responsibilities and managerial powers. The extensive and increasing resort to Crown agencies has revealed serious deficiencies in the system which, if left unattended, will only add to the existing state of confusion concerning the status and accountability of a large number of Crown agencies which now comprise virtually a second public service.
It is coincidental that in the response to a question on yesterday's Order Paper concerning Crown corporations, reference was made to an answer received in November, 1980, concerning the number of Crown corporations. I found it an interesting comparison to the number of Crown corporations
December 3, 1981

that had been listed in a rather lengthy study called the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability, or what is commonly known as the Lambert report. In 1979 the Lambert commission came to a conclusion about the number of Crown corporations. At about the same time an answer given by the government to a member's question showed that there was a discrepancy of approximately 40 between the high and the low. The high figure given in October, 1980, was 464 Crown corporations.
The regimes of accountability are tied primarily to financial management arrangements, while larger issues of accountability to Parliament for mandate and to the government for policy have not been adequately covered. This inadequacy for accountability will result in some decline in confidence in the Crown agency as a valid instrument for the implementation of public policy objectives.
According to the Lambert report, as of January, 1979, the official count was 429. As I mentioned earlier, just a few months later we were given a response by the government that the count was 464. I suppose there is some logical reason for this difference of 35 Crown agencies. I recognize the problems as many of the Crown agencies are dormant subsidiaries.
The first group of Crown agencies includes regulatory agencies, administrative or deciding tribunals, temporary bodies such as royal commissions and operating agencies like the National Film Board and central agencies. Departmental Crown corporations encompass such different entities as advisory and granting councils like the Medical Research Council, and regulatory agencies such as the Atomic Energy Control Board. Wholly-owned Crown corporations with varying degrees of commercial orientation and financial self-sufficiency include marketing agencies, such as the Canadian Saltfish Corporation, a number of corporations conducting business for the government, such as Defence Construction (1951) Limited, and a smaller number operating in a wider market like Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. The 21 proprietary corporations are mainly engaged in commercial operations, for example, Air Canada and VIA Rail Canada Inc. But they also include financial guarantee and insurance concerns like the Export Development Corporation and the Farm Credit Corporation.
Other government corporations seem to have few common characteristics other than the fact that they have been purchased, created, or sponsored by the federal government, and range from the Bank of Canada through de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Limited and the Standards Council of Canada, to the Belleville Harbour Commission.
Under the heading "Mixed Enterprise Corporations" are listed 24 enterprises, ranging from the Canada Development Corporation to the Blue Water Bridge Authority. These are share capital corporations owned or controlled jointly by the federal government and other governments, organizations, or individuals.
I should like to quote from page 279 of the Lambert report where the following passage occurs:
Crown Corporations
It is simply not possible to rely on the present schedules to the Financial Administration Act, which cover such a small number of the agencies and where the criteria for classification are minimal and inconsistently applied.
I should also like to put on record one of the recommendations contained in the report of the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability which appears on page 289 of the report and reads as follows:
16.1 the Schedules to the Financial Administration Act be replaced by a more comprehensive set of schedules in accordance with four categories:
(1)	Ministerial and other designated departments
(2)	Independent deciding and advisory bodies
(3)	Crown corporations
(4)	Shared enterprises
and that when any re-scheduling occurs such decisions be tabled for the information of Parliament.
The Financial Administration Act of 1951 established a general framework for the government, Parliament, and almost the entire spectrum of Crown agencies with respect to financial management and reporting. A change since 1951, as a result of the growth in the number of Crown agencies and the failure to include them in the schedules, is the weakening of the Financial Admnistration Act as the cornerstone of the management and accountability relationships among Parliament, the government and the semi-autonomous agencies.
Since 1951, a large number of government corporations, such as the Canada Development Corporation, the Canada Council and de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Limited have been created or acquired without being scheduled under the FAA. As a result, provisions for their accountability to the Crown are essentially idiosyncratic, founded either on the provisions of their particular constituent acts or on the powers available to the Crown under the general corporation law under which they were incorporated.
The management and accountability relationships of agency and proprietary Crown corporations to the government and Parliament are largely founded on the financial control provisions of the FAA. These include government power to approve annual capital and, for agency corporations, operating budgets and resulting contracts and major expenditures. For the Crown corporations which operate under schedules C and D, the minister would appear to have the power to issue policy directives in the form of unanimous shareholder agreements. These corporations include Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Loto Canada Incorporated, Eldorado Nuclear Limited and the Northern Transportation Company Limited.
The government readily admits that it does not have the capacity to give policy direction to Crown corporations. Public sector boards must reconcile themselves to some continuing surveillance and controls. It is in this light, I believe, that the following recommendation has been made concerning the Crown agencies that the Lambert commission has named. Recommendation 18.12 of the Lambert report reads as follows:
The annual reports... be automatically and permanently referred to the appropriate standing committees of the House of Commons, and that they

December 3, 1981
Crown Corporations
provide a thorough description of the activities of the preceding year including both achievements and problems, a record of reports issued and directives received, and plans for the coming year.
The managerial requirement for insulation from the political process can, at times, be in conflict with the need to be responsive to the national interests as determined by the government. Although it may be somewhat tiresome so to do, I feel that in conclusion I must read yet another recommendation found in the Lambert report. Recommendation 19.21 reads as follows:
-the designated minister be required to undertake a review of the mandate and operations of Crown corporations not less than once every ten years and further that the results of such reviews be tabled in Parliament and referred automatically for study and appropriate action to the relevant standing committee.
Obviously, the point is that at the moment we have some difficulty and conflict between the assumed independence of many of the Crown corporations and the fact that they are operating with some policy directions from ministers or from the government. We have some difficulty, as Members of Parliament, in adequately questioning and receiving reports from these various Crown corporations. We sometimes get an attitude, if they do appear in committee, that they are independent, either of the government or of Parliament. It is sometimes very difficult for us to impress upon these same Crown corporations that they owe their lives to this Parliament. In fact, the continuing operation of many which receive moneys in the estimates each year is conditional on approval of the estimates.
We made this point somewhat forcefully a few years ago when we were having difficulty with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We tried to indicate to the corporation that the public had a right to know what was going on within the corporation, since the public purse was financing the operation to the extent of almost $400 million at that time. As to today, of course, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation uses up approximately $600 million from the public purse.
We took a rather unusual step, back in those days, in illustrating that while we perhaps did not have any specific lines of reporting to hon. members, we had one ultimate weapon. That, of course, was to cut their budget. This we did, with some success, back in 1973 when we were operating a minority government. It caused quite a stir at the time, and this point is obvious to everyone, because even though the government's estimates are listed in the name of a Crown corporation, any cut in the moneys which is assumed to flow to a Crown corporation would be a cut in the government's estimates. However, the point was made. The point, of course, is simply that many Crown corporations owe their continuing existence to the moneys which they receive through the estimates. In that respect, I suppose Members of Parliament can exercise some measure of control. However, this is a rather indirect and, I think, unwieldy type of weapon. I believe the minister has given some indication that he intends to introduce a bill at an early date which would change the reporting responsibilities of the Crown corporations.
For what it is worth, during my last remaining couple of minutes I would express my personal opinion that if the Crown
corporations are to be executing the policies of the government, then the government should be directly responsible for the operation of the Crown corporations. That is a personal point of view. I doubt that that point of view will get very much support. However, I feel very strongly that if the government is responsible for the financing, if the government must answer for the hundreds of millions of dollars that are transferred to the Crown corporations every year, and if the government is to answer in this House for the method and manner of operation of the Crown corporations, then the best way to resolve the difficulty is to ensure that the government also exercise control over the operation of the Crown corporations. In that way we would get rid of any difficulty that anyone might have, and we would not have the conflict of interest which exists at the present time.
I guess that I am dreaming, but that is the way I would like to see it. I would like to see the government take over the responsibility entirely. However, if it is not to be that way, and I presume that arguments will be produced to illustrate why it cannot be that way, then we must at least see a better reporting responsibility to Parliament so that the hon. members themselves will be able to ensure that the moneys which are being spent by the Crown corporations are being wisely spent in the interest of the general public.

Mr. Speaker, I had not originally intended to speak on Bill C-339 this afternoon. However, I was so moved by the cogency of the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) that I thought I might contribute a few comments and lend some support to his bill.
I must confess that when I first looked at Bill C-339, and especially when I read the explanatory notes, I had a sharp reaction. I would like to read the explanatory notes which state:
The purpose of this bill is to put Crown corporations on the same level as private companies, to render Crown corporations subject to private law and to take away their privileges under public law.
My knee-jerk response was that this legislation was a poorly disguised effort by the sponsoring member to knock Crown corporations per se. After listening to the hon. member for Vaudreuil, it was clear to me, however, that that was not the motivation behind the bill, and I welcome the fact.
There is a habit in this House, and I think across the land, to knock Crown corporations, to view them, a priori, as somehow antagonistic to the public interest. They are viewed at worst as monsters, at best as an unnecessary drain on the public purse. Often in that connection the point is made that Crown corporations are unwieldy, are the victims of elephantiasis, are unaccountable to Parliament and to the public, and are in many ways less satisfactory as an instrument of public policy than are, say, government line departments. I would be the first to admit that many in my own party hold such views.
Sometimes the views I have described or summarized are accurate; and all of us can think of some corporations to which
December 3, 1981

these descriptions might apply. Certainly there are inefficiently operated Crown corporations in Canada, as there are in any democratic society.
1 would argue, though, that on the whole Crown corporations are an effective instrument of public policy. Some perform very useful functions. In fact, often the functions they perform could only be fulfilled by Crown corporations, or they could be performed best or most effectively by Crown corporations rather than directly by a department of the federal government or the private sector.
Crown corporations are set up because there is the need to have from time to time an arm's length relationship between certain government agencies and politicians so as to avoid interference, to give the agencies an element of freedom, to allow them to pursue a course without day-to-day interference by bureaucrats-and I use that word in the best sense of the word-by politicians or, for that matter, by the public or the media. That is why the CBC, Canadian National Railways and many others were established as Crown corporations: to give them a degree of independence from bureaucratic, public or governmental interference.
I take considerable pride in the fact that it was a Conservative government which fathered a number of our great Crown corporations. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a case in point. Canadian National and the National Film Board and others could also be mentioned.
All of us now and then have problems with the CBC or with Canadian National or with any of a number of others. We complain, strongly and legitimately so, about how they do this or that or do not do this or that. But most of us, I think, would admit that these corporations perform most useful functions that could not be performed nearly as well if they were directly under the thumb of a government minister, of a department, of Parliament or, again, for that matter, of the public.
The railway system in Canada-and I am thinking now of the Canadian National Railway system, rather than of the Canadian Pacific-forged a country out of a vast and thinly populated land. It literally helped Canada become a unified country, from one coast to the other. If the railway had been left entirely to private enterprise, the job would never have been accomplished. In fact, as we all know, most of the component parts that led to the formation of the Canadian National Railways system were once in private hands. Private interests just did not perform the job that needed to be done. The government had to grab the bull by the horns, take the initiative, bring these component parts together, and out of them form a state corporation, if you will, on the basis of which we forged a country out of, as I say, a diverse and thinly populated land.
The CBC is another case in point. Just as the railway brought Canada together geographically, so also did the CBC bring Canada together culturally. To repeat, while we have problems with the CBC-especially when we politicians do not make the national news at night, or for whatever reason; allowing for such possibilities and setting them aside-we must recognize that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
Crown Corporations
does a darn fine job in this country. Those of us who knock it do so outrageously unaware of the facts.
Having expressed the importance in principle of Crown corporations as vehicles for national policy, I hasten to add that we have allowed some of these corporations to get out of hand, often wildly. There may well be, as the hon. member for Vaudreuil has pointed out, too many Crown corporations. I suspect that is the case when the government is unable to answer the simple question, "How many corporations does the federal government own?" We have probably reached the point where there are too many. That question was actually put to the responsible minister at a meeting of a standing committee of the House. But the minister could not tell the questioner, a member of the House, how many Crown corporations within a hundred were responsible to Parliament.
Crown corporations have been permitted to become unwieldy, to become gross, much larger in size and much better endowed in funding than needed to be the case given the job at hand. I share with the hon. member for Vaudreuil his concerns about some Crown corporations' lack of responsiveness, of accountability to Parliament and to the public, and of manageability. And I share his concern also about their sheer ineffectiveness in getting the job done that they were set up to do. Many of the points he made, are, in my mind, valid and are ones with which most of us in the House could agree.
Yet, to stress once again the importance of Crown corporations, let me express some real, fundamental, and genuine personal fears about Crown corporations in Canada. The first is that I think too many of them are concentrated in central Canada. I am talking now primarily about the headquarters of Crown corporations. For the life of me, I cannot understand why, by definition, Crown corporations, government departments, agencies, commissions, boards, or what have you, have to be located in almost every instance in central Canada, often in Ottawa; if not in Ottawa then in Toronto or Montreal, but still in central Canada in any event.
To my mind, we in Parliament should pursue, as a matter of public policy, the objective of spreading the industrial benefits of government as widely as possible across this great dominion. Crown corporations, or government in any form, are as much an industry as General Motors, Chrysler, Ford or General Foods. They generate salaries and, in turn, those salaries have a rippling effect throughout the economy. Every community that is directly touched by a Crown corporation benefits.
Why should Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal-central Canada, in general-be the exclusive beneficiaries of the direct presence of government? When a Crown corporation is headquartered in Montreal or Toronto, for example, its purchasing is automatically done in the community in which it is located. If we located the headquarters or main arms of Crown corporations in areas other than just central Canada, that would benefit all the communities concerned and, I suggest, the country as a whole.

December 3, 1981
Crown Corporations
Apart from the economic dimension, another reason to spread Crown corporations across the country is that government, in whatever form, should be as close as possible to the people it is intended to serve. Not every Canadian lives in central Canada. Prince Edward Islanders, myself included, are Canadians every bit as much as Ontarians and Quebecers. We have a right to be directly served by Canada's Crown corporations and by other agencies of government through having the instruments of the state located as close as possible to us.
I do not expect every Crown corporation to be moved to our tiny province. Maybe none of them could be. But, certainly, the region of which we are a part is entitled to be considered a suitable setting for some Crown corporations. It is important that government, in every way, be geographically near the people it must serve. In short, we want a piece of the action and, as Canadians, I think we are entitled to it.
A disproportionate number of major Crown corporations is currently headquartered in Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal-in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. If Crown corporations must be housed in central Canada, I would feel much better if northern Ontario, for example, were considered, and not always Toronto or southern Ontario in general. Northern Quebec should also be considered. It is not out of the question. There is nothing etched in stone which says that a Crown corporation is necessarily inefficient or ineffective because it is headquartered somewhere other than in big metropolitan areas of Canada. It is now possible, with modern communications and technology, with computer systems and other modern methods available, to harness a nation, to have government spread out in a way which perhaps was not possible when most Crown corporations were established in their current locations.
The second and final point which causes me great concern is that, to the extent that Crown corporations have any presence in what is sometimes disparagingly called the hinterlands or the periphery of the country, many of them are steadily withdrawing direct services from those parts of the country.
We are all familiar, for example, with the VIA Rail question, which has been well debated already in the House; so, the facts are widely known. But suffice it to say that in my province of Prince Edward Island, for example, there has been a steady withdrawal of Canadian National. I think that fact has profound implications not just economically or in terms of transportation but also in terms of the visibility of the federal government on the Island. The same is true of the whole Atlantic region and of many parts of western Canada. To use Prince Edward Island as an example again, we first lost direct passenger service on Prince Edward Island in 1969. We later lost a major part of the Carload Centre, which is the main office for the administration of the movement of heavy freight to and from the province and within it. Canadian National then took away the main part of the Car Repair shop, where rail cars are repaired and maintained, both on a routine and emergency basis. Lately we lost half of the Canadian National Express office. The VIA Rail cutbacks were but another step-and probably not the last one-toward the total elimination of Canadian National's presence on Prince Edward
Island. If Canadian National is to be withdrawn completely from our province, ignoring the resultant economic and transportation and service disadvantages, just consider the impact on the psyche of the people there. They will see something of their national government removed from them at the very time when that same part of government, CN, is being aggrandized elsewhere in the country.
I think it is important that Air Canada, the CBC, CN and all other Crown corporations have a strong and visible presence in every part of Canada. The more their presence is chipped away in certain parts of the country, the more Canada itself is withdrawn, in a very tangible fashion, from the citizens affected.
Concerning the Atlantic provinces, there has been a propensity-almost an obsession-on the part of the federal government to consolidate the provision of its services either in the heartland of the country, the major metropolitan areas- including Vancouver, for that matter-or in major centres within the outlying regions, to the exclusion of places like Charlottetown and similar smaller centres. I believe this is bad for national unity. It could be demonstrated-but it would take more time than I have available-how harmful to national unity that practice is. It is also bad in terms of sound management. And, most important, it is bad because it is one step farther on a course which will alienate Canadians from one another and pit one region of Canada against another. I think we can be administratively efficient, rational and effective in government without resorting in every instance to bigness-to what I call governmental elephantiasis.
In conclusion, I apologize for being somewhat loquacious because I know that at least one other member wishes to speak. I have considerable sympathy for the rationale of the bill put forth by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), which we are now debating. I congratulate him for his initiative in sponsering the bill and urge all members to give it favourable consideration.

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes remaining I would like to put some of my perceptions on this problem on the record. I suppose I should congratulate the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for bringing this proposal forward, but it never ceases to astound me that government members should criticize Crown corporations and their operating procedures. I have heard this criticism in private members' hours and in committees. Government members attack the bureaucrats involved with public agencies, but somehow there is a lapse in logic, a failure in perception. They attack the servants but not those who set the policies. I never hear them in question period criticizing the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) or the others who are ultimately responsible for the government policy which should direct these corporations. Government members should insist on accountability and clarity of policy, but that never happens. I wonder how that lapse occurs. I am constantly astounded by these attacks.
December 3, 1981

I wish hon. members opposite would bend their efforts in a much more meaningful way.
I can certainly identify with the comments made by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan), but again I have some serious questions about his party's approach. The hon. member put on the record clearly that truth is a phenomenon that occurs only in the eye of the beholder. Anyone who says the creation of Canadian National Railways was an achievement should hide his head. It resulted from the bankruptcy of the old Canadian Northern Railroad and, I suppose, Grand Trunk Pacific. There was a colossal mess. In the early part of the twentieth century the Liberal Party supported promoters and wheelers and dealers so that they could rip off the public enormously. The whole system collapsed in a mess, and, at about the time of World War I, the taxpayers of Canada picked up the mess and paid off the financiers and wheelers and dealers. CNR was not a mechanism to weld Canada together or to bind the thin band of population across the country. It was a pay-off to the banks and financiers who operated it in such a manner that it could not function properly. I wondered whether the Liberal Party would take credit for fathering such a monster! Over the years it became evident that the government was required to run it in a responsible fashion, and over the years it has eventually developed into a very credible transportation system.
However, we still hear constant criticism. The federal cabinet is the group that makes policy, and it is very unfortunate that the criticism of hon. members opposite is not directed to the individuals responsible.
I would like to deal with some questions of principle. A Crown corporation is an agency of public policy. I am certain all members of the House believe in a mixed economy. I am certain of it because of the remarks of the hon. member for Hillsborough and the hon. member for Vaudreuil. If we are going to intervene in a mixed economy, we should do it in a very effective way, yet we leave Crown corporations hanging, neither fish nor fowl. We tell them to act like private corporations, to make profits and not to create expenditures for the government.
Clearly one of the basic problems here is that this government has not made up its mind as to what it wants to do with Crown corporations, and I will give a couple of examples. This government is not prepared to clarify its policy. It is not prepared to say that Crown corporations are agencies of public policy. It is not prepared to say that Crown corporations are created for social purposes and that they should be effective and accountable. That does not happen. They are left to hang.
With respect to accountability, we do not see reports to the committees of this House on a regular basis. No reports are laid before Parliament and studied by committees. The committee system is virtually incapable of handling this properly, and I lay that at the feet of the government, but the government attempts to reflect opposition criticism regarding its policies.
The credibility of Crown corporations in this country is stretched very thin when they are used as a mechanism of
Crown Corporations
patronage. They are a means of pork barrelling to an extent that would make a bank robber blush. One of our most prominent Crown corporations inherited a defeated Liberal cabinet minister. Who knows what connections or capabilities the individual had? He might have been the best president ever appointed to that corporation, but the public in Canada did not believe that or accept that. It severely strains the credibility of any organization when one of its prime functions is patronage. This is just not acceptable.
Getting back to the question of being neither fish nor fowl, I would say that Air Canada is probably one of the best airlines in this entire country. There is no doubt about that, but the purpose of that airline is not clear. What does the government intend to do with it? I leave Vancouver weekly, often on the old "red eye special" coming down here at midnight. I have a choice. I can travel on a one-third full Air Canada aircraft or a one-third full CP aircraft. As time passes, the airlines use stretched DC-8s, then DC-8s and then 727s, often with only a third of a load. I cannot see the sense in promoting two or three national air carriers in a market which does not warrant it. What is the policy? What social goal is to be achieved? These things are not clear.
With respect to Petro-Canada, I think it was on October 23, 1973, during a period of minority government that Tommy Douglas stood in the House and made one of the most definitive speeches on energy policy ever made. He advocated and demanded that an energy Crown corporation be created. It was not until the next Parliament that the government managed to address that. It was perfectly content to let foreign multinationals run the country. The government spoke in horror of what would happen if we ever let public enterprise, which, it was said, could not run a peanut stand, into the oil industry.
The government finally did create Petro-Canada but left it spinning its wheels for years, from about 1976 until 1980. No definite purpose had been established for it. Now we see Petro-Canada as a jewel in the dubious crown called the national energy policy. Petro-Canada now has a clear window and a mandate, but I would bet dollars to doughnuts that even Petro-Canada will be corrupted when it comes to throwing benefits to the private sector and placing the burdens on the taxpayer and the public sector. There will be that kind of split. This is what we get continually from both the other parties in the House, and it is a very serious situation.
Government members cannot have it both ways. They want to criticize Crown corporations, but let them go after the government. Let them go after the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Communications, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc). Let us not go after the Crown corporations. Let us direct our attacks properly. I regret it when members of the governing party criticize Crown corporations but do not go to the source. They should be criticizing the policies of their own government.

Mr. Speaker, this is my first opportunity to take part in a debate, although I have been on my feet during

December 3, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
question period and on motions. Before I get into what I would like to discuss-I think this is a very important matter-I wonder if we might be able to call it six o'clock.
