speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Don't worry about it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
I thank the House leader of the NDP very much for his advice. He tells me not to worry about it, and I won't. Thank you, sir.
I will start at the point where we are looking at a massive oil import bill in the 1980s when we really should have achieved energy self-sufficiency. This country should have full employment and full use of its productive capacity. We should have applied our minds, brains and interests sensibly toward putting in energy transportation systems that were and are still necessary, and ensuring we have the refinement capacity that we need for the heavier and sour types of oil. We should have moved faster in delivering gas to the east coast as an oil substitute. We knew these programs would have to be put in place eventually. If they had been put in place in a timely, planned manner, we would not be looking at an energy shortfall of some $8 billion this year. In the period 1981-1985, it is estimated that imported energy costs as a result of the shortsightedness, and in fact blindness of this government, will
amount to between $55 billion and $60 billion. This will place further pressure on our balance of trade account and on our foreign exchange reserves.
I have read many of the speeches of senior executives of major companies in the industry. I was very impressed with the quality and the amount of research that went into them. I read that the former chairman of the National Energy Board and now vice-president of the Royal Bank's global energy group, estimates that the spending required in this country in the next 20 years on energy alone will be approximately $1.4 trillion in current terms.
We see all kinds of moves on the part of the government to keep us from foreign ownership and to prevent foreigners from having more than 50 per cent of the industry. I guess there is some political sympathy for that. Surely the priority is energy self-sufficiency as fast as we can get it.
It is interesting to note that if you go back in history you find that emerging nations have been developed by foreign interests. As they come up to a wealth-creating capacity, they start to buy back the ownership of their interests. How is this country, with government policies and a budget such as we were given on November 12, ever going to create the wealth needed to supply the demands of capital in the quantities that these senior executives within the country estimate are required just in the energy field?
We only have something like seven years' supply, 7 billion barrels of conventional crude oil remaining in western Canada. Our shortfall is something like 400,000 barrels a day. We now have to deliver ourselves into tar sands and in situ processes. We are having to take, use and put into refining capacity sour and heavy type hydrocarbon oils. All of this is dead in the water while this country struggles with uneconomic matters and budgets that interfere with anything positive in the way of creating wealth, creating our own capital and paying for things ourselves. The combination of the constitutional package, Bill C-48 and the budget, that package of three pieces of legislation, will mean almost total socialization of the counry. The members across the aisle have not learned from those countries that have already tried the state ownership route that it will not bring sufficient wealth to a country to enable it to support the welfare system and answer the demands of the citizens put upon it.
The tragedy is that in the field of energy the free enterprise system has a proven record. It has served the people of Canada very well. It is true that massive amounts of money have been made through free enterprise, but also massive sums have been paid in taxes, and that has been an important element in the cash flow and in the treasury of this country.
I venture to say that if we look at the history and at the spending pattern of the government and if we look at the history of PetroCan, we will find that in two or three years from now PetroCan, with its massive power over the industry, will again be surrounded with the same group of Liberal friends as it moves in to exploration. I would be surprised if
December 3, 1981

that had not already happened, Mr. Speaker. The losses will be for the people of Canada to bear and the wins will be for the selected backers of the Liberal Party of Canada.
These three pieces of legislation are a massive intervention against the market and the private sector. I do not think there is any member of the House who can say that Parliament is still in control of the programs or the spending power of the nation under the series of Crown corporations that we have put in place. Too many of them cannot even be audited by the Auditor General, and we have not addressed the whole matter of control and accountability over Crown corporations in the Financial Administration Act. Also, no matter how hard the Standing Committee on Public Accounts works, all of these matters keep slowly being buried in the process of more and more studies.
It is a tragedy when the House cannot control the affairs of the nation and have the bureaucrats account for their actions. Bill C-48 has cut the heart out of Canadian operators. It is not only the multinationals that are injured by this bill. They are injured all right, but they have to stay here. They have no place to go. In the other markets of the world they are already established. It is the wholly Canadian-owned companies that are hurt by this bill, the operators, the geologists, the drilling companies, the trucking companies, the supply and service companies, the technologists. They are laying off people, and you can just see the lay-offs within the different sections of the energy industry that are taking place all across the country.
The National Energy Program delivers to Canadian operators something in the neighbourhood of $4 to $7 per barrel in profit. In the U.S. it is a profit of $15 to $25 per barrel. It is no wonder that the trucks are taking the rigs south. It is no wonder the Canadian operators are moving their working capital, talents and expertise down south where the whole exploration industry is booming, where there is a demand and a call for the industry. All of the rigs in Canada are quiet. Only a fraction of our capacity is being utilized. We have not given the industry an incentive to go from shallow well technology into deep well technology as a result of the national energy policy of the Liberal government.
As a result of this, we will have to face some tragedies, and that is the reason the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has such a low profile these days. He came in very proudly and announced he had an agreement with Alberta, and then a subsequent fast, quickie agreement with British Columbia, and then an agreement with the province of Saskatchewan, the oil producing provinces. The premiers thought everything would stabilize. He could not hear the voices of the advisers, the presidents and the knowledgeable people in the industry who kept telling him that the government was not leaving enough cash flow for the private sector to take a meaningful part in exploration and development.
It is now my understanding that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the premiers of those provinces have realized they have made a serious mistake. I gather that they are now returning to the drawing fables to draft a program
Canada Oil and Gas Act
under which they will have to take less for themselves and allow more for the industry so that it can get going.
How will we create this $1.4 trillion in current dollar terms in the next 20 years unless we give the companies in that creative sector, that engineering and risk-taking sector, room to move and some incentive to risk their dollars? Most of the winning technology today is a combination of outside and domestic technology. Why should we penalize so severely the foreign technology and know-how that we need? Why should we make this country so unattractive to the Canadian operators that they now have to go to other markets of the world to survive?
The 8 per cent gross revenue tax effectively reduces corporate earnings by 25 per cent. The retroactivity policy involving 25 per cent of all the holdings of oil and gas companies in the federal or Canada lands should not exist in a country that is bragging about its fair taxation policy.
The principle of retroactivity that exists in Bill C-48, which is now very definitely a Liberal government policy that was announced to the nation on November 12, means that retroactive earnings will now be taxed. Never before has a free country had to contend with this. Not only has retroactivity become a government policy, but they have now removed from under the taxation base of Canada the ability to pay retroactive tax so that you have to pay that tax from other earnings.
I was saying before five o'clock that we were just getting used to the ten years of recovery from the taxation policy set down in 1971. As soon as the oil operators in the country have started to get a handle on the rules of the game, low and behold, on November 12, the government pulls the rug out from under the taxation system and absolutely destroys the decision-making base of this country.
This country cannot progress in conditions where anyone in the industry who is willing to work and take a risk has to wait for some government bureaucrat at some desk in the concrete towers of Ottawa to say yes or no. The country in those circumstances is bound to come to a complete halt. Is socialism worth it, Mr. Speaker? That is what will be delivered to the people of Canada. It will destroy the base that has made this country great. That is what the November 12 budget does, together with Bill C-48. It is the same socialist, elitist thinking that is in Bill C-48 that is also in the November 12 budget. How we can hang on to the bounty, the welfare and the pension plans that we have learned to expect from our system of government in Canada is beyond me.
In the months preceding the budget, with the PetroCan acquisition of Petrofina and CPI acquisition of International Paper, and all the concentration of ownership within the business community and the state sector, we have delivered $17 billion on our foreign exchange reserve account. If one cannot imagine how serious that is, one just has to remember that the reserve base was at $3.7 billion and the government had to borrow $1 billion to bring it back to over $3 billion just a few weeks ago. Yet lying in the wings, as a result of the degree of corporate concentration that this government has allowed through its national energy policy and its pre-budget

December 3, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
era, we have committed ourselves to $17 billion on demand in our foreign exchange account. Can we imagine the pressure it will have on the Canadian dollar? Will there be any chance of interest rates coming down to a reasonable spread above the inflation rate of the land? The incompetence of the government and the mismanagement of the economy will be recorded in the annals of history in terms of absolute treachery and what has been done to a once viable and healthy country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite may laugh but these words will haunt them in years to come. We have spent a good deal of time on Bill C-48. It deserves a good deal of our attention because it was poorly drafted. Even the government brought in over 100 amendments to satisfy its own officials that in fact the bill would work. It would not accept any reasonable amendments from the opposition parties, therefore we must now state that the bill is not deserving of passage. It should be taken out of the House, pulled apart and redrafted so that Canadians receive the oil and mineral wealth of the north and offshore. The government should provide incentives to create competition. Then companies would go into areas with tough weather conditions, ice-periods of time when there is no daylight and so forth-conditions which make it difficult to explore. There must be incentives for people and companies to go into those areas as well as offshore. Most of us cannot even visualize drilling on a rig a number of miles offshore in rough waters.
Tonight I should like to outline the picture of energy we now face and to determine why the bill will not work or will not be of assistance in reaching the goal of self-sufficiency. Also I should like to deal with a number of groups who have mentioned the reasons for their concerns in regard to the bill. On a net basis we presently import some 400,000 barrels of oil per day, which is roughly 22 per cent of our daily needs of approximately 1.8 million barrels per day. At current world prices of some $44 per barrel, oil imports cost Canada some $17.6 million per day or $6.4 billion per year. The situation will become worse in the next few years.
At present our domestic oil supplies come from fields in western Canada and from the Syncrude and Suncor plants.
Western Canadian reserves of conventional, light and medium crude, which account for 90 per cent of present production, are now more than 60 per cent depleted. Production from existing fields is declining at a rate of approximately 10 per cent per year. Production capacity of existing fields is now about 1.1 million barrels per day. By 1985 it will have declined to about
850,000	barrels per day, and by 1990 to only 500,000 barrels per day. Obviously the Government of Canada had to get a grip on the situation, establish some priorities and devise a strategy to move Canada toward self-sufficiency.
I should like to refer to some potential sources of increased domestic supply. There are undiscovered conventional supplies of oil in western Canada-there is no doubt about it. We can extract additional barrels of oil from heavy oil and from the tar sands, but the National Energy Program and present negotiating conditions are not allowing these plants to go ahead. But the potential is there. Also there is an ability with present technology to draw the in situ capacity from depleted wells in the conventional fields of western Canada. The first such plant, the Imperial Oil plant at Judy Creek, is now on hold because there is not sufficient incentive for the company to invest money to bring the plant onstream.
Of course, we know there is oil in the frontier areas of Canada-the north, the Beaufort Sea, the Mackenzie Delta, and off the east coasts of Newfoundland and Labrador. It is clear that the National Energy Program is geared toward the offshore and the north. Its whole approach to self-sufficiency is that we can catch up on our imports and control them through conservation. It is an important theory because conservation is an easy way to protect the consumption of barrels of oil. However, our record in the past has not been good. It is improving, and hopefully it will continue to improve. Part of the plan is the use of conservation until the late 1980s when oil from offshore and from frontier areas can be brought onstream. Supposedly we would have self-sufficiency by 1990. When we consider the budget and what is contained in this bill, it is obvious that the government is geared toward gutting the industry in western Canada and promoting, as much as possible, government control of the industry offshore and in the north. As the hon. member for Capilano said, as a result hundreds of millions of dollars are being forced offshore, south of the border; thousands of trained professional people are being lost to the United States; and hundreds of rigs are no longer drilling in our basin. Of the 10,000 exploratory wells that were expected to be drilled in western Canada in 1981, only 6,400 will be completed, while a significant part of the oil service industry has been emigrating to the United States in search of employment and adequate returns. Major enhanced recovery initiatives, such as the Imperial Oil Judy Creek project, have been shelved.
It has been estimated by the Canadian Petroleum Association that, in terms of activity levels, the industry has stepped backward about three years as a result of the National Energy Program. It has had a devastating effect upon oil drilling in my area which produces two-thirds of the conventional oil in the nation. The largest Canadian industrial park, which has as
December 3, 1981

its main components oil servicing and oil well drilling companies, has been devastated; $100 million has been lost in that small region of Canada, along with thousands of jobs. It is difficult to understand why the government would create a policy which has driven many experts away from that area of Alberta into the United States.
I should like to refer to a few statistics which have appeared constantly in Edmonton newspapers. For example, hundreds of trailer camps sit idle in Edmonton industrial yards. During the past year more than 650 people have been laid off in the industrial trailer camp manufacturing industry in Alberta. Since the fall of 1980, the Territorial Company in Edmonton has cut back its manufacturing and service staff from 500 people to 271. Six other industrial camp producers in the Edmonton area cut their staff by 30 per cent to 75 per cent. These are people who just a few years ago put their money on the line. They bought a piece of property, put up a building, hired their neighbours to come in and build the trailer camps that would provide catering capacity for the oil drilling industry. Some of them bought small service rigs to assist in the drilling industry. Many of the companies that drilled were unable to make a decent return, and so had no choice but to either leave their rigs idle or move to the United States.
During the past year, manufacturing employment in Alberta has dropped by 8,000 jobs. That is a significant number in a province that had been booming. The demand for workers has increased in other areas, and that has absorbed some of the people who had been thrown out of their jobs.
Other areas, such as the construction industry, have been able to absorb some of the unemployed. The Edmonton Journal conducted a survey of specific businesses. The result shows that more than 1,200 people have already been laid off in the industrial camp manufacturing and camp catering sector. That is a small but intense sector. Company officials predict that the prospects for this winter look even worse. Some industry estimates place the employment impact at between 20,000 and
25,000	jobs, including about 8,000 jobs lost in the oil patch and 15,000 jobs lost in related industries.
Many of these people were producing for the north-for camps and catering facilities working in the Beaufort Sea. I hope that activity will continue in that area so that more people are not laid off there.
There is a lack of incentive for business in the bill, Mr. Speaker. It has been demonstrated that profitability in the United States is about four times higher than in Canada. Quite clearly, then, the government has placed its energy priorities in the offshore, and Bill C-48 was supposed to set regulations to attract industry into that area.
The bill is also supposed to regulate the Canada lands. Obviously there is a great deal of potential in these areas, so we could have expected the government to bring in a bill that would provide incentives and encourage companies to work in the north. But there are only disincentives. There are back-in provisions and there are extraordinary taxes. It does not even
Canada Oil and Gas Act
allow the deduction of interest as a legitimate expense. Instead of incentives, we find provisions in the bill that will go a long way toward reducing competition, discouraging investment and deterring the industry.
The taxes contained in the bill will have the effect of discouraging all but perhaps three or four companies from working in the north. Of course, Petro-Canada will be the favourite son. As far as real competition in the north and the offshore is concerned, however, there will be virtually none.
Anyone who has heard me speak on this bill in this chamber before will know how strongly I feel about the value of competition in a sector that is supposed to make us self-sufficient in oil and gas in the future. Competition has been very successful in the past, but it has virtually been made ineffective by this bill. I do not intend to go through that argument again. I have already spent some time explaining why the bill will have that result again.
Competition is essential when we deal with an industry such as the resource industry with its implications for our businesses, our economic wellbeing, our very lifestyle and our employment situation. This is the one industry that was growing rapidly and employing new people. At one time it was growing so rapidly that we could not supply enough geologists and chemists to meet the demand.
One of the reasons why competition in this industry is so important is that we now have on the books a bill that states that companies must table their core samples and drilling results after one year.
In many cases, company geologists will find that, although another company drilled a hole a year earlier and found nothing, they, using a different technique and with different abilities and different intellectual capacities, can go back into that area, drill again and find gas and oil. One of the largest gas fields in North America was discovered in this way. A large company had drilled in northwestern Alberta, but it was a dry hole. A year later another company, Canadian Hunter, checked the results, went back to that area and drilled again. It found the largest field of natural gas in North America.
Other small companies with good geologists have been extraordinarily successful in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. They have studied the core samples of other companies, and a year later have found what was missed. That is what competition does, Mr. Speaker.
Two or three companies can explore a huge area, such as the offshore in the Northwest Territories and Yukon. They can have the same geologists, the same people throughout their whole bureaucracy, so there is no big gap in intellectual capacity. If they do not make a find then, as things stand under this bill, other companies will not be interested in going in to test again because they will not be able to afford it.
This area has the greatest potential for oil and gas in North America but we are putting a law on the books that provides incentives for only two or three companies. I find that very hard to understand, Mr. Speaker.

December 3, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
On the one hand, the government is saying that we need to be self-sufficient by 1990 and that we can do that by developing the north and the offshore. On the other hand, it seems to bend over backwards to discourage the very activity it seeks. The only area in which it has been successful is the nationalization program which results in many hundreds of millions of Canadian dollars going out of the country when they are needed to develop our own industry. And this money does not produce one more barrel of oil, Mr. Speaker.
The taxation regime which this bill puts in place imposes a
10	per cent basic royalty; a 40 per cent participating royalty after a 25 per cent return on investment; an 8 per cent gas and
011	production tax; and a unique 25 per cent back-in tax. As the hon. member for Capilano said, no other country in the free world has done this. The total of these taxes is over 83 per cent, Mr. Speaker.
The government can claim that it plans to give an exploration grant depending upon the degree of Canadian ownership, and that it does not allow deductions for legitimate business expenses such as interest. That is a very small incentive for an area of so much risk such as the north. Most companies would not consider going into an area like that unless the potential return on investment was between 20 per cent and 25 per cent.
Some countries in the world have used a different system to encourage companies to go into high risk areas. In these countries, a company which finds a well that has a production capacity is allowed to use all the wealth from that oil production to pay off its debt first rather than to pay large interest costs and other costs such as royalties and taxes. Once the debt is paid off, the government then comes in with its royalty and profit tax. This system is much more successful than ours and is having tremendous success in countries such as Norway. I believe that is something we should seriously consider for our northern regions because of the high costs of exploration in those areas. As well, as I said before, we will really only allow three or four companies into the north, companies which can operate under this tax regime.
Let us look at the effect that that may have on self-sufficiency. Let us take a look at a small area around the town of Leduc in the Nisku-Drayton Valley of the province of Alberta. We have been exploring in that area for over 30 years. Tens of thousands of holes have been drilled by hundreds of companies, and the success rate over those 30 years has been very good. Even today, in that very area, we are still discovering oil and natural gas. Just a few weeks ago we drilled a new well which is producing 700 barrels of oil per day. Therefore, if only three or four companies start operating in the north, in an area which is 50 to 60 times the size of the area I have mentioned, unless they are extremely lucky, they will not achieve the same kind of production that could come on stream in the next four or five years if we had good competition and a number of experts working in that area.
The back-in provision in Bill C-48 causes me a great deal of difficulty. I cannot disagree more strongly with this tax. These
were not rules upon which companies went into the north and risked their capital. People went into the north, took the risks and stayed a long time away from home, often for questionable returns. Those rules were not there at that time. Companies went up into that region because they expected to find something. They were prepared to take profits that they were earning from producing wells in other parts of Canada and place those profits in the north through incentives that we made available such as a depletion allowance.
Now the minister is saying, "Well, we have a right to this back-in provision because the Canadian taxpayer has, in fact, already paid for it." That is just a lot of nonsense! If incentive is provided for a company to go in there, it does so in good faith. However, when it has made a discovery and a back-in provision is put in place, it is no wonder it puts little trust in the government. How can one have any trust anymore? What private company will put its capital on the line when it is not sure what the government will come up with two years or three years down the way?
Even if we, as a government, wanted to put in a provision which would allow a 25 per cent part of the play to a Crown corporation, surely we should have made that effective in 1982 or 1983, which would have allowed companies to prepare for it. I know that the Dome Petroleum Company, which has spent a lot of time and effort and has been very successful in the north, has placed before us a proposal regarding the 25 per cent back-in in Canada lands. I think it is a proposal which should be given consideration. However, if we want to impose such a tax, and I certainly do not think we need to, surely we should have put the tax in place as of 1981, 1982 or 1983, with 5 per cent one year and 10 per cent the next, or something of that sort. That would have been more fair to the companies which are spending time and effort in that region.
As my time in this debate draws to an end, I want to place on the record the concerns of another group regarding this bill. They are the concerns of the people who have lived in the north for many years. The majority of them are native people. They have particular concern with this bill because it is coming at a time when their land claims are just now moving toward settlement. If a lot of drilling does go on in that area, they are unsure whether they can lay claim to the land where a drilling rig is situated. That concern is not defined in this bill. It is not settled anywhere. I can see only one section which pertains to this matter, Section 5(7), which states:
-nothing in this Act abrogates or derogates from any aboriginal title, right or claim that pertained to the aboriginal peoples of Canada prior to the coming into force of this Act-
While the section is included in the hope that it will, in fact, protect native people, they are very concerned about this bill. Nothing in this bill will exempt lands from being claimed. It is unlikely that lands under development will be surrendered by the government to natives claiming them. Harry Daniels, the outgoing president of the Native Council of Canada, has pointed out the very problem that lies in this section. He stated that:
December 3, 1981

-once the drill rigs are up and production centres on the drawing boards and approved by government, there will be no turning back. Do you realty think that under those circumstances the government would withdraw those lands?
These are legitimate concerns. When we look at the COPE settlement, lands that were under exploration at the time were withdrawn from the negotiating area.
Another area of concern is the Norman Wells development. Under this bill, the area around the Norman Wells production sources and refining area is not included. Section 10(2)(d) provides for equitable participation by the aboriginal peoples affected by the particular exploration agreement. This is fine, and this is a good section. However, where will these people get the equity? From where will they get the money? In most instances, these people have no funds at all. They have no capacity for raising funds to participate in an equitable sense. In the southern provinces, in Saskatchewan and Alberta, we have set up trust funds for future generations to participate in the wealth from oil and gas. It would seem to me that we could learn something from this and apply it to the Northwest Territories and Yukon, as well as the native people in that area. It would make sense if we were to put a section in this bill setting up a trust fund which would come from the earnings of oil and gas production in the area, so that these people could use that money to begin equitable participation in the north and, hopefully, make some discoveries on their own. However, without that type of suggestion or initiative, there is simply no way that they can get the equity, the billions of dollars that it costs to drill a well offshore in the Beaufort Sea or in the Mackenzie Delta. This is something which should have been considered, and Section 10(2)(d) will really be meaningless unless we have some way of providing the initial capacity for equity in the north.
For all these reasons, and there are many more which my colleagues have stated, this bill should be withdrawn, pulled apart section by section, and redrafted so that under the new provisions we can reach energy self-sufficiency by 1990 or soon thereafter. If we put this bill in place now, even though some of its rules will assist, we will not reach that goal. We will not have the kind of competitiveness necessary in the north. We will not have the necessary oil companies and people in that area, and we will fail our country miserably.
For that reason, I say that it would be impossible for me to vote in favour of Bill C-48. I hope that the House will seriously consider all the reasons that my colleagues and I are putting forward.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I saw the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in the House this afternoon and it was my hope he would be here tonight because there is something I wanted to say to him. It takes a big man in this life to admit a mistake. The National Energy Program is surely a mistake of tragic proportion for Canadians. The Minister of Energy has had an opportunity, since becoming the minister and having spent some time as
Canada Oil and Gas Act
critic when we were in government, to learn something about the oil industry. In all fairness to the minister, I think he is a big enough man to admit a mistake.
This National Energy Program will be changed. We are not going to change it here tonight on third reading, but it is going to be changed because there is no incentive left for the oil industry to go out and explore for the oil and gas we desperately need. Strangely enough, there is still 40 per cent of the Canadian population who believe we do not have a problem even today. Some 40 per cent of Canadians do not think we have a problem in terms of future oil and gas supplies. They think this has all been rigged, and that somehow the government and the major oil companies have perpetrated a fraud on the Canadian people. The National Energy Program will be changed, and I would have thought that the Minister of Energy was a big enough man to recognize the need for such a change at this time.
The minister has said there are some anomalies in the program and that Premier Lougheed and the Alberta government can sort out these anomalies and give the industry a few little handouts here and there which will encourage the industry to go back to work. This is not something that requires a band-aid solution, and the Alberta government cannot do it all by itself.
Let me assure you that the National Energy Program needs to be changed in its basic, fundamental thrust. It is completely out of tune with the reality of the industry and the needs of the Canadian people. Essentially, the reason for that is that there is no incentive left.
I have been involved in the oil and gas business for 20 years. The new oil prices under the National Energy Program are very attractive. If I could believe, first of all, that we were going to get that kind of price for our oil and, second, if I could trust the government not to go in and confiscate what I had found, I might be prepared to go and look for it, but I do not trust the government. Therein lies the fundamental problem with the investors today who want to go out and invest in the oil and gas industry.
The investor does not believe in the prices which have been projected forward and, moreover, he believes that if he does find it, the government will not allow him to keep it. Why should he believe that? Every time any investor has gone out and found oil or gas in this country, the federal government or provincial governments have stolen it from him. Why should an investor trust a government today? I would not.
I am prepared to accept the fact that part of the downturn in the oil and gas industry we have seen in Alberta-and we have seen a massive downturn in activity-is a result of the fact that we cannot export our gas. We have huge reserves of shut-in gas in Alberta today and we cannot export it and we do not have the pipeline to deliver it to eastern Canada in place as yet. 1 accept that fact as part of the reason our industry has suffered a slowdown. The National Energy Program has gone much further than that in causing the disaster we are experiencing in my province of Alberta today.
13712

December 3, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Let me return to the main objectives of the National Energy Program. When the program was introduced a year ago in the House the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said the objectives were security of supply, fairness in terms of revenue sharing and an opportunity for Canadians. I guess there is not a member in the House or a person in Canada who would not agree with these noble objectives. We all want energy security, we would like to think revenues are being fairly shared and, above all, we would like to think there is an opportunity for Canadians. Those are admirable objectives.
Has the National Energy Program really provided us with a program to achieve energy security? Do we in fact have a fair sharing of revenues, and has the program created an opportunity for Canadians? From my perspective, the energy program has failed on all counts. In spite of what the Minister of Energy continues to say, there is absolutely no hope that we will be self-sufficient in oil by 1990. I am not going to go back into my arguments; I spoke for 40 minutes a few weeks ago explaining why we are not going to be self-sufficient in oil. This is a myth and a delusion and the Minister of Energy and the officials of Energy, Mines and Resources know it to be a myth and a delusion. It is a sham to pretend to the Canadian people that we can be self-sufficient in oil in 1990. That is simply a falsehood. It is done to sound nice to the Canadian people. It is decisive and it represents confidence, and Canadians above all need confidence. "Let us not face the truth; above all, let us not face the truth. Let us bury our heads in the sands and let us deceive one another", they say.
I can recall Mr. Gillespie, the former minister of energy, saying in 1974, "There is no problem, Canadians, we have a program in place for you and we will be self-sufficient in 1980." Oh, yes, we are self-sufficient in 1980. Certainly we are; we are buying 400,000 barrels of oil a day. This government and the minister of energy are no less deceitful than the minister who preceded him, Mr. Gillespie.
The National Energy Program will result in the need to at least double our imports of foreign oil before the end of the decade. This is a matter of simple arithmetic. There is no great complexity to this at all. Our domestic reserves are declining. Our total consumption is estimated to remain about the same, and there is no viable method in place for making up the difference in the next decade. The minister knows it and Energy, Mines and Resources people know it. Those are the facts. This is not only my opinion, it is the opinion of many knowledgeable authorities in Canada who are not trying to deceive the Canadian people. That is energy self-sufficiency for Canadians? That is oil self-sufficiency by 1990? Forget it, because it is not there.
Let us talk about fairness in revenue-sharing. I suppose that fairness in revenue sharing depends on your point of view. If you are the federal government, you would be rubbing your hands in glee because you just took $55 billion from the Canadian people and you think that is a fair share of revenue. The Alberta government did all right, too. They did not do any
worse than the federal government. It got a big slice of pie. The province of Ontario got its pound of flesh.
The consumer is paying 75 per cent of the price for gasoline and heating fuel in the form of government taxes and royalties between the federal and provincial levels. The government leaves the industry 25 per cent to find the oil, produce it, refine it and deliver it to our automobiles. Some may say that is all right, that there is nothing wrong with 25 per cent, that it seems like a good number because, after all, these oil companies are making huge sums of money.
Can we really look at anything in terms of the absolute amount of money which is made? In this case we are looking at literally billions of dollars which oil companies have to spend to build an oil sands plant and hundreds of millions of dollars to drill in the Beaufort Sea and Hibernia. These are also large sums of money which have to be spent. I suggest that the oil companies' rate of return, the amount of money they receive from their invested assets, is less than that of the manufacturing industry in Ontario. In 1980, the oil industry in Canada had an 11 per cent rate of return on its total invested capital, as compared to 13 per cent for all manufacturing industries in Canada.
Is 25 per cent adequate? If it is, why is the oil and gas exploration industry not taking advantage of this opportunity? If this opportunity is so great, why are 150 rigs in western Canada shut down for lack of work, and why have the 214 rigs drilling in western Canada left the country? Tell me why an additional 48 rigs will leave the country in the next few months? And why is it that 161 oil well servicing rigs are not working today and 92 oil well servicing rigs have left the country? An additional 52 oil well servicing rigs will be sold or shipped out of Canada in the next few months. The difference between a drilling rig and an oil well servicing rig is that a drilling rig is used for the original discovery and the oil well servicing rig comes in afterward to be used for remedial work and to make the oil well continue to produce at a sustainable level.
If the National Energy Program is such a great opportunity, why is it that the oil and gas industry has lost the services of
8,000	field workers? Those 8,000 men have worked on those drilling and service rigs as well as all the other equipment involved in the oil industry. Why did 8,000 of these workers lose their jobs? Many of them have left Canada and will not be back.
If this is such a great opportunity, why is it that our independent oil companies have moved in droves to the United States, Australia and other countries? If 25 per cent of the revenues is such a great deal in Canada, why are these companies moving out of Canada in droves? These companies have moved $3 billion worth of capital out of the country in the last year. Did the government not think Canadians wanted to explore in Canada if given an adequate opportunity and the incentive? Does this indicate a fair sharing of revenues to you, Mr. Speaker?
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has said that some elements of the oil and gas industry have expressed
December 3, 1981

disappointment about the impact of the energy agreement on cash flow. Well, how about that? He goes on to say, "I believe this approach reflects, in most cases, a preoccupation with short-term prospects". When a company is literally facing bankruptcy, as many small oil and gas companies are today, and I do not exaggerate that fact for a moment, is it not surprising that one would be looking at shorter term prospects? If you need evidence, just talk to a banker in Calgary. He will tell you that there are at least a hundred small oil and gas companies which will not be around at this time next year if there is not a change. If you want to buy oil and gas reserves, there is ample opportunity to do so because there are many for sale in Calgary and Edmonton today. As I said, if you were in this position, would you not be looking for shorter-term prospects? After all, you may not be around long enough to look at long-term prospects.
The minister of energy says, "I would think that the ability to explore and develop in Alberta, or anywhere else, would not be enhanced by conveying to investors an overly dark picture of industry prospects on the basis of some short-term and entirely predictable factors." What does he mean? Does he think that oil companies can persuade investors to risk their money on oil and gas exploration by simply telling them that the National Energy Program is a wonderful opportunity and that these investors should get on board? Does he really believe that private investors are that naive? Is the minister suggesting that the industry should be telling private investors that the National Energy Program is a wonderful opportunity to make money? Is he suggesting that we lie to them and try to deceive them into investing their money?
Investors know the facts and have read about them. That is why the oil and gas index on junior oil companies listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange has declined by more than 35 per cent since the introduction of the National Energy Program. I might say that the junior oil companies in Canada have suffered more than the industry as a whole because they have been affected to a greater degree than any other part of the industry. They do not have the cash flow to sustain their operations as do the multinationals which have downstream benefits from petrochemical and refining operations from which they will be able to sustain themselves.
However, the junior oil and gas companies have risked large ammounts of money in the search for oil and gas reserves, and in many cases they have those reserves in the ground and have not yet had the opportunity to develop a sufficient cash flow to sustain themselves because their assets are invested in exploration. They invested their assets in the ground before the National Energy Program began because they felt they had an opportunity to make a dollar.
The minister says that there has been a dispute between the industry and the government over netbacks on oil and gas. Netback is a term commonly used in the industry and it means the net amount left over after expenses and taxes have been taken from gross revenue. The minister went on to say that when the government calculates the netbacks, "we assume the producer is reinvesting heavily and therefore qualifies for tax
Canada Oil and Gas Act
write-offs." Well, indeed he does. There is no question about that. If he reinvests, he qualifies for tax write-offs. The minister went on to say that the government uses what the government calls an effective tax rate. The effective tax rate is the rate of tax paid after having taken all write-offs. This statement is absolute nonsense. Do hon. members assume that an investor or anyone else does not have to pay his full rate of income tax? Is that the assumption we should make? Sooner or later every investor knows that if he is going to put a dollar into his pocket, he is going to have to pay a dollar to the Crown.
One does not assess business opportunities based on avoiding income taxes. That is what the minister is asking the industry to do, and that is what he is asking the investment community to do. He is asking them to assess their opportunities based on the fact that they can continue to write off, write off, and write off. However, there comes a day when perhaps one does not want to write off any more. Perhaps a person does not want to be in the oil and gas business anymore. An individual investor drills a well and finds oil and gas. Perhaps he wants to go on and do something different and pay his taxes. Perhaps he does not want to reinvest in another oil or gas well. Should he not be allowed to assess his investment without having to take into consideration the fact that he is compelled to go back in and reinvest his profits in an oil and gas venture? The minister's statement is absolutely dishonest, and he knows it. Investors make decisions on paying their income taxes, not avoiding them.
Finally, the third cornerstone of the National Energy Program is opportunity for Canadians. I would like just one Canadian to tell me what opportunities have been created for him by virtue of the National Energy Program. Let hon. members opposite tell the 8,000 rig workers who have lost their jobs what a great opportunity the National Energy Program has provided for them. Maybe the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) would like to go and talk to those 8,000 workers in Alberta and tell them what a great opportunity it has been for them. Let him tell the investors in the small Canadian oil and gas companies what a great opportunity it has been for them. They just lost 35 per cent of their investment, but let the parliamentary secretary go and tell them what a great opportunity it has been for them. Let him tell all the contractors and the engineering firms who were making plans to help build Cold Lake, the in situ project in Alberta. Let him go and tell them. Let him tell all the contractors and engineering firms connected with the Alsands project what a great opportunity it has been for them. Let him tell the manufacturers of equipment in Ontario and Quebec what a great opportunity the National Energy Program has been for them.
Finally, let him tell the consumers what a great opportunity they have had when gasoline prices and home heating fuel prices have doubled since the National Energy Program. A super opportunity! Let him tell the thousands of people in

December 3, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Calgary who were formerly employed in the oil and gas industry and have had to move their families and their homes to the United States to make a living what a great opportunity the National Energy Program has been for them.
In summary, the National Energy Program, in terms of energy security, fairness and opportunity, is an unmitigated disaster. It is a disaster for which all Canadians will pay dearly. They are paying dearly for it right now in the prices of oil products such as gasoline and home heating fuel, and the tragedy of it all is that they are not getting a thing for it. The provincial and federal governments are getting it all, and the consumer is getting nothing. He is not getting energy security, he is not getting opportunity and he is not getting fairness.
I have said that the National Energy Program has denied investors the incentive to invest in their own country and denied workers jobs. Above all, Canadians have been denied the economic growth that would come from a healthy oil and gas industry.
Let me turn more particularly to Bill C-48 which we have before us this evening. Bill C-48 is particularly important because it deals with the opportunity to find truly enormous reserves of oil and gas in our frontier areas offshore, in the Arctic and in the Northwest Territories. On one point I agree with the federal government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and that is with respect to the prominent role Canada lands should play in the future development of energy in Canada. On that point I fully agree. Discoveries in Canada lands should account for an increasingly larger share of exploration and development in the future. The importance of Canada lands to Canada cannot be stressed too much. They are absolutely critical to our energy security and, moreover, they provide us with an opportunity of untold proportions to build a strong Canadian economy by putting people, capital and equipment together to capture the enormous wealth under Canada lands and waters. We really have a fantastic opportunity. We have an opportunity no other country in the world I can think of has to build a strong economy and give the best standard of living to every Canadian, if we want to go out and grasp it and develop our resources in the Canada lands. However, there will have to be some prerequisites to that. We will have to allow the private sector to go out and do it because no government can do that for us, unless we completely nationalize everything in the country and abandon all concepts of the private sector.
The amount of money required to develop our resources in the frontier areas in the Northwest Territories and offshore is staggering. The Royal Bank, to quote a number-I do not know whether hon. members want to believe it or not, but others have come up with the same number-has said that we need $400 billion in the next decade to do that job. I really wonder whether we want to pay taxes to that extent and let Petro-Canada do it. I am not going to get into the Petro-Canada argument tonight, but I will say that Petro-Canada has not done one doggone thing for Canadians since it was invented. It has not found any oil or any gas. It has just cost taxpayers a bunch of money. However, this wealth cannot be
captured without incentives to industry, and this is where Bill C-48 completely fails to come to grips with our future. Not only do we have a lack of incentives for industry but we also have confiscation and a regulatory environment which will discourage exploration. That is what Bill C-48 is all about. It is about confiscation, retroactive confiscation and regulation.
This government has a mentality which says, "Jeepers, we cannot allow anybody to make a dollar. If we allow somebody to make a dollar, that has to be wrong". The mentality is that it has to be wrong if we allow anyone to make a dollar, so we will not let anyone make a dollar. The government says we should not allow our resources to be developed by that rotten, dirty old private sector!
My most serious concern-and it has been expressed time and time again in the debate on Bill C-48, not only by myself but also by other members of our party-is the retroactive 25 per cent back-in provision outlined in Clause 27 of the bill. I will acknowledge that the government has moved from its original position of expropriation without compensation. I suppose we can give the government a small amount of credit for at least recognizing that it should not steal without giving a little bit back. The government moved to a scheme which is intended to provide for recovery of prior expenditures made by the initial oil finder. The government will reimburse a company, if it goes out and finds oil, a small portion of its costs. This is called ex gratia compensation, but it is totally unfair. It provides only for prior expenditures made in the discovery area related to successful and developed hydrocarbon accumulations, and ignores the inherent value of the reserves taken by the Crown.
It sounds like a nice argument. The government tells you to go out, find it and then it takes 25 per cent and pays what it cost. However, it will not pay for dry holes that have been drilled. If 12 dry holes are drilled at a cost of $50 million a hole, which is what it costs in Hibernia and the Beaufort Sea, the government will not pay for that. However, if there is a find, it will pay 25 per cent of the $50 million.
Do hon. members really believe that is fair? I have used the word expropriation. It is a strong word. Nobody likes expropriation. To a lot of people expropriation means stealing. Is it difficult to imagine what other term would apply in a situation where assets are literally seized unilaterally without any semblance or attempt at negotiated settlement?
The Saskatchewan government expropriated to potash companies. I will give the provincial NDP government some credit, and it is not often I have cause to say anything good about them. However, at least it sat down and negotiated a reasonable deal based on the fair market value.
The Quebec government wants to take over the asbestos corporation. It is sitting down and talking to the owners, negotiating in good faith what it believes to be a reasonable market value. Not this government, no sir. It expropriates with no semblance of compensation cost. It reminds me of Iran and Libya. Those are the kinds of governments those countries
December 3, 1981

have. They just walk in, take it, and if you do not like it, lump it.
The definition of adequate compensation in the case of a government expropriation is always a contentious issue, but Canadian governments in the past have always recognized a basic fundamental principle that fair and equitable compensation for expropriated assets is not related to historical cost but is based on the market value of those assets.
I find it paradoxical that Petro-Canada, the federal government's own oil company in its acquisition of Petrofina and other companies, accepted fair market value as the appropriate benchmark in its takeovers. It paid a premium over and above the market value for the companies it acquired. I cannot understand why the proprietary rights to petroleum reserves should be treated differently. Will somebody explain that? I do not understand it. Why is it that the federal government pays a premium over fair market value for certain assets and will expropriate other assets at a fraction of the cost? It does not make any sense to me.
Witnesses have stated in connection with the Hibernia field-and for those who do not know where it is, it is offshore Newfoundland-that the present value of the proposed compensation that the federal government proposes to pay when it expropriates the 25 per cent interest is in the range of five to ten cents per barrel of oil, after tax. In the case of Sable Island, which is a gas field, we hope, the value of the compensation works out on an after-tax basis to a mere one cent per
1,000	cubic feet of gas. These estimates of ex gratia payments have been calculated using the government's own formula.
The market value of the reserves taken by the Crown is difficult to determine because such estimates must be based on unknown factors 10 to 20 years hence. It is particularly difficult to establish market values of fields such as Hibernia and Sable Island where the prospective economic and regulatory environment is still unknown. This is also true in the Canadian Arctic. Let us forget about the economics of offshore Sable Island and the Arctic. Let us accept a recent study of an independent consultant in Canada who values Canadian conventional oil reserves at $2.50 per barrel for oil and 40 cents per 1,000 cubic feet for gas. The point I am trying to get across is that ex gratia payment offered in Bill C-48, ranging from five to ten cents per barrel and one cent per 1,000 cubic feet of gas, does not come anywhere close to the fair market value of the reserves being seized.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and other members of the government argue that the back-in provision is simply payment for taxation foregone as a result of earlier tax incentives. Where is the logic in an argument that uses a system of tax incentives which was introduced with the specific intent of encouraging high-risk and high-cost exploration to justify retroactive measures? It reminds me of the budget; what was an incentive yesterday is a loophole today. lished, the government realizes its share of the proceeds automatically through royalty and tax payments.

The fact is that the rationale used by the government is indefensible.
The proposed 25 per cent back-in provision is particularly difficult for a number of companies. This 25 per cent back-in provision is in addition to a 25 per cent interest already acquired by Petro-Canada under previous legislation. Under the 1977 amendments to the Canada oil and gas regulations, Petro-Canada obtained a 25 per cent interest in a number of prospects in the Canada lands. With the passage of Bill C-48, this right of Petro-Canada no longer exists and will be replaced by the 25 per cent retroactive Crown share.

I say that the native people of northern Canada feel betrayed at a time when native claims are being negotiated. This bill can only bring about needless complications. Passage of this bill at the present time will only add to the complexities of native claims and will only make settlement of them more difficult. That was made very clear by the native organizations that appeared and testified before the committee.
I have said before that Yukoners regard this bill as a gigantic land grab of Yukon and Northwest Territories by the government. The Progressive Conservative has always hoped that these territories would one day become provinces. What will happen when that day comes? What will happen if the people of Yukon and Western Arctic decide by a referendum that they wish to join confederation as provinces and petition the federal government to that effect? What happens when those resources have been exploited by the government, not for the benefit of the Yukoners who stand to gain absolutely nothing and not for the financial benefit of all Canadians or even northern Canadians, but for the financial benefit of the Liberal government?
We are witnessing the curious spectacle of a government which has shown no ability to run those operations already under its control, setting out to engage in operations which require a high degree of skill and know-how which, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary South, this government certainly does not possess and which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his parliamentary secretary have not displayed, even to my limited knowledge of the industry. It could not run the Post Office and so had to get rid of it. It is a government which not only cannot make the trains run on time but cannot even make them run at all, yet it sets out to bring in new oil and gas supplies.
It is a government which took a healthy economy and allowed it to run down, to be destroyed, while the ministers

The topic was Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited. One of the tasks of the special parliamentary committee on national trading corporations was to look into how Canada can increase its export trade and thereby help small and medium-sized businesses. The special parliamentary committee had difficulty obtaining information on the Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited.
Before setting up any new corporations or systems, it is always wise to see what existing systems are doing and whether or not they are successful. Because I did not receive a satisfactory answer from witnesses appearing before the committee, I tabled a question on the Order Paper dated June 19, 1981. Question 2,559 specifically asked:
What was the date of incorporation of the Export Finance Corporation of Canada Limited and what was its purpose?
Did the corporation meet its obligations and goals and what is its present status?
The answer given to me by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs of Canada was that such a corporation was federally incorporated on June 4, 1959, under a special act of Parliament assented to on that day. The department stated:
The object of the corporation was to Finance and facilitate exports and imports and the exchange of goods and services between Canada and any nation of the Commonwealth of Nations or other nations, and between agencies or residents of Canada and such nations, or agencies or residents thereof.
The department's answer went on to say that in so far as the act was concerned, the company had met its legal obligations by having filed its financial statement and annual summary for the year ending March 31, 1981, with the director of corporations. The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, however, was unable to comment on the performance of the company with regard to its goals and objectives.
Not receiving an answer to my tabled question, I raised the question during question period in the House on November 23, 1981. I would like to quote my question from Hansard at page 13079:
Would the minister inform this house on the success or failure of this corporation in meeting its objectives in Financing and facilitating exports and imports?
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs replied:
Madam Speaker, of course it is not a simple matter to determine a corporation's ability or inability to achieve its objectives.
-there is no legal or even political obligation that would allow us to make sure whether or not it is meeting its objectives successfully.
As a parliamentarian in this House of Commons, I feel I have the right to ask for such information and to be provided with the accurate data. I pursued my question further. On December 1, 1981, I received further information from the
deputy minister addressed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). The deputy minister confirmed that such a corporation was incorporated on June 4, 1959. His reply states that the corporation was given ample financing powers to achieve its objectives. At the time of the incorporation, the capital stocks consisted of ten million shares with a par value of $5 each. The deputy minister went on to say that the corporation is currently dormant. The current capital base stands at $20,000 and is owned by seven major Canadian chartered banks. The board of directors, which meets once a year, consists of 14 officers from these banks and is currently chaired by Mr. J. J. Dowsley from the Toronto-Dominion Bank. If the corporation is dormant, why did I receive, on form 3, an annual summary under Section 133 of the Canada Corporations Act, dated March 31, 1981, from the active board of directors, 14 of them to be exact? The answer from the deputy minister goes on to state:
In April, 1968, the Board of Directors of the corporation decided after consultation with the Minister of Finance and the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, to stop accepting new business due to the imminent incorporation of EDC in 1969, and to the pattern and direction of short-term interest rates in the New York market that made Fixed rate medium and long-term export Financing rather difFicult for the corporation.
If the board of directors in 1968, in consultation with the Minister of Finance, and the Export Credits Insurance Corporation decided to stop accepting new business due to the incorporation of EDC in 1969, then how can the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs of Canada state that the company has met its legal obligations by having filed with the director of corporations its financial statement and annual summary for the year ending March 31, 1981?
I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. McCauley) whether the seven major Canadian chartered banks are using the Export Finance Corporation of Canada, Ltd. as a gimmick to avoid payment of taxes to the government?
There are just too many unanswered questions surrounding the Export Finance Corporation of Canada, Ltd. Therefore, I appeal to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) of Canada to tell the House what is the status of this corporation since it stopped accepting new business since 1969, and why is it still in existence? Have the banks benefited from any tax write-offs by keeping it in existence even though it is doing no business at present? Since Canada is losing its fair share of exports on the world market, will this corporation be reactivated to finance and facilitate exports?

THE BUDGET-EFFECT ON INSURANCE POLICIES AND RETIREMENT SAVINGS PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak tonight on the effect of the budget on insurance
Adjournment Debate
policy holders, insurance companies and RRSP holders. I placed a question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) on December 2 regarding the effect of the budget's new tax measures on the ability of average Canadians to save through insurance and RRSP policies. The parliamentary secretary answered only the part of my question dealing with RRSPs. But what about insurance policies?
I was pleased to see that, on November 19, a Liberal backbencher, posed the same question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the minister stated:
I would be happy to consider any refinements that can be possible in these measures.
So I hope we will be hearing about some of these refinements tonight because there is considerable concern across the country at this devastating new tax.
Changes are needed now because average Canadians simply cannot afford these new taxes. They will cause higher unemployment, greater reliance on government operated pension plans, more welfare recipients, less self-initiative in general, because people can no longer attempt to fend for themselves, and here, Mr. Speaker, I offer a few examples of what individuals and insurance companies are saying about the new tax proposals:
As women now outlive men by an average of six or seven years, and inflation has led to a diminution of their available resources, industry has pointed out that 80 per cent of individual life insurance policies in 1980 were bought by people with incomes of under $25,000. If working guidelines around the arbitrary application of the accrual tax concept on both insurance and annuity contracts cannot be worked out a large supply of long-term capital for national development will disappear. Personal initiative to province income maintenance on death and retirement will be discouraged, leading to increased pressure on government and will aggravate Canada's ability to compete in world trade. The insurance industry will not be able to sustain its field or home office staffs. This will increase unemployment and, more importantly, harm millions of Canadians who cannot afford accountants and lawyers, but rely on our agents for counsel.
That is agents of insurance companies, Mr. Speaker. Here is a statement by a life insurance salesman who lives in Winnipeg. He states:
I am bound to protest against the recent budget proposals which single out for attack whole life insurance, which is the best means of protecting dependants against the premature death of the main supporter of the family.
As you know, many people, including government, have been expressing great concern about the elderly poor, especially widows. To the extent that new tax measures discourage the purchase of permanent life insurance there will be no more elderly poor and more widows who will be dependent on the taxpayer for support. I know of no other advanced country which attempts to tax the income on life insurance savings, an income which no one can touch during the lifetime of the policyholder, and if it is touched under the present system, the gain will be taxed. In other advanced countries the provision of protection to dependants through life insurance is positively encouraged, not discouraged.
As you know, permanent life insurance provides a means for gathering millions of small amounts of savings into large investment pools which have done much in the past to develop Canada. The inhibiting of these savings will slow down the development process.
If the government is really serious about being positive in its attempt to develop this country, it should be seeking to encourage savings through life insurance rather than by taking negative action to scare people away from protecting their families.

December 3, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Also, Mr. Speaker, I have received this from a constituent who is very concerned about these new tax measures, and she points out:
I can appreciate their attempt to close tax loopholes for the rich, but not threaten the financial security of millions of ordinary Canadians while all they are trying to do is save for retirement or an untimely death which could bring a great hardship on a young family.
Another constituent, an employee of an insurance firm, states:
There are three portions of the proposals which concern me particularly:
1.	The budget would require a policyholder to report accrued investment income on his or her policy or annuity every three years even though no income is actually received.
2.	A portion of many life insurance policies will be taxed on death-a proposal similar to one made in 1977 which on closer examination received the disrepute it deserved.
3.	In addition, the budget proposes that the amounts paid by employers for health and dental benefits be included in the taxable income of employees.
If deferred profit-sharing plans are virtually eliminated, this will affect many small-business owners and their families who are trying to build adequate retirement plans. Non-related DPSP employees will have their contributions reduced up to $2,000.
Interest on borrowed money for deferred income plans such as RRSPs and DPSPs will no longer be deductible.
It is vital that a concerted effort be made to persuade the government to desist from its apparent plan to discourage individual estate and financial planning. Many Canadians are proud enough to want to be totally independent and not have to rely on government welfare and pension plans, which are inadequate, unreliable and costly.
I hope we hear some words of encouragement from the parliamentary secretary tonight that the government is considering dropping these taxes on insurance policies.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE BUDGET-EFFECT ON INSURANCE POLICIES AND RETIREMENT SAVINGS PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to respond tonight to the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) because there are some misconceptions.
Some information has not been widely disseminated with regard to these two topics, RRSPs and whole life insurance, and I think it should be.
First of all, the budget makes no change in the amounts deductible as RRSP contributions. The only difference is that now there is no special incentive for borrowing money to make RRSP contributions, since the interest on money borrowed to put into an RRSP will no longer be deductible from noninvestment income. Individuals using their own funds, however, and investing these in RRSPs are not affected. Canadians can still obtain great benefits from contributing to RRSPs because of the deduction for the contribution itself. A person, for example, contributing $3,500 to an RRSP who is in a 25 per cent tax bracket will save $875 in taxes in the year that that contribution is made, which is a major saving.
The tax on accrual of investment income earned with life insurance policies will not affect the retirement savings of most Canadians. The investment income on life insurance policies purchased through RRSPs will continue to be sheltered from tax. For other policies many low and middle-income people will find that the investment income will not be taxed because of the $1,000 investment income deduction which is currently in the tax system. This deduction ensures that for taxpayers with no other investment income any amount of investment income from life insurance policies up to $1,000 will be exempt from tax in a year.
It is important to note that before the budget, many lower and middle-income individuals had to pay tax when they surrendered life insurance policies before death because all of the investment income was taxed at one time when it was taken out of the whole life policy. Now that income can be reported as it accrues, and it may escape tax completely because it is covered by the $ 1,000 per year investment income deduction.

Madam Speaker, it is appropriate that the House should be dealing with this motion today because it coincides with the release by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation of the latest statistics showing another sharp decline in housing starts. Today we are facing the worst housing crisis in the history of the country. It is perhaps without parallel since the Second World War. Today Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation reported another 30 per cent decline over one year in the number of housing starts.
We are told by none other than the minister responsible for housing himself, in a document which was leaked-the minister later tried to disown it but it has his signature on it; it was submitted to his cabinet colleagues-that we need 220,000 housing starts a year. We are told by the same authority that the best we can hope for is 135,000 housing starts. That is a shortfall of 80,000 housing starts. Included in that is the critical situation facing the country in rental accommodation.
We are told by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and by Statistics Canada that the major metropolitan areas of the country are now facing a zero vacancy rate. We have already arrived at that unhappy state in the city of Oshawa. We are close to it in the city of Toronto. We are almost there in the city of Calgary. If anyone reads this morning's Citizen, he will see we have practically arrived there in the city of Ottawa.
What does that mean? Let me again quote the authority of the Minister of Housing as contained in that famous leaked document. The minister predicted that this situation, this dire shortfall in rental accommodation in the country, would create a black-market situation. He even went so far as to talk about key money.
Anybody who remembers World War II will know what key money is. Key money is that black-market device whereby, if you are desperate for an apartment, you go to the doorman, give him $100, and in exchange for that $100 pay-off he will advise you that there is an apartment available. He will then take you to show you the apartment. For another tip, he will arrange to give you a lease on that apartment, in exchange for which you have to pay him every month you are there.
That is the black-market situation we are facing in this country which has been created by the deliberate negligence of this government.
