speechtext: To the knowledge of the government, during the past five years, did Canadian public officials or private individuals appear as guest speakers before the Soviet Institute of the U.S.A. and Canada and, if so, in each case (a) what was his/her name (b) was the speaking engagement solicited or did it occur as a result of an invitation from the Soviet authorities (c) were other Canadians, official or otherwise, present during the presentation and, if so, what were their names?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SOVIET INSTITUTE OF U.S.A. AND CANADA
speechtext:
To our knowledge during the past five years the only Canadian public official to appear as a guest speaker before the Soviet Institute of the U.S.A. and Canada was Mr. Ivan Head in 1977. Mr. Head at that time was the Prime Minister's foreign policy advisor. He was invited to speak before the Soviet Institute and to our knowledge no other Canadian public officials were present during this speaking engagement. In June, 1981, at the request of the Alberta government, Mr. Horst Schmidt, the Alberta minister of economic development, visited the Soviet Institute in question for discussions with its senior representatives. Three Canadian Embassy officers were present during this visit: Ambassador Geoffrey Pearson, Minister Counsellor Peter Hancock and Second Secretary Robert Poetschke.
Against this background, while agencies of the federal government, such as the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC), do have official exchange programs with the U.S.S.R. Academy of Sciences, a branch of which is the Soviet Institute of the U.S.A. and Canada, we do not have any specific exchange programs of an institution-to-institution nature with the Soviet Institute in question. As such there has not been a federally-sponsored program involving Canadian officials or private individuals either on exchange with or speaking at the Institute of the U.S.A. and Canada. We understand that there have been occasions over the past five years where on an ad hoc basis, private individuals or Canadian official exchangees doing research in Moscow, have been invited by the Soviet side to speak before the Institute of the U.S.A. and Canada. While it appears that in most cases these invitations have been initiated by the
December 4, 1981

Soviet side, there have been instances when Canadians visiting Moscow for business or touristic purposes have visited the Soviet Institute. Against this background it has generally not been the practice of the Institute of the U.S.A. and Canada to invite Canadian officials, including embassy representatives, to participate or sit in on these private visits or speaking engagements. In view of the personal and unofficial nature of these speaking engagements, the government considers that it would not be appropriate to identify the names of those individuals who have visited the institute.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
That this House condemns the failure of the government to foresee or avert the crisis facing the Atlantic fishing industry, regrets that Canadian-owned fish processing plants facing closure have not attracted the same active support from the government as have foreign multinationals in other parts of Canada experiencing similar difficulties, and urges the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to listen sympathetically and respond positively to the four Atlantic Ministers of Fisheries when he meets with them on Monday, December 7, 1981.
He said: Madam Speaker, the issue that is in front of the House today is extraordinarily important. The tragedy is that the situation that is facing the east coast fishery was clearly foreseeable. For many months the government has been in a position to know that some kind of plan of action had to be put in place. If one looks at the newspaper headlines from as early as August of this year, one will see that they are indeed enlightening. I quote from The Globe and Mail of August 13: "Fish production cuts widespread, east coast situation may get worse." August 12, The Globe and Mail: "National Sea Products to shut three major plants." Again in August: "National Sea shutdowns leave 1,800 out of work."
My colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), wrote to the government in August. The hon. member is a former minister of fisheries. An article in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald was headlined: "McGrath warns Atlantic fishery about to collapse." An item in the Financial Post was headlined: "Rough waters for fish exporters." More recently, on October 21, we see in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald: "Fishery hit hard by poor U.S. market." The October 21 edition of the St. John's Evening Telegram says: "Rompkey says Ottawa is prepared to help." That, of course, refers to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey). In October 17 The Globe and Mail we see an article headlined: "Hard times down east."
I am glad to see that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) has been able to return to the chamber because I know the minister is concerned. He has told us so. The minister knows there are problems in the east coast fishery because he has told us there are problems. As I said to the minister in committee earlier this week, a very great parliamentarian named Winston Churchill once said of problems: "Don't speak to me of problems, the problems will speak for
December 4, 1981

themselves; come up with a plan of action." This government has not come up with a plan of action. That is why it is to be condemned for a situation on the east coast which is getting worse and for which there is no response whatsoever from the Government of Canada.
The minister was in committee, as I said, where he told us what the problems are. He told us about the problems of marketing, commodity quality, problems over capitalization and the problems of too many licences and more fish plants being built than he thought was appropriate. However, during all this time, except for a short interruption, it has been the Liberal Party in power and this minister who has been the minister of fisheries.
There is no answer. We know there are plants facing imminent collapse in the Atlantic fishery. It is no secret that one company in Newfoundland is in critical condition. It is no secret either that that company has put before both the provincial government and the Federal government a plan of action which will require some support and help from both levels of government. I know the minister knows all about this. However, there are other plants the minister may be hearing about unless something is done.
It is incredible that after all these months the minister will only on this coming Monday get together with his provincial counterparts. When we asked him what he is going to say to his counterparts, what sort of plan of action he might put forward on behalf of the federal government, this is what he said:
But I intend to say to my provincial counterparts on Monday, and in fact to give them all the information we have, because I think there is a certain amount of misinformation floating around.
The minister smiles. There is always a certain amount of misinformation floating around, especially when ministers are making speeches.

When the opposition is asking questions, the misinformation is what comes back by way of answers. The minister is saying here that when he meets with the provincial ministers on Monday, he will give them all the facts. Isn't that interesting.
What facts does the minister think he can give them that they do not already have? Is he going to tell them there is a plant in imminent danger of collapsing because it does not have the financing it needs? Is he going to tell them that there are other plants that will be closing unless they receive help soon? Will he tell them that in Newfoundland there is 30 to 40 per cent unemployment in these areas? Is the minister going to tell them again that we should not catch so many fish or we should fix up the fish better before selling them?
Is the minister going to tell them what he told the world in his speech of October 3? Talk about misinformation. Everybody asks what was meant in that speech. The minister said we have to export less fish, or at least we need to have less people
Fisheries
exporting fish. The minister smiles. He says, "Yes, now the hon. member of the opposition has it straight." He says we have finally found out. He made the speech on October 3, but is only now getting it sorted out and only because we are asking questions. When the minister talks about misinformation, he adds to it.
What is the minister going to tell his provincial counterparts? Is he going to tell them that he intends to bring in legislation to cut down the number of exporters? What is his real position? Should we be exporting fewer fish or selling fewer fish? Should we not be selling more fish in more markets?
I can go along with the minister when he says there has to be better quality control. I understand, as does everyone else, including the ministers who will be meeting with him on Monday, that the American market is not what it was a few years ago.
What these ministers will want to hear is not what they already know. They are not coming to Ottawa to be told that there is a lot of misinformation floating around, as the minister told us in committee a few days ago. They will be coming to Ottawa to hear from the minister what is the federal approach. We have not heard that. We hope we will hear it today.
It is the responsibility of this government and this minister to tell us what is being done and to put a plan before the provincial ministers. No one is suggesting that this minister or the federal government must necessarily come up with all the answers or be fully responsible to do everything that is needed. But the federal government is the lead government in this matter. The federal government must present a plan. We want to hear from the minister today. We do not want any misinformation. The minister smiles. I do not know whether that is a smile of shame or anticipation. In either case, we will be grateful for some information today.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, it is not really a laughing matter; I know the minister knows that. The situation on the east coast is extraordinarily serious. We are not talking just about corporations; we are talking about people; we are talking about families; we are talking about men and women whose very livelihood and future are threatened. When one considers that the annual incomes of fishermen in Newfoundland, as a consequence of the very difficult time they are now facing, are down to around $4,000 a year, and that is including unemployment insurance, then we are facing not only an economic tragedy but a social tragedy.
We would like the minister to speak to us today and to tell us what he is going to do, Mr. Speaker. We do not need to be told what the problems are, we can see them. I would hope that the minister is not going to say that by asking questions we are spreading misinformation.

I do not know whether that was an attempt at humour on the part of the Chair or what, but it did disturb somewhat the excellent line of reasoning and logic that I was attempting to develop at the time. Mr. Speaker, whether we are talking about the east coast, with which I am less familiar, or the west coast, with which I am more familiar, the state of the fishing industry in Canada is deplorable. Whether we are talking about marketing, about too many vessels too highly capitalized chasing too few fish, or whether we are concerned about an extremely important problem facing the fishing industry on the west coast-and I am sure it is the same on the east coast-the problem is one of energy prices. The energy component in cost of doing business, of farming or even catching fish has been a serious disadvantage, a serious inhibitor and a serious income depleter of west coast fishermen, and I am sure energy costs also injure the east coast fishermen. The west coast fisheries has been in a crisis for a number of years. We now learn from recent events that there is an imminent crisis for the east coast fisheries.
I was about to say before the Chair rose on its own point of order that while we have learned that the lobster or inshore fishermen have done fairly well in Prince Edward Island this year, other fisheries have been far less successful. We have also learned from news reports and from questions posed in the House that there are a great number of processing plants that are being threatened in the Atlantic region. No one can treat these matters lightly, especially when we have an economy facing a recession. There are 128,000 fewer jobs available in Canada in all industries, including processing, manufacturing and the resources industries, than there were just three months ago. We are told marketing is down and we have too many people in the business. On the west coast, the Pearse commission has recommended a royalty in which the fishermen will be asked to finance themselves into oblivion through a buy-back program. We have a similar situation now happening in the east coast fisheries. It is odd that in the days when perhaps one third of the world goes to bed hungry every night, when we are beseiged by groups such as OXFAM and Save the Children, church agencies and other relief agencies, apparently we have a glut of fish on the east coast.
We have a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who goes to Nairobi and makes a speech at the alternative energy conference saying how much Canada needed and wanted to become involved in assisting the Third World. I am suggesting to hon. members that fish aid is one way to assist the elimination of a good deal of the world's hunger, disease, oppression, and perhaps even the rising militarism of the Third World. We need an expansionary budget policy not only in the fishing industry but to stimulate our whole economy, so that we might then be in a better position to assist the Third World.
December 4, 1981

Canadians are suffering through high interest rates and the lack of a visionary and expansionary budget. Not only the fishing industry but all segments of our economy suffer, from housing to manufacturing. Someone once said that if your neighbour loses his job, then you are in a recession; but if you lose your own, you are in a depression. In the last month 40,000 job opportunities have disappeared in this country.
I would just like to suggest that there is no point in looking for the villain of the piece much beyond the federal government. The federal government is the one that is and has been traditionally, historically and constitutionally responsible for fishing. Fisheries have almost entirely been under the jurisdiction of the federal government. If salmon stocks are down and enhancement programs are failing, the department has to close or threaten to close the Fraser river to 450 gill netters in my riding. This is because stocks are down, escapements are too low, or there is overfishing in one segment, overcapitalization and increased efficiency of gear used by modern fishermen. If there exist so many fish boats that they have to start buying them back with fishermen's money, on whom do we lay the blame? Don't blame me, I'm NDP!
I look forward, not just with interest but with fascination, to what kind of remedies the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) is prepared to propose to solve the very serious problem affecting not only the area from which I come but the area he represents. I know he will be hobbled in his efforts by lack of funds. He will be like the minister of housing; he will express all kinds of sympathy and he will ask everyone to accept it, but what they need is his help.
Whether or not the minister of housing knew about the budget in advance seems to be open to some question or dispute. At least on the night of the budget he said that he was very pleased he would not have to resign because he got through a program which, at its biggest, might provide 15,000 homes. He cut off all hope of increased rental accommodations. We in the Vancouver area could have used the 15,000 homes in Vancouver. He cut off all hope in my riding that there would be more rental units built soon.

This could be done, even if he had to do what was done

for Third World countries through powdered milk shipments; there has been a subsidy program for dried milk for years. The government must do something. The need is urgent. It is of crisis proportion.

I hoped it would be something more than sympathy or kind words. I anticipated that he would rise to tell us that he had convinced the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), who is also from the Atlantic provinces, that he will have to change some of the budget provisions and spring a little more money to assist because words will no longer solve complex problems. The government must do more than fine tune; it should reverse the direction of the mad lunacy of its economic policy which has brought the country virtually to its knees. I am referring not only to the fishing industry, but to the housing, agricultural, resource and marketing industries as well. In fact, today we heard talk about Uranium City.
In closing, may I repeat that we look forward with a great deal of anticipation, hope and even prayer that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans from the province of New Brunswick will, in his usual civilized and very eloquent way, lead us out of this fish wilderness into a new day of hope not only for Atlantic fishermen but for west coast fishermen as well.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the chance to make a few brief remarks before the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) replies. I am not an expert in fisheries. If any group is in need of help or assistance from the government and in need of some sympathy from the larger forces of public opinion outside the government, surely it is the fishermen of the country.
Recently as a member of the energy committee I met with some west coast fishermen of the UFAW in Vancouver. I personally heard their particular concerns. While they are fishing on the west coast, I think their concerns have relevancy to east coast fishermen with which this motion deals.
The motion refers to "the failure of the government to foresee or avert the crisis facing the Atlantic fishing industry." As the energy critic of the NDP, I wanted to raise this point before the minister replied. I am referring to the difficulties faced by fishermen because of energy costs. This was one of their concerns when I spoke with them in Vancouver. There was almost a desperate feeling at the meeting. I heard personally from trollers their concerns about great increases in energy prices and how they were being squeezed. They told me

Fisheries
that they could not really increase the price of fish, but they were being squeezed by costs, especially energy costs which were continually rising; eventually it will not be worth fishing. They told me about the difficulties. They mentioned the Pearse report and the difficulties concerning it.
I do not want to focus on that particular matter now, but I should like to focus on energy costs. Fishermen have told me that they are already suffering. We must remember that diesel fuel costs will rise greatly next year. They told me that there was some sort of a subsidy in gasoline at the present time. But my question is simple. Is the minister prepared to approach the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and ask him to revise his budget, and to ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to redistribute some of the $20 billion the government will receive from those energy agreements over the next five years? I am not referring to drivers of automobiles; perhaps they can look after themselves. It will be tough but they will have to do it. Some of the groups would be fishermen, farmers, and seniors who have to pay extra oil costs. Can we not do something to reduce energy costs to fishermen, perhaps by changing the federal tax paid on the diesel fuel oil that they use.
I hope the minister will not say that that cannot be done. Under Bill C-48 which we have been debating, Dome Petroleum and other companies like it will be given a 93 cents subsidy on every dollar spent on drilling. That is a massive subsidy. I am very familiar with the petroleum incentives program and under that program we will provide something like $2,000 million in subsidies over the next five years. That is nearly $3 billion, Mr. Speaker. Can we not do a little bit for the fishermen and help them with the cost of their fuel?
This motion stands in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) who has always shown great concern for the fishing industry and for the ordinary people of this country. His riding is neighbour to mine. I hope that in the course of his reply to that hon. member the minister will
announce some concrete proposals to help in this situation. Perhaps he could specifically address his remarks to the question of energy costs for fishermen. That is a problem about which I think something should be done.

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in some ways I wish that the debate were a little less formalized and that we could proceed with questions and answers. In many ways, there are a lot of questions to be asked on these issues. The motion stands in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser). I must confess that when I read it I was suprised to see that it begins as follows:
That this House condemns the failure of the government to foresee or avert the crisis facing the Atlantic fishing industry...
If there is one area in which I gave ample warning for years, it is in the area of the danger of returning to the boom or bust cycle, having experienced the bust cycle of 1973-74. In fact, I might tell the House that one of the people with whom I co-operated very positively at that time is the former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie).
When I inherited the fishery in 1974 there were two main problems. One was the low catch rate because of overfishing by foreign fleets, particularly off the northeast coast of Newfoundland and Labrador. The other problem was the low throughput in the processing plants. We addressed those two problems and if anyone bothers to read the policy document published in 1975, they will see that the first priority was the establishment of Canadian jurisdiction over the offshore zone, which meant that we would control the amount of fishing, the restoration of stocks and the stock expansion that followed. So I find that there is not very much substance to the charge of the opposition that we did not foresee the possibility of a crisis developing.
The record will show, and I will quote it, that I have publicly warned about the danger of overexpansion in the past few years and about the need for processing companies to get their act together in the highly competitive marketing field. Unfortunately many of my words fell on deaf ears.
On May 19, 1977, speaking in St. John's, Newfoundland, I pointed out that the new 200-mile zone, which many were hailing as opening the door to a huge fishing bonanza, was "less a pot of gold than a garden needing work and care." My actual words at the time were:
We are going to need great self-discipline to avoid repeating errors of the past: overcapacity, overlicensing, overfishing.
Later that year, speaking in Yarmouth, I expressed grave concerns about expanding the fleet, a move that was being pushed very hard, particularly by the provincial politicians and mainly in Newfoundland. I said on that occasion that "for advice on fleet expansion and the like, we look first to the state of the stocks and to the fishermen." I also said: "Even when we replace fishing units, we must make sure it is not disguised expansion." These were not isolated statements; I repeated them consistently, both in this House and elsewhere.
December 4, 1981

The federal government, with the responsibility for managing this country's ocean fisheries-and this was pointed out by the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose)-went to the limit of its mandate to attempt to keep the industry on an even keel. We said repeatedly that more discipline was needed in export marketing to compete with the single desk marketing operations of our Scandinavian competitors. But the processors told us bluntly: "Keep out of marketing, that's our business." So we kept out, and today that is where the most serious problems exist. Perhaps we should have insisted on getting involved in marketing at the government level. If we had, I am sure the screams would have been long and loud from our friends sitting on your immediate left, Mr. Speaker.
The record will also show that we have resisted the pressure for a massive expansion of the fishing fleet. We have deliberately held in check the growth of the offshore fleet. The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) should listen to that- we resisted the massive expansion of the offshore fleet. That was done with great difficulty in the face of the $900 million fleet expansion proposals announced with much fanfare by the provinces of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia at the time. I am not partisan, but one of those governments shared my political faith.
As another measure to attempt to keep the fleet's catching capacity in line with the available resource, we introduced the foot-for-foot replacement policy. Again, this policy was unpopular in many quarters, but if we had not stuck by our guns the present situation would undoubtedly have become much worse.
Fleet overcapacity is certainly a factor in the current situation on the Atlantic coast, just as it is on the west coast. A recent study of vessels fishing within 200 miles of Nova Scotia showed that if the fleet capacity were brought in line with the available resource, an annual saving of around $25 million could result. In other words, we have a sector of the fleet that is inefficient to the tune of $25 million.
The other major factor in the current situation facing the Atlantic fisheries is, of course, the overexpansion of the processing plants. I have some interesting figures regarding the growth of processing plants in Newfoundland. The minister of fisheries for Nova Scotia became quite indignant after reading only what the agencies carried, and with some reason, I think, because that province has kept the lid on its processing capacity rather successfully. I wish Newfoundland and Quebec had done the same. In 1973 there were 61 registered plants in Newfoundland. At the latest count that total has mushroomed to 225, a 269 per cent increase in 1973 and a 53 per cent increase since 1977. The federal government cannot be blamed for this state of affairs as plant licensing is strictly a provincial jurisdiction. I am not trying to pass the buck when I say this; I am trying to establish some facts. In fact, during the period 1977-79 my department received 48 requests from the province of Newfoundland for us to comment on new licensing applications. We advised against the licensing of 34 of the 48 on the grounds that the resource could not maintain that number. In spite of our advice, 22 of the 34 were built anyway.
Fisheries
Although there is no question that this mad rush to build processing plants in the mid and late seventies has substantially contributed to what is currently ailing the Atlantic fisheries, I can understand and, to a certain extent, sympathize with those in the provinces who are responsible for the decisions. The apparently rosy prospects for the fishing industry following the introduction of the 200-mile limit were obviously a great temptation to open the floodgates in provinces which were grappling with high unemployment and lagging economies. I am sorry that they did what they did, but at the same time, as I said, I can understand it. However, at the moment my sympathy cannot help the situation.
It is important to look back and assess the situation in which the Atlantic fishing industry found itself in 1977 when the 200-mile zone was brought in. In many ways, the industry was riding the crest of the wave. The resource picture was reasonably good. Fuel was comparatively cheap. There was no need to steam hundreds of miles to get to the resource, and our number one market was just across the border. Canada enjoyed huge advantages which most countries, and our competitors, did not enjoy, such as close proximity to the resource, close proximity to the market, and a good fishing tradition. Additionally, the infrastructure was all there, ready to be put to work. We already had overcapacity, and if ever an industry had a chance of a lifetime, surely that was it.
However, what happened in the space of four short years? I previously mentioned that one of the moves which courted disaster was overinvestment. However, that is not the only shortcoming that I lay at the door of the industry. Despite our pleadings, processors did not move in the direction of orderly marketing but continued to engage in destructive price undercutting among themselves. In fact, a good part of this year's problem was triggered as a result of dumping by competing processors in the U.S. market.
Again, in the face of repeated warnings and cajoling by my department, industry did not make a determined attempt to consistently market top quality products. The day has gone when our export customers or our domestic customers, for that matter, will accept anything that is put on the counters. Big fast-food chains, such as McDonald's, want fish of first quality, day in and day out, not just five days out of six. If they cannot get it from us, they will go elsewhere, and I am afraid that they do.
One can also lay a measure of blame on the industry for a lack of initiative and imagination concerning the introduction of new product lines. I imagine that is one of the reasons consumption of fish in Canada has dropped off somewhat lately. Again, this does not apply to all companies. As is evident, I believe, in the riding of the hon. member for South Shore, some have made very creditable efforts. Consumers are always looking for something different in their food diet, but I am afraid they are not getting too much from most of our major companies. However, we can only advise on this matter, we cannot direct.

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
I might add that officials from my department and officials from other governments have been thoroughly looking at the marketplace and its potential in recent years. However, when we have offered advice, I am afraid that in many cases it has been thrown back in our faces.
The motion before the House seeks to condemn the government for not providing active support for processing plants facing closure. By that, one supposes that the government is being criticized for not throwing a large sum of taxpayers' money into bolstering companies which are in difficulty. If that were the quick and easy way to solve the troubles of the fishing industry, then I imagine that I would be very enthusiastic about it. However, simply pumping money will not do the trick. We have surely learned that since 1974. That is not the panacea many people are seeking. It might be, perhaps, a band-aid solution, but it will not be a permanent cure. What is needed to cure the ills of the fishing industry is a basic restructuring, a reordering of the way we operate, in order to reduce input costs in relation to market prices, thereby increasing profitability.
When we look at the current fish export statistics, the picture does not look all that grim. For the first nine months of 1981, Canada's total fish exports were worth more than $1,100 million compared to $898 million for the same period last year, which means an increase of 22 per cent. At that rate, it looks as though we will once again hold the top spot in world fish exporting. We will be the main fish exporting nation for 1981.
Here are some figures for the same nine-month period. Exports of fresh and frozen seafish, whole or dressed, are up 32 per cent in quantity and 24 per cent in value, while exports of fresh and frozen seafish, fillets and blocks, total 130,000 tonnes valued at $330 million, compared to 118,000 tonnes and $282 million last year. Exports of smoked, salted and cured fish increased by 21 per cent in quantity and 35 per cent in value. Canned fish exports are 12 per cent higher over this period last year.
If these export totals are coming up consistently higher than last year-and let it not be forgotten that exports are the life blood of the Canadian fishing industry

then one might be excused for asking why so many of our fish producers are in trouble. If the catch is up and the prices are up, then the problem obviously lies in weaknesses and inefficiencies in the processing and marketing structure. Certainly, high interest rates and a soft U.S. market are contributing factors to the current situation over which we have little or no control. However, a large proportion of the problem is one which is within our power to control. I might say that the problems began to emerge before high interest rates reached the level that we saw some eight or nine months ago.
How, then, will we tackle the problem? The motion before us asks that I listen sympathetically and respond positively to the four Atlantic ministers of fisheries when we meet on Monday of next week; but I hope their suggestions will be a little more constructive than the ideas which they were espousing a few years ago. However, I intend to do more than be a sympathetic listener. Contrary to what one may have been led
to believe from the remarks of the hon. members opposite, for weeks officials of my department have been concentrating their efforts on the best ways to restore the Atlantic fishery to the state of health it should and could be enjoying. I will be placing a number of options before the provincial fisheries ministers from the Atlantic coast which could be undertaken to set us on the road to recovery. They are not stop gap measures but, rather, moves that should be of long-term benefit to the industry.
I would now like to mention some of those possible options. One option, obviously, would be for the government to become directly involved or take equity in an integrated fishing company in order to learn, and also possibly to forestall an undesirable level of concentration. Another suggestion would be the nationalization of the offshore fleet to prevent large, integrated companies from exercising excessive influence over the supply of raw material and to introduce, as I said when I related some earlier figures, an element of rationalization and efficiency in the catching of offshore fish.
There are those who say that government should be a participant but not a total shareholder. That option, which I call the Panarctic model, could be one of the midway points in any decision we could reach. Obviously, we must rationalize the capturing of fish and avoid the sort of mad race for the fish that we saw last winter.
With the permission of the House, I would like to call it one o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, when we rose for lunch I had indicated a number of possible actions which I would be discussing with my provincial counterparts and with different segments of the industry. I would hope members of this House, as we come to this House for legislation, if and when that legislation is required, will support our position.
I had talked about suggestions that had been made for perhaps direct government intervention in some processing enterprise. As well perhaps the fleet should be brought together under one management system or possibly a mix of government and industry participation in order more properly
December 4, 1981

to utilize the existing capacity, and possibly reduce it in some cases.
I had started to talk about the rationalization of the harvesting capacity. A suggestion which is being looked at very seriously is one of allocating the offshore quota to participating companies on a share basis which would allow them to make their plans for harvesting and resist the traditional race for the fish which, as we saw last winter, brought about some of our present difficulties. In some cases we may want to reduce the size of the fleet. This appears to apply to the west coast fisheries. This, of course, is a program which would be undertaken in full consultation with fishermen and fishing enterprises.
There has been some suggestion that the small and medium-size processors lack the capacity to play a role in the offshore and perhaps by getting together in some consortia arrangement this would be a good way of allowing them to participate, yet not have everyone buying capacity or aggravating the fleet problem.
As far as the distribution of fish among processors is concerned, we could go for organized and national harvesting. There are those who suggest auctions as a method of making fish available to those processors who do not want to buy large trawlers.
It has been suggested that we look at reducing the cost of fuel to increase our competitiveness. I must say that this appears on the surface to be rather attractive. However, I have to say that the implication for all Canadian industry is pretty serious if we do go to one industry. There is already an effort to help fishermen and farmers with the cost of fuel, and certainly in relation to our competitors we do enjoy advantageous fuel costs.
There is one area in which some movement is necessary, and this is the area of rechanneling investment in processing. I am a believer of modernizing existing capacity, not increasing it. In many cases plants can be made quite competitive and profitable by upgrading. We have already started working with DREE in this endeavour in quite a few areas. I hope we can negotiate a federal-provincial agreement to limit the capacity of the processing sector. I know that some provinces have voluntarily restrained the processing capacity movement, but I will be taking a much firmer line on this issue to my provincial counterparts. Some are advocating foreign investment, not so much control but equity in operation, which in some cases would perhaps give us access to markets which we have traditionally been unable to enter. This will be the subject of considerable discussion in the months to come.
I have to say a word about the improvement of quality and quality consistency. We have insisted on putting some money into this program and have been quite successful in some areas. I have written to my provincial counterparts under whose jurisdiction this matter rests and asked them to regulate the landing of fish so that at least fish would be landed in the best condition, preferably bled and gutted. I will be discussing
Fisheries
this matter with the provincial ministers next Monday. To discuss this issue when so many other industries have set standards which they meet consistently shows that we still have some way to go. For example, I ask hon. members if we could even consider that non-pasteurized milk be put on the market without some considerable consumer resistance. I am not saying that fish which is sold in Canada is bad, but that we do not have a system which guarantees absolutely consistent high quality. Surely this must be a goal which we must seek.

speechtext:
My colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), says we should have "Canada approved." Certainly we should have "Canada approved" and we do, to some extent. However, the standard can be higher than that which we have thus far maintained.
Another question I would like to deal with is market discipline and market orderliness. I have no doubt that jawboning is not going to be sufficient in this area. Some sectors of the industry have already indicated that they believe that this is not only inevitable but desirable. Only through some legal framework which forces discipline will companies not be tempted to undercut each other in the marketplace.
I might say that the hon. member for Vancouver South has tried to make me sound as if I were against an increased effort in marketing. Obviously he knows that this is not what I was suggesting. I was suggesting that we should do the same as our best competitors-particularly the Scandinavians-to get a number of people marketing as a group, as Canadians. In some cases, of course, there may be up to six or eight partners in one marketing organization.
But the philosophy that we must catch every fish in the sea is also one that must be carefully considered. This year I advanced the idea to the industry that we should perhaps catch according to the market potential and market predictions. These quotas could always be adjusted during the season if the estimates are low. Some countries have been doing this very successfully.
Within the framework of these policies, we must make room for the protection of the small processor and the small operator. I have no doubt that whatever co-ordinated marketing effort comes about, there has to be one location where the small operators can find a haven without having to be forced into working with a major player who would, of course, overshadow him.
An hon. member has mentioned the use of fish as food aid. We are using some now and will be using more in the future and my cabinet colleagues have responded favourably to this policy. One of the difficulties is that some countries are not equipped with the holding facilities necessary to distribute and handle certain species of fish, especially program products. We are talking increasingly with CIDA about producing and preparing for the food aid program, particularly using saltfish which does not require the same amount of conservation expense.
13744

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
Over-the-side sales for species of fish in which the Canadian industry has very little interest must become organized and not left to the whims of people who may have a market because they have a relative in some part of the world. I believe if the industry stopped having a total knee-jerk reaction to this question but came in with the government in a joint operation where we could take advantage of certain markets where vessels are used to freeze fish bought directly from our fishermen, we might be able to gain some considerable advantage. I am amazed at those who advocate that Canadian fishermen should be total prisoners of the local fish merchant and that somehow it is immoral if we let those who want to come in from offshore buy about 2 per cent of the fish that we have on the east coast. I can tell the House that the fishermen do not consider it immoral. In fact, in some cases it is the only weapon they have to negotiate.
Of course, there are those who say that you can bust your way into the markets of the world, that you do not have to have agreement with the Common Market or an arrangement with foreign nations because somehow Providence has ordained that the world must buy our fish. I am afraid that is a very naive outlook. The idea that somehow it is not right for foreigners to buy fish from Canadian fishermen, possibly using their vessels to freeze fish in some cases-again in a very well controlled situation-that somehow we are betraying the plant workers, to me is akin to saying that we must have the largest warehouses in the world filled to capacity regardless of whether we have the markets.

I thank hon. members. I will finish by briefly saying that the options I have listed are being examined and discussed and we have had good working sessions with the Fisheries Council of Canada and with representatives of the industry. The problem is not new but was recognized. In some cases it has taken a more dramatic form and we are now trying to address that situation. In fact, it is only in the last week to ten days that we have had firm proposals.
As far as the federal jurisdiction is concerned, where we are responsible for the setting of quotas and their allocation through the licensing system, and for the establishment of the fleet capacity and its impact on the market, I think we have fulfilled our role well. In the two areas which escape our jurisdiction, namely the processing capacity and quality control-however, in quality control we share a joint role- unfortunately we have not had full co-operation.
That being said, the policy of trying to establish a vigorous fisheries industry which has professional fishermen, that is, people who do not see it as employment as a last resort, but people who invest their livelihood and skills into fulfilling what
is a very rewarding profession when it is managed properly. That remains the goal of this government.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the limited time that I have available to me this afternoon, I have somehow to resist the temptation to respond to all of the areas covered by the minister in his speech. There is one area, perhaps, which I will not go into right now but requires some passing comment. It is the last comment the minister made with respect to the over-the-side sales. He said that these must become organized and that companies must get involved.
I merely want to remind the minister that during our administration we put together a rational over-the-side sales policy which included all the players and had the support of all the players. Unfortunately, it was scrapped by the minister when he resumed his responsibility of Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. I say that with sadness because if he had continued he would not have been in the' difficulties in which he found himself last summer. But perhaps he likes to be in difficulty.
We meet here today in this debate in the midst of a crisis situation which is, in my opinion, unprecedented and unparalleled. A recent publication from the Canadian Institute for Economic Policy by Professor Donald J. Patton of Dalhousie University which arrived on my desk yesterday said this:
The Atlantic fishery is currently facing serious problems, with almost all major companies suffering substantial losses on their fishing operations. Poor markets, high interest rates and unprofitable fishing have led to widespread production cuts. Hundreds of employees have been laid off through plant shutdowns in a region of the country that already has high unemployment. But while there appears to be no immediate relief in sight, these problems should not obscure the long-term value and importance of the fishery as an industry-
Then he went on to say:
It is becoming increasingly clear that unless difficult policy choices and actions are taken now, Canadians will not fully benefit from the future development of their fishing industry.
When the minister spoke today we expected that he would take the House and the country into his confidence and let us hear about some of these difficult choices. We all agree they are difficult choices. Unfortunately, all we heard was the minister's usual song: blame others, blame the provinces, blame the processors, absolve yourself.
The minister reminds me of Alice in Wonderland. He is there, but he does not quite know what is going on around him. As the Mad Hatter said, it gets curiouser and curiouser.
A few days ago in this House my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), put a question to the minister with respect to the plight of one of the companies referred to by Professor Patton. He talked about the fact that this company was in serious difficulty and that unless it heard from the minister within the next few days with regard to a proposal it had before the government, it would be forced to close down. That shutdown would result in the lay-off of 2,500 people directly employed by that company and 1,600 fishermen who depend on that company.
December 4, 1981

1 am sorry the hon. member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) is not in his seat. If that company goes under, that spells doom to nine towns in Newfoundland, most of which are in the riding of Burin-St. George's. It will be a death sentence to the towns of Bonavista, Grand Bank, Fortune, Burgeo and Gaultois, and I could go on. Nine towns in the province of Newfoundland with a total population in excess of 20,000 depend exclusively on this company for employment. This company has a payroll in excess of $40 million.
I do not believe the minister is taking this seriously. If that were the only company in trouble, I suppose the proposal could be seen in isolation; but we cannot look at it in isolation because the minister and all of us know there are other companies in trouble. Other companies have proposals before the government to bail them out. We are talking about an industry that is totally Canadian owned, an industry which employs in its fish plants over 8,000 people, an industry which owns a fleet of 150 trawlers employing over 3,000 trawlermen, and an industry which produces over $500 million in goods and services in the Atlantic provinces.
We are talking about the keystone of the very fragile and weak Atlantic provinces economy. That places a particular responsibility on the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc). We are entitled to expect some direction from him. We are entitled to expect some indication of assistance from him. He talks about band-aid treatment. He says he will not give in to band-aid treatment, and that is how he describes an infusion of capital. He talks about long-term solutions. Unless he applies band-aid treatment now, he can forget long-term solutions because many of these companies will be forced to close their doors, and in the process we will lose what is left of the most important and, indeed, the only important market we have, the United States market.
Where does the minister sit? He is a member of the inner cabinet. He was a party to the decision to bail out Chrysler, a multinational employing Canadians. I make no comment on that. He was a party to the decision to bail out Imperial Oil, another multinational, again employing Canadians. I make no comment on that. He was there when the government bailed out Massey-Ferguson. He was there when the government wrote off over $100 million for some obscure computer company of which we had never heard.
Where is he when the Atlantic provinces fishing industry is bleeding to death and is on its knees? He does not take the industry seriously. He thinks it is bluffing. He referred to that in his speech today. Every time the industry gets into trouble, it comes with cap in hand to the federal government. That may have been true in the past. That has happened before. It has happened several times before. It has not happened since the declaration of the 200-mile economic zone. It has happened now because of circumstances beyond the control of the industry, such as high interest rates, a softening of United States markets, increased competition as a consequence of the strengthening of the U.S. dollar, the weakening of European currencies and a change in consumer habits in the United States market.
Fisheries
We all saw it coming. The minister says he saw it coming. The minister says he warned the industry about a boom-and-bust psychology. He saw this coming and did nothing. What happened last summer when the Nickerson National Sea organization announced it was closing down three major plants, one in Nova Scotia, one in New Brunswick and one in Newfoundland, because it could no longer afford to carry inventories due to interest rates? That was in August. The minister knew, as we all did at that time, that that was merely the beginning and that the closing down of these Nickerson National Sea plants would set off a chain reaction, and it did. At one point in time, in my province alone, over 15 fish plants were down. It happened to coincide with a failure in the inshore fishery in many areas. The minister probably will come back with statistics to refute that, but let him tell that to the inshore fishermen who have to get by with little or nothing this year. It coincided with the failure of the inshore fishery, but the fact is that at that time the minister had a responsibility to move in and he did not. He did nothing.
I and others asked him to sit down with the industry because in that industry there are people who are highly professional and highly qualified. There are highly professional and skilled people within the various provincial fisheries departments. I know from my own experience with the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans that there are highly skilled professionals who are probably the best fish managers in the world. I get the impression that the minister sat there in isolation and did not take their advice. Perhaps he even refused to see them. Certainly he refused to sit down with the minister of fisheries for Newfoundland who repeatedly requested meetings with him. I think in his entire tenure since 1980 he has had only one or two meetings with the minister of fisheries for Newfoundland. Indeed, during that period he has had only one meeting with the Atlantic provinces ministers. Granted, there is a meeting taking place on Monday or Tuesday in Ottawa with the Atlantic provinces ministers and the minister responsible from Quebec. I maintain that meeting is six months too late; it should have taken place late last summer or early last fall. We have lost valuable time.
Basically we are facing the problem which speaks to the need for market diversification. The minister talked about quality control. Certainly we need to improve the quality of our fish. We need to put in place incentives to produce better quality fish. However, the bottom line is that unless we diversify and reduce our dependence on the U.S. market, there will be more trouble down the road. All the band-aids or long-term solutions in the world will not address the problem.
This is not the time to talk about a reduction in production capacity or a reduction in fleet size. I was hoping the minister would talk about the problems of fleet renewal. Most of these companies face that problem. Many trawlers are out of date, antiquated and have to be renewed.
We talk about overproduction capacity. The minister cannot, like Pontius Pilate, reach for the silver bowl and

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
absolve himself irrthat area. No, he cannot absolve himself from responsibility. The minister has the power, which has been described as a draconian power, under the Fisheries Act totally to manage the industry. He has no power to manage or license plants on shore. However, the fact is that if we had a rational system of fisheries management where you do not have a boom-and-bust catching situation, the plants would not have to expand in order to accommodate that. This is part of the problem, what we used to call the glut, except it is a man-made glut.
Why does the minister not sit down when putting together a fisheries plan and rationally discuss this with the fish processors, the fisheries unions and the provinces? The minister knows where I stand on jurisdiction. He knows full well that fisheries management can no longer be the sole prerogative and responsibility of the federal government, constitutional rights notwithstanding.
The minister has to share those managerial responsibilities with the provinces, the producers, the representatives of the fishermen, whether it be the Newfoundland Fish Food and Allied Workers or the fisheries associations of the maritime provinces. He has to take them into his confidence if we are going to have a situation that is orderly fisheries management in the Atlantic provinces.
The minister has finally succeeded in antagonizing everyone. He has everyone against him including the fishermen's unions, the fishermen's associations, the fish processors and the provincial governments. Why? Because the minister has chosen in the midst of the worst crisis to face the industry to sit in his ivory tower in Ottawa and pretend that everything is fine. It is business as usual-don't get excited, don't make any waves.
I expected the minister to come to my province when these plants closed down last summer, and most are still down, and meet with the government, the Newfoundland fishermen's union and the processors. He had a chance encounter with them when he was in Marystown to preside over the launching and christening of a new fisheries patrol vessel which I had directed to be built in Marystown. He had a chance encounter, and a very unsatisfactory one at that. He does not have to take my word for this; he need only talk to the members of the Newfoundland fishermen's union, the processors and the people along the south coast of Newfoundland to know how totally unsatisfactory that encounter was and how totally unsatisfied they were with the responses they received from the minister.
All the minister does is muse and philosophize when the situation requires action, action which this minister has the power to carry out. He talks about basic restructuring and exports. Why has the minister not been able to get guarantees from the European Economic Community? It is not enough that we should allocate quotas within our zone. I agree with him that may be necessary in order to break through the tariff barrier which now discriminates against Canadian fish. However, if that is necessary, it should only be done with guarantees. At this point in time we do not have the guarantees.
Why can the minister not get the support of the Government of Canada? If the British government is providing opposition and giving him problems, why does not the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talk to Margaret Thatcher? Their industry in terms of their total economy is not nearly as important as ours, especially in the case of the Atlantic provinces. I am sure the British government would be reasonable if they had a responsible approach from the Government of Canada.
We know full well that the German fleet is tied up with no place to fish. That should be our ace in the hole, but we have not been able to use it effectively. In my opinion, we have not been able to deal effectively with the opposition we are receiving in Brussels from the British government. That is the responsibility of the minister and his colleagues in cabinet, and nobody else.
Who is responsible for the high interest rate situation today? The Government of Canada. Who is responsible for the failure to diversify our marketing opportunities? The Government of Canada. Who is responsible for failing to meet with the industry and the provincial governments and look for and accept their advice? The government that has the major responsibility under the Fisheries Act and under the Constitution of Canada, the Government of Canada.
It is not enough to go on attacking provincial colleagues and blaming the provinces and processors, blaming everyone but yourself. The fact is it is this minister who got us into this mess. All is not hopeless, all is not lost; he still has the power to get us out of it. But I am not sure he fully appreciates or understands the seriousness of the situation.
The Lake Group may be forced to close its operation if it does not hear within the next few hours a positive response from the Government of Canada. Not only the Lake Group, but many major processing companies in the Atlantic provinces are facing the same problems, such as cash flow problems, marketing problems and bank problems. They are heavily into the banks. How long are the banks expected to carry on? How long will this minister continue to allow the banks in Montreal and Toronto to call the shots in the Atlantic provinces? We have an intolerable situation which I do not believe this minister fully appreciates.
During my brief tenure as minister of fisheries, I set up on the coast of British Columbia an advisory council that I could deal directly with and receive policy advice from. Even the minister admits that has worked well. That was the first of three advisory councils we were to establish, one in British Columbia, one in the maritime provinces and one in Newfoundland. Just like the over-the-side sales policy we put together, the minister threw that out the door as well. If we had that mechanism in place today and a minister who was prepared to listen, I suspect we would not be in the mess we are at the present time. This minister does not fully appreciate the gravity of the situation that we face in Atlantic Canada today.
December 4, 1981
