speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a debate like the one we are having this afternoon clearly confirms the interest of the members of this House in an industry that is extremely important to Canada, namely the fisheries industry, and I believe that both the government members and the opposition parties realize that the basic purpose of today's debate is to find positive solutions to providing for a genuine renewal of our fisheries industry.
I listened earlier to the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), Newfoundland, and I could not help smiling when he referred to various measures that should be taken, because I remember that when he was Minister of Fisheries, he gave permission for trawlers of 100 feet and over to fish in the Gulf of the St. Lawrence. In my constituency, the gulf means 400 miles of coast line, from Sept-Iles to Blanc-Sablon, including Anticosti Island. Obviously that decision was severely criticized by the inshore fishermen. What we are trying to
Fisheries
do today is to define ways of helping fishermen. There is a danger, when discussing the fisheries industry, of always thinking in terms of profits for the large processors, and forgetting the fishermen. In fact, throughout his speech, with only a few exceptions, the hon. member to whom I was listening spoke in generalities and blamed the department and the minister for the present situation in the fisheries industry.
I think it would be somewhat overconfident to say merely that the fisheries industry is doing as well as any other industry. Everyone knows what the world economic situation is like, and obviously the fisheries industry is just as sensitive to national and world development problems as other industries are. Now, what do we have to do? Trying to evaluate the situation is one thing, but finding solutions is an entirely different kettle of fish!
This morning and this afternoon, the minister talked about programs for restructuring the fisheries industry. I think there is an interesting aspect to this subject and it would perhaps be useful to invite the opposition parties, the fishermen and the co-operatives and processors to think about what is involved in restructuring the fisheries industry. In Quebec there is an additional problem because responsibility areas tend to overlap. I purposely included fishermen, co-operatives and processors, and I feel we should also involve the provinces in defining responsibility areas, because this is truly a field where all concerned should not only be consulted but should also have a say in the matter, if we are to draft legislation and regulations that will help fishermen to truly develop the industry within this sector. Of course, I could speak about fisheries throughout Canada, but I should like to see the Department of Fisheries focus its concern a little more on my part of Quebec's middle and lower north shore, because it is a region that is anxious to see a renewal of the fisheries industry.
The minister talked about thoroughly reorganizing the department and the fisheries industry, and although we do not necessarily want to be the ones to initiate such changes, neither do we want to be a step behind. We want to be treated as equal partners and we want to get our point of view across. In this respect, I must congratulate the minister who, during his eighteen months in office, has helped us tremendously to modernize our fishing facilities. When discussing fisheries or any other subject, it is very easy to talk in generalities, because in the final instance, everyone is for motherhood and against sin. Helping people is fine, but hitting on the best way to do this is another story, and I must admit that in this particular area the present minister has done excellent work in our region. I know that the member for St. John's East, Newfoundland, is familiar with my area-his sector is not very far from mine-because once you get to Blanc-Sablon, you are just opposite Sainte-Barbe, and I think the people in Old Fort Bay, Middle Bay and Saint-Paul often deal with Newfoundland.

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
In this easternmost part of Quebec, the problem is the lack of infrastructures for fisheries. There is also the marketing aspect, how to sell the fish, but if we do not have the infrastructure, our fishermen today will never be able to bring new life to the fisheries industry or be able to interest the younger generation in the industry. I see my colleague from Bonaventure-iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bujold) who also obtained funds through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in order to provide for appropriate facilities for the fisheries industry in his area, and that, too, is a tremendous boost for the Fisheries industry, not only in eastern Quebec but throughout Canada.
Another positive contribution is the fact that DREE is working together with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to provide comprehensive assistance projects. And I say this with great feeling today, because the north shore fisheries have always been neglected, and we want to put an end to this, because we have people who are highly motivated to develop this sector, and we shall no longer let ourselves be victimized- I agree with the hon. member for St. John's East, Newfoundland-by the big processors who are rushing to apply for large grants in order to build even bigger ships to provide work for a few highly modernized, very well equipped, even too well equipped fishermen, while our inshore fishermen are left to fend for themselves. Our inshore fishermen must come first on our list of priorities.
I would now like to talk about the role of research in bringing about a renewal of the fisheries industry. No one has mentioned research yet. Nevertheless, it should be one of the department's principal tools for considering solutions for the future. I think Canada is particularly fortunate in having oceans to the north, south and west: the Arctic, the Pacific and the Atlantic. We have a resource that belongs to all Canadians, and we still tend to be very conventional in how we make use of that resource. Our universities should be given a chance to develop an interest in modern approaches to the fisheries industry and to look for ways of making us far more competitive, not only on national but also on international markets.
Now that the Gulf region is gaining its own identity, I would also invite the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) to try and set aside a specific location in the Gulf area for research in Quebec. As you know, the people of Quebec have traditionally been fishermen and the Gaspe Peninsula depends on the sea and on fishing, as do the Magdalen Islands and the north shore. We would like to be able to increase our presence in the Canadian fishing industry. We shall be able to do so if the government gives us the means to be very active in the field of research. I wanted to say this because this sector has perhaps been left to cope for itself in the past. We have been content with unsophisticated fishing methods, but to be able to compete with Scandinavian and northern countries, we
need extremely sophisticated techniques in the fishing industry.
Another basic element, Mr. Speaker, is information. In my own region, we know that information is distributed, but its quality and regularity could be increased. Our fishermen, whether in Blanc-Sablon, La Tabatiere, Old Fort Bay, Middle Bay, Saint-Paul, Harrington Harbour, Cheverie, Natashquan or Riviere-au-Tonnerre, do not have enough information, and in this regard, if I may make another positive suggestion to the Minister, I would ask him to co-operate with the Department of Employment and Immigration to hold winter courses which are better adapted to the needs of our fishermen, as they have perhaps more time in that period of the year to receive information from his department. It is often said that information is power, the newspapers being called the fourth estate. I believe that it would be a good thing for the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to provide this power for our own fishermen. I say this because it is a comment which I heard during our travels along the middle and lower shore. The fishermen want to fish regularly, they are not lazy as is often suggested in the industry, but they would like to be in constant communication with the department because when comes the time to innovate and to create, they would truly be well informed and would achieve a major sense of self-fulfillment and commitment, as well as greater co-operation with the department.
Another element which concerns my area and which will certainly interest the hon. members opposite, especially those from Newfoundland, is the question of quotas. In this regard, I believe that the department does not deserve to be congratulated because, while we are very proud of our minister and even of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans officials, a major mistake was made this year when setting the quotas, and as a result a ban on fishing has to be imposed at the beginning of October. A week later, the department reconsidered its decision and said that there was no problem and that fishing could continue. In our region, this brought about the early closing of some fish processing plants. I wonder, Mr. Minister, if it might not be advisable to have separate quotas for the province of Newfoundland and for the province of Quebec, at least for that zone of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, so as to make sure that there is no conflict between the quotas of either province. Of course, any man fishing with a trawler of 100 feet or more and working with the latest in the way of fishing gear is way ahead of a competitor using traditional fishing methods. I draw that to the attention of the minister and, if possible, I would like to hear his ideas on that because, with respect to quotas, the fishermen are not on the same footing, and I think it is important to do justice to our inshore fishermen.
Another point I would like to raise has to do with the quality and processing of the fish and the new plan. I think that the department wants to innovate in fisheries, not only in Quebec
December 4, 1981

but in all fishing zones in Canada generally. In Matane this week officials of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans held an important meeting with groups of fishermen, and the minister gave them a few reports to look over, and those fishermen and those associations made a few remarks to the minister. I hope that the time for meetings is not over or drawing to a close, but that such meetings will only be suspended for a while and that the minister will take concrete measures to implement his policies.
I know that DREE is willing to invest fairly large sums of money in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and that people are ready for action. We must not try to do everything at once of course, but we must take one step forward because if we do not stop consulting people right and left, both at the federal and the provincial levels, we risk discouraging the fishermen. The people want to feel that the department and the minister are willing and ready to act. They have to get this feeling otherwise the fishermen will no longer show their good faith and willingness because they will be inclined to say: it is always the same thing, we always get the same statements and we are no longer interested in co-operating with the department.
So I would urge the minister, after the Matane meeting, to get things moving, to free some funds so that in 12 to 18 months from now, we may see the results of his political will. One last point, because I think my time is almost up, concerning the responsibilities of the federal fisheries department and the provincial level. It is crucial, Mr. Speaker, that the spheres of authority of all parties involved be clearly defined and identified. We are quite happy that the constitutional debate is over, but it is most important, now that there will be negotiations on the distribution of power that the definition and the limitations of all governments be clearly identified, otherwise it becomes a buck-passing game in which each side says : this is a provincial responsibility or this is a federal responsibility and the buck goes back and forth. We have to put an end to this administrative buck-passing game and define clearly the spheres of authority of each party and of each institution involved.
I have here a book written by an author from Sept-Iles on the North Shore, Louis-Armand Santerre, entitled "De Sept-Iles a Blanc Sablon, 750 kilometres par voie d'eau." The book explains or tells the history of the Quebec lower and mid North Shore, which covers half of my riding of Manicouagan.
I would urge the speakers who will follow me to make down-to-earth statements because some of the people I am talking about, do not even have a television set and come from a long line of fishermen. That is most unfortunate because often, when listening to hon. members and even to ministers during our proceedings in this House, we get a feeling that things are being said generally, vaguely, so that ultimately no one in particular is concerned and no specific guidance is given to those who will have to decide on the measures to be taken to
Fisheries
find solutions to present problems in the fishing industry. I am being explicit because our people have to know, to hear exactly what solutions are being put forward by the opposition. I myself, as a member of the party in power, am trying to be critical of the department itself while avoiding sterile speeches condemning this or that individual. What is important is finding solutions. I insist that hon. members who speak after me must concentrate on solutions.
All hon. members must denounce the problems facing us, that the fishing industry is now up against. But the people of whom I spoke a while ago would like to hear from those hon. members who are directly concerned with fisheries what proposals and solutions are possible. That is very important, because in our meetings with our constituents these bread and butter issues are always being raised. Here, we hear very seldom about them. We hear a lot about hon. members' pious wishes and good intentions, as well as their rather vague ideas, but nobody ever really tries to define the problem. What I should like the minister to tell me is how we are going to proceed to modernize our fishing gears? How, with the assistance of our universities, are we going to develop new techniques to catch and condition fish? What new techniques could we develop? How could we secure the co-operation of universities, co-ops, industries, fishermen and the various provincial governments? How could we ease the regulations to make it easier for fishermen to get out there and catch fish? How could we guarantee fishermen a minimum income, when it is not possible to extend the scope of the Canadian Saltfish Corporation Act over a wider territory than the one already identified?
Could we not set up for the fishing industry something similar to the Canadian Wheat Pool as we did for wheat, to guarantee our fishermen income stability, because the problem of this industry stems from the fact that there is no income security there, a factor which discourages our youth from joining the industry, while western farmers enjoy income security thanks to a relevant legislation. Fishermen in my area do not have income security and certainly would like to get it. The whole issue of unemployment insurance benefits for seasonal fishermen is being raised again: they will try to find ways to find additional income. That is why I wanted to call hon. members' attention to this problem. I am aware that my time has run out, but I merely wish that by next year, we might have taken a step forward in the right direction. I am most grateful to hon. members for listening to me and to you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to express my views.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this special debate which I hope will highlight the financial crisis which presently faces the east coast fishing industry. I submit to you, sir, that it is a great day in the life of anyone when he can go fishing. This

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
activity, whether it be for pleasure, protein or profit, is being seriously restricted at the present time in Atlantic Canada. This is a fact which the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) learned firsthand in November when he had the pleasure of visiting my riding and I had the honour of hosting the visit.
Within the past week, those of us in the official opposition who are interested in the problems facing the fishing industry met with the leaders of this industry from the Pacific region, from New Brunswick, from Prince Edward Island, from Nova Scotia and Quebec as well as Newfoundland. All of these people told the same story, that unless a miracle occurs between now and the end of June, 1982, the entire industry on both coasts faces complete and total financial collapse.
When we consider the number of people, towns, cities, villages and auxiliary industries that are dependent on the fishing industry, this is truly a startling revelation. Many of us who have been associated with the industry for a long time knew from firsthand knowledge that all was not well in certain sectors of it, but few of us realized the depth of despair and the pessimistic outlook which was portrayed by industry leaders.
Despite a remarkable resource development and recovery since the 200-mile limit was declared in 1977 and a favourable outlook for further stock growth of codfish in the Gulf and east of Newfoundland, the entire east coast fishing industry is operating today in a fog of uncertainty. National Sea Products, one of Canada's largest fishing companies, has seen its financial situation deteriorate steadily. On November 4, it put out a press release stating that the company's net loss for the nine months ending October 3, 1981, was in excess of $3 million. Over the 21-month period ending October 31 the company's net working capital declined from $20.8 million to half a million dollars, yet the minister seems to think that this is not a serious situation.
H.B. Nickerson and Sons, another Canadian fishing company, has had similar cash flow problems. The Lake Group mentioned by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) is also facing serious financial problems. This large Newfoundland company closed its trawler operations at Grand Bank, Fortune and Gaultois and I believe that only the Fortune plant has been reopened.
In all cases, spokesmen for these companies gave similar reasons for their financial problems. They cited four principal factors for the rapid decline in the industry, namely, growing market weakness for their products, high interest rates, operating cost increases and inappropriate government policies.
It would seem that the soft markets for Canadian fish have been due to weak demand in the United States in recent months for several key products, plus what I can only call the strained attitude which seems to exist between Canada and the United States, brought about by the hamhanded manner in which this government implemented its Foreign Investment Review Act as well as its national energy policy. We see this attitude reflected in the stalemate which exists in the negotiations on the fishery and boundary treaties covering the controversial Georges Bank area.
I fear that Canadian fishermen will long remember the lack of this government's ability to reach an amicable political solution on the Georges Bank issue which, I submit, could have been obtained if a conciliatory attitude had been taken by Canada when dealing with our best friends and our largest trading partner.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext: What do you advocate-that we give in?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
The minister interrupts and asks what I am advocating. I will repeat it so that even he will understand. I have great admiration for the minister and I know he has worked hard but he could work a little harder on this one.
I said that I submit the situation could have been different if there had been a more conciliatory attitude taken by Canada when dealing with our best friend and our biggest trading partner. That is what I advocate.
The lines of communication are down. They are not clear between our two countries. There is too much static. No one will ever convince me that further consultation rather than confrontation would not have brought about a more desirable settlement of what I call a very thorny issue between our two countries. Our fish markets are soft as well because of a relative drop in several European currencies which has eroded Canada's price advantage. There have also been very weak prices and poor demand for Canadian herring in Europe. This is due to the resumption of the North Sea herring fishery.
Another item affecting our sales has been tariff and nontariff barriers in Spain, Japan, the European Economic Community and in Portugal. These have been raised in an attempt to force Canadians to agree to granting further fish allocations inside our 200-mile limit. This, of course, should not be happening.
When speaking in Marystown on October 3, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) said that there had to be realism when it comes to negotiating with other countries for advantageous entry into their markets or for the removal of barriers to those markets. He also said that if it costs us a few thousand tons of fish from our waters to sell many more thousands of tons of Canadian fish products, then we must assess the deal and not perpetuate some myth that we must catch every fish in our zone. Such a concept is fool's gold, he said, and that what is required to achieve entry into markets must be done.
This is high sounding rhetoric, and the minister is obviously following the course he expounded. He is giving away fishing quotas to foreign fleets-within our 200-mile zone. When he does not give them what they think they should have, they come and take what they feel they are entitled to. We learned this fact only on Thursday of last week when I pointed out that 25 Spanish draggers and two Mexican trawlers were fishing on Flemish Cap in the northwest Atlantic fisheries zone. They have reportedly been overfishing in that one small area near the Grand Banks where cod stocks are endangered, thereby making a mockery out of this country's quotas on fish.
December 4, 1981

I asked the minister in committee if he had any idea as to how many tons of fish the Spanish and the Mexicans are catching, what effect this overfishing would have on Nova Scotia and Newfoundland cod stocks, and what action the government was taking to encourage these nations to discontinue their destructive practices. The minister's officials replied that they did not know how much fish was being taken because neither Spain nor Mexico are members of NAFO. Therefore, they are not obligated in any way to abide by NAFO rules or to report catches.
We were told that the impact on our cod stocks is indirect. The government is making representations, through NAFO, against the countries following this practice. I think this points out a weakness in our Department of External Affairs. I submit that Canada, through that department, should be making diplomatic protests, loud and long, to the Spaniards and the Mexicans. This apparently has not been done.
Since the minister holds strong views which, as I just reported, he stated in Marystown, I think he should also tell us how many tonnes of fish he has given away to foreign countries and what advantages he has received for Canada with regard to getting entry into their markets. I am sure he is aware, and if he is not, I will tell him now, that this policy is not acceptable to the Canadian industry, for although the industry desires to get new markets, it is not prepared to be blackmailed into giving tonnage to others in return for market concessions until all or any benefits which we may receive as a nation are given or frittered away. This is not the way to manage Canada's fisheries resources.
I mentioned a moment ago that the lines of communications between Canada and the United States are cluttered with static and the message seems unclear. This analogy is equally true within Canada. In my own riding, for example, in River-port, Nova Scotia, the Riverport Seafoods plant burnt down along with the government wharf on the afternoon of September 26.

speechtext:
I submit that the minister has added unnecessarily to their anxiety and worry over the future.
Again, on Tuesday, I asked the minister in committee what his plans were for the reconstruction of the wharf at Riverport. He replied, "The company in question has to decide if it is going to rebuild, and as soon as there is a firm commitment to rebuild, we obviously will be preparing the plans which might be slightly different from those for the previous wharf." In all honesty, I suppose that that type of answer is better than nothing. However, I ask the minister and the government, which has two cabinet ministers from Nova Scotia: why is it impossible to get at least one direct answer from anyone over on that side which would indicate that they plan to rebuild that wharf at Riverport in Lunenburg County? There has been a wharf on that site for decades. The fishing fleet and the homes of the captains and the fishing crews are there. I submit that Riverport citizens will not easily accept or readily forget the form of shell game that this minister seems intent on playing with their fortunes and their future. I ask the minister to reconsider his stand on that issue immediately, and since the wharf reconstruction is nothing more than economic pump priming, that he immediately start with plans for its replacement.
Another factor affecting the fishing industry has been the high interest rate policy of the government. This policy has increased the industry's fixed costs, and especially inventory holding costs, to which such a seasonal industry is especially vulnerable. In addition, operating costs, especially those for fuel, for fishing gear and for labour have been outpacing general inflation while market slumps have kept the over-all market price for the product below cost.
This government has not provided any help whatsoever to assist the fishing industry to overcome its high fuel costs and its bloated interest costs, which are a direct result of government policy and for which the cabinet ministers in the House and, in fact, the entire government, must assume entire responsibility. In fact, on November 30, 1981, in response to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), the minister said, "interest and fuel increases are only"-what did he call it? He said they were "irritants".

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
They are some irritants! It reminds me of Winston Churchill's famous phrase: "Some chicken, some neck." Some irritants, the government's fuel price increases and the high interest costs!
While these factors have triggered the current crisis, the cumulative impact of federal fisheries policy since the mid 1970s has so weakened this industry economically that it cannot withstand the present downturn. Licensing and quota allocation policies have induced too many participants to enter the fisheries industry. This has increased and concentrated fish landings in the summer when the fish flesh is soft. It is not of premium quality, and the markets are weak.
Seasonality, I say to Your Honour, is the most serious structural weakness in the industry today. The minister has the full responsibility. He has told us many times that he has the responsibility for controlling the Atlantic fishery. Therefore, he must take full responsibility for this unfortunate situation. Today, when the minister was speaking, he referred to me, for which I thank him. One always likes to hear one's riding mentioned in the House. The minister referred to "The hon. member for South Shore" when he said that it was he, the minister, who had resisted the expansion of the offshore fleet. I am like the minister, and I, too, wish the debate were a little less structured because we could perhaps get our points across a little better. However, at that time we were pointing out that some of the fleet was obsolete. In fact, some ships became so old that their continued use would endanger and could now endanger the lives of their crews. We were also saying that, to be competitive, the industry should upgrade its ships to take advantage of new technology, including some freezer trawlers for the inshore as well as the offshore fleet. That is what we were saying at the time.
Today the minister also mentioned some of the options he is considering. I hope I am quoting him rightly because I do not want to misquote him. One option was to buy into one of the large companies in order to learn more about its managing policies. He also said that the government may bring the fleet in under one management system. In other words, what he said indirectly was that the government is thinking about nationalizing the fishing industry-

-which is comparable to that which has already been done in the oil and gas industry. This is precisely the worry and the concern of the entire industry. If it is carried out, the government will have to raise the taxes of all Canadians even higher in order to bolster its unemployment insurance fund.
I hope the minister will understand when I say that I believe Canadians should have some freedom to operate a business in a free democracy. This is difficult for me to understand because, speaking on a more personal note, when I and some friends built our first dragger in 1947, we followed the course of cleaning and icing our fish at sea in order to land prime quality. The minister says they do not buy, Mr. Speaker. I will accept that, and I will deal with that in a moment.
But this policy diverts raw material and potential employment opportunities away from Canadian processors, thus creating unrealistic price expectations that are incompatible with the private sector development of the industry.

However, if the government can subsidize the factory ships of communist countries by guaranteeing them additional catches of squid or other fish species if they do not fill their holds with mackerel or herring, then I believe the federal government should pay the difference between the processors offered price and the foreign factory ships through the fisheries prices support board.
