In the long run, if that type of policy were followed it would bring a greater over-all return to Canada than that received
December 4, 1981

under the present policy. Also, it would be fair to all fishermen and workers, and it would not favour only a select few, which is happening under the present policy.
To place the fishery on a profitable footing in the medium to long term I submit that we must establish policies leading to the restructuring of the entire industry. I submit that the Canadian fishing industry is well placed to make a significant and ongoing net contribution to national and regional wealth, but this can only be achieved by the private sector if it is able to make some profit.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister and my honoured colleague have addressed a number of the issues, which clearly shows that far from failing to foresee the problems currently facing the Atlantic fishing industry, the government has warned all the participants right from the beginning of the pitfalls and the problem areas which would have to be dealt with on a continuing basis if the promise of the 200-mile fishing zone were to be fully realized for the benefit of all.
I have just a word to say on the 200-mile limit. Since the extension of the Canadian jurisdiction to 200 miles offshore, on the east coast and in Canada generally we have increased our share of the total catch of groundfish. This has increased the market value of Canadian fisheries production. In fact, a study recently completed by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, entitled "Canada's Fish Markets for the 1980s", forecast that Canada could export $3.25 billion worth of fish and fish products. This could be achieved by 1985. This is a 44 per cent increase in real earnings over 1980. The study reported that, to reach this goal, the quality of Canadian fisheries products must be improved if they are to appeal to the sophisticated tastes of consumers in other countries.
Since the implementation of the 200-mile limit, I do not feel that our industry has grown to the extent that the policies have tried to make possible. In my view, the industry has not done anything about meeting the requirements of the export markets. We may put the blame on the federal government for some things, but surely we cannot blame the government for the fact that food cannot be sold in world markets. Nor can we put the blame on the minister. The minister has tried over the past few years, and has discussed measures with the industry which he has proposed they adopt, to increase the market value of our groundfish and other fish.
There are many factors which have caused the distressing state of our east coast fisheries. I will dwell on four only. First is markets. This year I have seen intensive fishing of groundfish by the offshore fleet. This was done even after a poor 1980 year. The fleet caught its quota in the first three or four months of the season to the detriment of other areas, mine in particular. I saw the haddock they caught. Some fishermen had never caught haddock before and some plants had never processed haddock before. When our season began, our own industry could not participate in that market, which had been there for years, because of the dumping by the offshore fleet and by the dumping of the processors into the existing markets.
Fisheries
The big four fisheries firms compete among themselves. They dump into an existing market. They catch their quota right at the beginning of the fishing season. Some of the European competitors can provide better quality, and with the favoured exchange rate there is a serious marketing problem for Canadians. We have not been able to overcome the tendency of the big four to control their existing markets and to fail to find better markets or to put better fish on the existing markets.
Another problem is quality about which I shall speak later. But first I want to speak about our high interest rates. 1 have not seen any of the provinces, who are directly responsible for some of those processing plants, get into the fray by helping the processing companies. Instead, they come to the federal government. I am sure some solution will be found, but I would like to see some effort on the part of the provinces in coming to a solution.
Another problem is overcapacity. This year we saw plants open which had never before operated at that particular time of year. In fact, some had not operated at all for quite some time. We may well have overcapacity in some of the fishing areas. Perhaps our vessels will have to go looking for new sources of fish beyond the 200-mile limit and develop some of the underutilized species. We have not risen to that challenge since the 200-mile limit was imposed. This too is one of the main reasons that we are suffering at this time.
My colleagues have discussed the three basic factors which must be part of any analysis of the ill health of the fishing sector, namely the resource, the capital and labour employed in both harvesting and processing, and last, but certainly not least, is the marketplace. I have already discussed in general form some of the marketplace factors which I think have existed this last year.
At the outset I wish to remind hon. members opposite that time and again, even before fisheries' jurisdiction was extended to 200 miles, the minister emphasized the fact that while Canadians were gaining a fishing zone, they were also losing an excuse for poor performance in the fishery. The time has come when we can no longer excuse ourselves for poor quality fishery products and inability to compete.
Until now we have been unable to control the marketplace, yet we have, off the east coast, one of the greatest potentials for industry, particularly if one considers that we are dealing with food and the need for sources of food which exist in the world today and will exist in the future. This subject has been much talked about but we have never taken the concrete action required to control the marketplace rather than allowing the marketplace to control us as is the case today.
Obviously, there are some aspects of the marketplace which we cannot control. We cannot set the world price, nor can we demand that people eat Canadian fish rather than fish caught by fishermen from other countries, just as we cannot demand that people not eat chicken or pork.

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
There are some aspects to the industry which are under our control and upon which we must take action. We must stop fishing in a general way and begin fishing in earnest to meet market requirements. First we must determine, before the net is put into the water, where there is a market, and what product will sell. If we find we have a particular species which would sell in the market, we should offer a top quality product so that we may obtain the top price.
I would like to turn now to processing, quality and marketing. I believe that if we on the east coast can improve the quality of our fish, our marketing capabilities will follow. The processing, quality and marketing policies are also in the process of changing dramatically. Of course, processing is an integral part of the fisheries policy because it is the processors who provide a market for the fishermen's product. The processor also provides much of the shore-based employment in the region.
The primary responsibility for this sector lies with the provincial governments. However, the federal government remains involved in areas such as inspection regulations, export marketing and regional economic development.
Quality enhancement was one of the most important aspects of fisheries policies which were discussed in the recent document called, "Policy for Canada's Atlantic Fisheries in the 1980s". A major program has already begun. It will be maintained in an effort to ensure that the quality of Canadian fish products will continue to improve.
We have had a fishing inspection program for many years which was aimed in the beginning to ensure the health and safety of consumers. However, steps have already been taken to improve quality. For example, the department has given financial assistance to help upgrade handling and storage facilities. The department has provided equipment to the inshore fishermen to improve the on-board handling, off-loading and dock-side handling and transportation. These measures have helped but, we are told, much remains to be done. The implementation of this assistance is what I am concerned about and what I will be watching for in the next few months.
After extensive consultation with people in the fishing industry, the government has embarked on a major quality enhancement program. The major elements of the program involve vessel certification, quality protection on board, dockside grading onloading, dockside handling and transportation to plants, improved quality control in processing plants and finally, finished product grade standards.
In terms of vessel certification, regulations are being amended to require that all vessels have adequate on-board facilities for storing and chilling the fish in a manner which will preserve its quality.
On-board quality protection is an area in which Canadian fishermen have not measured up as well as their competitors. Competitive industries require that fish be bled, gutted and iced on board and prohibit the use of forks and pumps which damage the edible portion of the fish, and they insist that the fish be stored at depths which prevent physical damage. In
many sectors of the Canadian fishery, all of these prohibited practices are in use. I know that in this area the minister has given an ultimatum to fishermen about bleeding and gutting. However, I do feel that there are instances during certain times of the year when fish are caught that it is hard to believe that they would be of better quality by having them bled and gutted. I hope through consultation and meetings with the fishermen that this problem will be considered.
The department proposes that Canada should at least adopt the practice of chilling or icing the fish on board and restricting the depth of storage to 90 centimeters or less to prevent damage. I can assure the minister that in my area a good percentage of the fishermen are doing this already. There are perhaps other areas where fishermen are not doing this, and that may be one of the quality problems. It was not quality which prevented the sale of haddock last spring and summer. Those fishermen had had good markets and good prices for their fish. It was the fact that the inventories of the big companies, which the offshore fleet had caught so early in the spring, had been dumped on the market that brought the prices down. Haddock is not a commodity which we find in many other areas of the European markets coming into the United States. It happened to be a good selling product in the southern part of the province and this was detrimental.
Returning to the measures which are already in place, the discussion paper went on to say that by making these measures universal as well as by paying higher prices for fish gutted and bled on board, the department hopes to see a major improvement in quality. I have already stated in the House that I do not feel that gutting and bleeding fish is the only measure which makes for top quality fish. When fishing boats are out for extended periods of time, fish should be bled and gutted before processing back on shore, but when fish are returned almost immediately it is hard to believe that bleeding and gutting would make the fish of better quality.
Another area considered by the discussion paper was dockside grading standards which are being developed at this time. The standards will be based on firmness, odour, exterior appearance and degree of bruising or blood spotting. As previously noted, the department stated that first quality fish would be those bled and gutted on board, and I repeat that I question this being the only way to produce first quality fish.
If this program is to be successful, a concentrated program to train and/or licence graders is essential. To my knowledge there is no quality training program in Nova Scotia which would upgrade the quality of fish in the processing industry. The proposal now being considered is to elicit the help of the provinces in this task to undertake the training at fisheries training schools and in colleges.
If quality is a prime consideration, I certainly hope that the provinces play their part in the program.
The quality enhancement program at dockside will prohibit the use of forks and pumps which damage the edible portion of the fish. In addition, the department is working on a port-byport basis to ensure an adequate water supply at all unloading ports. It is hoped that there will be a fully approved water or
December 4, 1981

modified unloading system at each port by 1985, according to the discussion paper.
I welcome this because one of the chief ports in my province, the town of Digby, has a bad water supply problem and has not been able to find funding under DREE. Perhaps in the renegotiation of the DREE agreement, there will be some assistance in solving this problem.
Guidelines are being developed for good manufacturing practices which will ensure the production of high quality products. Voluntary compliance with the guidelines will begin this year and the possibility of including them in the regulations which govern plant registration will be considered.
The department is also drafting a finished product grade standard for a number of products including crabs, frozen pickerel fillets, frozen sockeye and pink salmon, groundfish fillets, frozen herring fillets and cured herring products. These graded products will be subjected to inspection, and the granting of an export licence will be conditional on their meeting the standards. I believe this will achieve one of the expectations of the industry respecting marketing better quality products.
In the marketing field the major new direction outlined in the discussion paper is the initiation of an export licensing system, and on that point, I remind the House that the minister has been seeking an orderly marketing system for the past number of years. I do not think the hon. member who spoke just before me was implying that we should register a complaint because the two countries to which he was referring are fishing on the open seas. They have a right to the open seas, as does any other country. Until there is a law of the sea agreement, we would not have any jurisdiction to oust them from the open seas beyond our 200-mile jurisdiction. If we did, I am sure that would be considered a major provocation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext: Fish war.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I would not even call it a fish war. I think it would be a provocation against a state. It is unfortunate that the two countries referred to do not belong to NAFO.
There was some mention about the EEC agreement, and we must remember that Canada negotiated to get orderly marketing arrangement with the EEC. Only recently has that been ratified by the EEC and, to my knowledge, the Canadian provinces and processors which were opposed to this have not stated whether or not it should be ratified by this country. However, the process of the negotiations did involve the provinces and the processors. It is my understanding that a decision will be made very shortly on the EEC agreement.
I know time is passing. There are many problems, but I believe they can be solved. This fisheries minister has always been able to sit down and discuss problems. It is a matter of the industry showing good faith. I remember back in 1974 and 1975 when this minister brought in a support program for the groundfish industry, which was failing at that time. The
Fisheries
industry promised it would come up with better standards and better marketing conditions for its fish. It seems to me that those conditions have not improved since then, and I for one did not feel it was necessary at that time for assistance from the federal government. I felt that the industry should have improved its own fish operations because there clearly was irresponsibility on the part of some of the big companies in expanding to meet a demand which they were not working to increase in the marketplace. I wish the minister luck with the problem. It is a major one, but I know he has resolved other problems in the past. He is having a meeting with the provincial ministers on Monday. To my knowledge, he has been meeting with representatives of the Fisheries Council over the last few months at least every six weeks. This demonstrates his willingness to discuss the problem. There may be some hon. members opposite who are not as willing to look at this problem.
I speak from experience because last spring when the problem arose with respect to the haddock fishery in South West Nova and at the southern end of my province, the minister met with both fishermen and processors. A $14 million stabilization plan was brought forward by the Fisheries Prices Support Board. However, the people who had put the inventory into the market were not willing to accept the plan and, to the best of my knowledge, did not come back with any alterations to the plan, and have yet to come forward respecting that $14 million program for haddock inventories.
I am pleased to have taken part in this debate today. I would have liked to comment on other matters such as sector management, which I feel needs to be discussed. I can see that the general over-all feeling respecting sector management is good in the sense that there will be Gulf sector, Newfoundland sector, Scotia sector and Fundy sector. However, there are problems which are worrying the people. The resource in a given area should be for the fishermen in that area, and there should be no lines drawn, particularly in the Scotian shelf area, between different areas. I realize that there will be discussions on sector management before its full implementation, and I look forward to some of those discussions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am happy to participate in the discussion this afternoon on the fishing industry on the east coast. Over the years the east coast fishery has been a valuable sector of the economy of Atlantic Canada, but in the last number of years it has been declining in importance, and we have had a great number of problems in the industry.
This afternoon my comments will be about a proposal the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is considering. It is a proposal regarding transferable property rights. I read a paper on this matter and, according to my understanding of the contents of that paper, one objective of the proposal is to allocate to certain sectors of the industry the right to own the fish that are in the oceans. They will have the right to catch those fish at places which are convenient to their operations. Another objective of the proposal is to provide for a more uniform and even flow of fish to the processors in order to

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
avoid a boom and bust or a feast or famine situation. I agree with this objective, and I can certainly endorse the principle, but there are some concerns I have about the proposal which I would like to voice at this time.
As I said earlier, the paper is a note on transferable property rights. It defines the proposal, explains its application and briefly discusses the benefits and some of the problems which could be expected.
The report defines transferable property rights as a distribution of fish quotas to individual fishing enterprises which may catch the assigned quotas at whatever time and, in principle, by whatever method they choose. Transferability implies that the quotas can be sold, traded, loaned, rented, etc. as can any element of private property. It tries to clarify that they would not constitute personal property as such, but once allocated initially by the Crown, there should be an implicit notion of contract which would protect the recipient against arbitrary withdrawal of the right. Nonetheless, it is almost certain that the federal government would enact regulations to place some restrictions on freedom of transferability to prevent quotas concentrating in too few hands, or in foreign ownership, for example. One of my concerns is that these quotas will be assigned to certain companies, and on the east coast at the moment, unfortunately, there are large fishing companies which are in extremely poor financial condition. They are almost bankrupt. If, heaven forbid, they do go broke, I am concerned that their rights might be transferred to other companies which may not even be located in the same province. Those companies would then have control of the fish and take it to that other province, eliminating completely a fishing industry in the former province. That is one of my basic concerns about this proposal.
The paper suggests that this proposal could in principle be applied throughout the industry, but for practical reasons it is most feasible to first test the concept in the offshore sector. The first and most important step in the application of the policy would be a division of the total quota, the total allowable catch, in a given stock among fleet sectors. Once the offshore share of the TAC is determined as a percentage, this amount of fish would be allocated among trawler operators over a certain long period of time and according to some initial formula. The major benefit of the transferable property right according to the proposal, as I understand it, is that many of the problems we now struggle with under the common property system will be eliminated. That may be so. Only time will tell.
We are all aware of the race mentality which is a result of fleets naturally trying to maximize their share of a quota. The result has been short seasons which operate regardless of when fish are schooling. Large fleets are maintained to maximize the catch, but they sit idle for long periods of time after the quotas have been caught.
Similarly, processing plants are pushed to their limit during the season and then must lay many of their workers off when
the glut of work disappears. After all, the fish have been caught, the processing plants have to lay off the workers. These feast and famine cycles have plagued the industry as long as the government has found it necessary to impose limitations on the period of the fishing season.
We must recognize that the problem is not an industrygenerated one, but an infliction caused by the government's decision to regulate. I am not saying we should not act to protect our fishing resource, but the problem is created by the government, so we have a responsibility to act to solve it. For that reason, we must examine very seriously any proposal which changes in a very major way our existing fishery. However, before embracing it as our survivor, let us examine it critically to see if it truly is a superior system.
The introduction of transferable property rights would be a complete reversal of our current theory of fish ownership and resource management. Presently we expect fish to be common property. Harvesting of it is controlled by licensing and restriction of the season. The transferable right claims that fish should not be common property but should be allocated by a yet undetermined system to the fishing enterprises. In theory, the race to harvest would end and the fishermen could concentrate their efforts on economical and efficient methods. That is something we all want. This would logically lead to a much more consistent flow of fish from the trawlers to the plants, eliminating the boom-and-bust aspect and the race mentality.
The discussion paper points out that the fishery is the last major resource industry where participants have no property rights in the resource itself. This is undoubtedly correct. However, we must be concerned about our method of distribution of the ownership. The concept is one that is most important in a country which operates under the rules of a free marketplace. Ownership of a resource as important as fish is of great economic value. If we do not distribute that resource fairly or equally, it will be very hard for any government to justify seizing the property for redistribution. In fact, the proposal of giving away a resource owned by the Canadian people is an important consideration we should all reflect upon. The rights to fish present to any owner a great possibility to generate a profit. The fish in the Atlantic Ocean are of great value. We should determine the cost of that licence. Will it simply reflect the cost of the paper work and administration, or will it reflect the true economic benefits gained by the new owner? The answer to those questions depends on how we define property rights.
Let us at this time take a close look at the beneficiaries of the transferable property rights and just how they may respond to its enactment.
The trawler fleets currently are of sufficient number to be able to harvest a large number of fish over a short period of time. That is what happened last summer. The trawlers caught the allowable catch for the year in a very short period. Consequently, the season closed. The fish plants closed and a great many of the plant workers were out of work after a very few weeks.
December 4, 1981

With the elimination of a formal season, the fleets will concentrate their efforts when and where the fish are schooling. This will result in a much more efficient harvesting of the stocks and a more even supply of fish to the processing plants. This is something we all desire. The probable result is a gradual elimination of older, less efficient trawlers which would lead to employment for less men but over a longer period of time. This will effectively lead to even more fishermen being out of work.
I hope the minister realizes the likely consequence of the establishment of the transferable property rights, and is prepared to try to establish alternative employment opportunities for those affected. That is one of my main concerns. We will have fewer people working longer periods of time. It is an important goal to try and attain. However, there will be greater numbers of people out of work. They will not be able to find alternative work.
The processing plants will be subjected to even more substantial changes. A more constant supply of fish will eliminate the peak period when all of our processing plants are running at 100 per cent production levels. It is reasonable to foresee a large number of the small, older and outdated plants going out of business. Not only will many jobs be eliminated, but this will likely happen in areas such as Prince Edward Island where smaller plants exist. They will lose out. The larger centres will benefit.
Our discussion today centres on the plight of our fish processing industry and the discussions the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) will have with his east coast provincial counterparts on Monday. I certainly hope that the minister will suggest that transferable property rights be examined as a possible solution. I hope at that time he recognizes it for what it is, a plan to stabilize the cyclical nature of the industry.
The fact that the industry is geared to the cycle will mean further strains on it in order to adjust. The transferable property right is at best a partial solution. The consequence and responsibility of causing unemployment and losing part of the industry must be addressed by this government in its meeting with the provinces.
At this time I would like to express my concern of this "notes" proposal that transferable property rights be introduced exclusively in the offshore fisheries, with the remainder of the industry being introduced to it at a later, as of yet undetermined, date.
We must realize that the theory and principle behind these management programs are opposite and contrasting. How will we explain to the struggling inshore fishermen why the government has given offshore trawlers exclusive ownership of a large quantity of unharvested fish while they must continue to struggle with the inequities of the present common property system? If fishing regulations are not uniform, conflict in the industry will intensify.
I realize that application and enforcement of transferable property rights will be much easier if it is restricted only to the
Fisheries
offshore fleets. Setting quotas and enforcing restrictions on catches will be, without a doubt, a huge task. If it is not done equally or if quotas are not closely adhered to, the system will break down. When a decision is made, it must be made in the context of all the fisheries. A fair and equitable system must be established to win the respect and co-operation of all involved.
I am sure that the minister is aware of problems created when the government fails to stick to its own set of rules. I rose in the House on October 14 to bring to the minister's attention the anger and frustration of P.E.I. scallop fishermen in the Northumberland Straits.
Actions such as this have caused much frustration and distrust of this government and have encouraged the belief that we have no management plan for our fisheries. The most enlightened aspect of the transferable property rights proposal is that the fishermen would gain more control over their fishing operation because they would not be subject to the unexplained whims of the minister.
In closing, I would like to encourage the minister and his officials to listen hard to the concerns and requests of the provincial ministers of fisheries when they meet in Ottawa on Monday. They are in closer contact with the fishermen and understand well the problems the east coast fishermen are now experiencing. The transferable property rights system has merit, but major problems still exist within it. They must be addressed and solved before the full merit of the new system can be judged by the House.
I want to reiterate, Mr. Speaker, that the principle as outlined in the proposal would stabilize the fishing industry, eliminate the boom and bust cycle or the glut of fish being caught in the short season, the plants operating over 100 per cent capacity into long hours of the night, and then all of a sudden the quota being caught and the plants closing down for the season. The principle behind this policy is largely to eliminate that. It is something I endorse on principle. However, as I said earlier, there are many things in the proposal that are of great concern to me and I hope that they will be brought to the attention of the minister. I hope the minister will pay attention to some of the concerns that will be explained or voiced to him on Monday by the ministers and deputy ministers of fisheries from eastern Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to say that the fisheries industry in Newfoundland is in dire straits would be a gross understatement.
The year of 1981 has been a disastrous year in fisheries, not just for fish plant owners but for thousands of fishermen and fish plant workers. In my few remarks today, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the House my own opinion about this situation, mostly as it relates to the inshore fishermen, particularly in my area. The major problem for the people on the northeast coast of Newfoundland this year was the lack of fish.

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
It was incredible, as I went around my constituency this summer, to see ten to twenty communities where absolutely no fish was caught, and then two or three other communities where the fishing could be described as being from good to excellent.
The scientists claim that it was because of the temperature of the water. While accepting that rationale, there are other factors that should be noted, factors that go beyond the short run and factors that go unnoticed because of lack of attention, generally speaking, to the long run.
I have always maintained that if fishermen on the northeast coast of Newfoundland could sell all the fish they catch, and if that fish were going into final production in Newfoundland, even at times when we have a poor inshore fisheries, the return to fishermen, fish plant workers and fish companies would not be classified as the disaster that it was this year.
The time is long overdue for provincial and federal governments to be working with the industry for the long run. It is not good enough that at times of economic distress in fisheries, governments turn on governments, searching for excuses to lay blame and, in some cases, to make up for their own shortcomings. There has been no plan or united approach to the fishermen.
Provincial governments control the issuing of licences to processors and buyers. The federal government controls everything from the low water mark out into the ocean, and never the twain shall meet. The big losers in this game that is being played about who is to blame in this disjointed approach are the fishermen, the fish plant workers, the fish plant owners, the Newfoundland people, the Canadian people and the people in other countries who want to purchase that product.
Let me be more specific. I shall first talk about the fishermen. In the federal riding of Gander-Twillingate there are 10,000 fishermen. Most of them have small boats, and a minority of them own what we call long liners.
In 1981, the vast majority of these fishermen had an absolutely disastrous year. Can one imagine a fisherman getting up at 3 a.m. steaming out to the fishing grounds, hauling his nets and returning home at 8 p.m. and not having made enough money to pay for the fuel that he burned in his boat for that day! That happened to thousands and thousands of fishermen day after day and week after week. The year of 1981 for most fishermen was the year when they had to go out in stormy weather late in October and into November just to try to get that extra stamp for unemployment insurance so that it would help them over the winter, or to provide them with enough income so they could at least keep body and soul together until the unemployment insurance cheque arrived. They made practically nothing this year.
Yes, there were fishermen who had a good voyage on the northeast coast this year; but for every one of these fishermen, I could show you 20 who did not have a good voyage. These experienced men and women-and that is the majority-who have thousands of dollars of debts on their equipment and on their boats hanging over their heads and who have bill collectors hammering on their doors, continue to experience extreme hardship.
While this natural disaster, this scarcity of fish continued, the provincial government's loan board deducted fishermen's loan payments as the fish came into the plants. As a result of its audits, the federal government deducted money as the fish came over the wharf. UIC nailed them with overpayments. The men went home with as little as S40 a week in their pockets in the months of July and August, the very months that they were supposed to be making most of their money.
To listen to hundreds of people recite that same story was incredible to me. I shall never forget it. In trying to help the primary producers, I spent a great deal of time this summer appealing to UIC, making formal appeals to them, and to the Department of National Revenue, and appearing before umpires on their behalf, writing reams of correspondence on each case. Eventually, out of total frustration I publicly denounced the provincial and federal government departments concerned. At a time when there were no fish, the system dealt these fishermen blow after blow. In fact, Mr. Speaker, at this very minute on Fogo Island in my district there are 484 cases of overpayments according to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The man receives a letter from the Unemployment Insurance Commission which says, "You owe us $8,000 from our audit for the last four years. If you have already sent your payment, then disregard this notice. If you have not, you have to do it immediately or we will pursue some form of collection".
While delving into this matter I was informed by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, from which I received no co-operation, that if I delved into the matter much more, because there was an RCMP investigation by the fraud squad, I could be charged with interfering with the judicial process.
There are only a thousand households on the island. Last week I sent out householders containing a questionnaire and statements to sign. If the system calls that interference with justice, then it should charge me right away.
When I said that there were no fish, I meant there was no cod fish. When we on the northeast coast of Newfoundland talk about fish, we talk about codfish. Generally speaking, it was a poor year as well for squid and other species. This leads me to the subject of fish and fish plants in the area which I know best, where 10,000 fishermen have experienced a poor year on the northeast coast.
I have heard the arguments today on both sides of the House. The argument used by the federal government and by the fishermen's union in Newfoundland is that there are too many fish plants. This argument is used in condemning the provincial government for issuing more processors' licenses these past five years than at any point in our history. It has caused some problems with the larger plants now experiencing trouble on the south coast of Newfoundland. It may have its merits. Even if the provincial government now admits or
December 4, 1981

claims that it is part of the problem, there is another side to the story.
The biggest issue in the fishery industry on the northeast coast of Newfoundland has always been that fishermen cannot sell every fish they catch. There are not enough plants to buy all the fish fishermen catch. When a community is told that it will obtain a fish plant and that the plant will sell underutilized species, species which it has not been able to sell in the past, the announcement is greeted with cheers. It is welcome news to see employment come into a community where there are only a few jobs in a local store, perhaps one in the post office, perhaps two men working with the department of highways in the winter, where families are on welfare and there are no employment opportunities. I defy any politician to deny these people employment opportunities. Also I defy any provincial or federal politician to deny that it will improve the quality of fish because they do notvhave to be trucked 200 miles to the closest plant.
If there were more dialogue between the provincial government and the federal government, I am convinced a happy medium could be found. Then and only then could both governments discuss the real problems in the fishery which are prevalent in good and bad years. I believe these problems are at the core of the whole affair. Solving these problems would go a long way to relieving a situation such as the one this year. For example, in good and bad years we dump tens of millions of dollars worth of fish. In some countries it would be considered a continuing national scandal and disgrace until it was corrected. With the starving millions of the world, how can we justify the use of only female capelin in our fish plants while the male capelin are dumped into the water? Approximately 60 per cent of the capelin caught are dumped because they do not contain spawn. How can anyone justify, every year there is a good fishery, the dumping of 30,000 pounds of herring from one small boat if the plant is overloaded or there is an August glut? This is the case boat after boat. How can anyone justify the dumping of fresh squid because of a boat quota by the fish plants or the over-the-side sales to foreign boats? No one can justify the figure of $20 million to $30 million of dumping off the Newfoundland coast in good years, just as no one can justify the dollar value of fish dumped this year, a bad year in the fishery. A fisherman can go out at three o'clock in the morning, spend all day on his boat but not make enough money to pay for boat fuel. He passes over miles of mackerel; he can see them on his sonar. He cannot catch them because he cannot sell them. That is the reality on the northeast coast of Newfoundland; this is happening.
The real problem must be addressed, but I do not honestly believe it will ever be addressed because the experts who are supposed to know, say that it is impossible to correct, that it cannot be solved. I am referring to the problem of what happens to the vast majority of fish after they are landed. The man on the street presents the argument; the man on the northeast coast of Newfoundland asks simple questions which I have heard hundreds of times in conversations in kitchens late at night over cups of tea. The questions are: Why do we
Fisheries
export most of our fish in a relatively raw state? Why do we export so much fish in cod blocks, in barrels or in frozen blocks? The answer given by everyone who is supposedly an expert is always "tariff barriers". The issuing of a processor's license on the northeast coast of Newfoundland in 90 per cent of the cases is the issuing of a license to semiprocess or not to process at all.
I am not suggesting that this problem could be overcome within one or two years or even three or four years, but surely that is the direction which should be followed eventually to final production. Are we to accept the simplistic argument of tariffs for all time? Are we doomed forever by shortsighted government policy which indicates in effect that fish will be exported from a fish plant in Canada to a fish plant in Massachusetts? Fish are being shipped from a fish plant in Newfoundland to a fish plant in another country to be processed, to be sold, to be marketed in that country and then possibly even sold back to us. We export our jobs, we export our profits, we export our economic advantage. If there is one thing that we have in Newfoundland, it is fish. We did not have much this year, but we still have fish. Yet, because there is no long-term planning for the industry, no economic planning, no provincial planning and no consistent rapport between the two levels of government, we are losing the one great advantage we have over other countries.
The provincial government controls everything from the low water mark on land and the federal government controls everything from the low water mark out into the ocean. Because never the twain shall meet for long-term planning, we will continue to export our fish from Newfoundland fish plants to fish plants in other countries, we will continue to dump fish, we will continue to persecute fishermen and we will continue to play games, all for the short term. The time is coming when fishermen, fish plant workers and fish plant owners will come to the conclusion that the solution of problems in the fishery is much too important a question to be left in the hands of politicians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe I can really accept the closing remarks of the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker). Politicians have become so involved in this matter that I do not know how the problems of the industry can be unravelled or how it can be put back in the hands of private enterprise and responsible individuals who did not do so badly prior to the interference of the politicians. Perhaps we should get the politicians out of this and let the industry operate on its own, as it did for many years.
I do agree with what the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate said however, with respect to the activities of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey), with whom the hon. member should be very well acquainted. I would suggest to the hon. member that he should arrange a special meeting between the minister and the Standing Committee on Fisheries and

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
Forestry. Hon. members could then explain to the minister in person the problems with the harsh, unreasonable assessments that are being made retroactively for three, four, five or even six years. I am respectful of the community I shall name, Mr. Speaker, but these assessments are made by somebody born, say, in the community of Estevan, trained in accounting and transferred to St. John's, Newfoundland, where he or she is ordered to reassess the income tax returns of the fishermen. A person like this knows no more about the realities of the fishermen's business than a goose knows about Providence, and this ignorance is illustrated in the reassessments. This procedure is cruel and unreasonable. There is no understanding of the difficulties and the costs that fisherman incurs when trying to make a living.
I urge the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate to invite the Minister of National Revenue to meet with the fisheries committee so that the inequities, the cruel, unreasonable and illogical inequities of retroactive income tax assessment, can be revealed to him. Not all those reassessed are innocent, of course. Some have been careless about filing their returns, but for every one of those there are probably two dozen innocent people mortgaging their homes and their boats and going without necessities in order to pay taxes on assessments made by people who do not know what they are doing.
I appreciate the comments of the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate and I offer my sincere support to him in any action he wishes to take against such unreasonable behaviour by an otherwise responsible minister.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) has problems and, to a large degree, these emanate from the fact that for the last ten or 15 years successive ministers have decided they could run the industry better than it had been run hitherto. The minister who initiated such behaviour may have had some grounds for it, but things have not improved.
I think we should examine the licensing structure, Mr. Speaker. The licensing regulations change without notice. For instance, there is the case of a man who has a licence to fish in the Bay of Fundy and the Atlantic for scallops. When he goes to renew his licence, he finds that now he is constrained to a seven-mile limit. Unfortunately, however, he does not look at the licence when he picks it up and misses the fact that he is no longer allowed to fish in the broad area he used to. When he goes to inquire, after he has been apprehended outside the seven-mile zone assigned to him, he is told that he is no longer eligible for the licence for that area. So he has been deprived of his fishing area without notice-and without noticing. Now it is too late for him to re-establish himself.
What happens in such a case, Mr. Speaker? I will give you the example of a young man in my constituency who bought a boat with which he expected to do some scalloping. He had a letter from the minister which indicated that he was eligible at one time for a licence. He bought a boat worth $100,000, mortgaged his home, but now he finds that he does not have the kind of scallop licence that he thought he had and there is no way he can get enough scallops within the seven-mile zone. Now he finds he cannot get the licence for which he thought
his boat was eligible when he bought it. I suppose that officials in the department will say that he should have known that. I submit, however, that a fisherman has no way of knowing from one day to the next what his licence will be. The information is not posted or circulated to licensed fishermen in advance. The change is imposed at the will and pleasure of some regulatory individual in the department.
The young man to whom I refer happens to be a very strong supporter of the minister's party, but I plead publicly on his behalf-give him the licence that he must have to save his home, to save his boat, to save his honour! I will plead for others who support me or who support the people on our left, because it is my job in this House as a representative of a fishing community to seek fair play. I do not care what a person's political stripe is; if my services are needed, they are available. I say publicly that this man, along with many others, should get his licence.
I should like to put on record another example of a licensing problem, Mr. Speaker. A person in my constituency bought a boat which already had a licence. When he went to transfer a licence from a boat that is now unsafe to the new one, he was told he could not do that. He could not transfer a licence which he had owned to a boat which he now owned. He was told he would have to get another boat if he wanted to use the licence from the unsafe boat. I have known this man for only ten years. He and his family have worked like dogs. Whenever there were fish and scallops to be had, he was out there, no matter how long it took. He has equipped two sons, and a third one is working for him. To date he has surrendered a total of eight licences because he wanted new boats. He needed the diversity of fishing capability which he had in those licences, but they have been taken from him. In my view, this is partly because Halifax has the control of fish and fishing licences for New Brunswick. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the officials in Halifax could not care less what happens in the Bay of Fundy or in the province of New Brunswick.
I am sure that the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate and the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) would join me in appealing to the minister on behalf of communities which have no opportunity to make a living other than through the fishing industry. For generations that has been their sole source of support. When the licensing and quota regulations fall on an isolated community with such severity that it can no longer make a living, then I submit that the minister has to look into the situation. The islands of Campobello, Grand Manan and Deer Island are isolated fishing communities. There is no other way that people can make a living in those communities. When quotas and licences and disadvantages are imposed upon those people by regulation to the point that they cannot make a living, then I ask the minister, in the name of mercy and consideration, to look into matters. Licences should not be taken away. The value of licences should not be reduced by regulation without notice, or the communities will be destroyed. We are all very concerned about the amount of fish left in the ocean. Mr. Speaker, people have been fishing in those areas for nearly three centuries and there are still fish

there. I agree that we must have quotas and that there has to be an element of regulation, but if the people have been able to look after themselves for that period of time, that indicates to me that they should have a little recognition and help, and not be totally neglected. Fairness and justice is the least they can expect.
Yesterday, I believe the deputy minister discussed aquaculture, a subject which has been close to my heart for over 20 years. My interest started when I first saw the work which could be done and the wealth created from fish culture, or aquaculture. It is a subject which our government has not chosen to support except, perhaps, for a little research. However, it has had some knowledge of the subject. For instance, concerning salmon aquaculture, I believe that a man was seconded from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. His name is MacDonald, and he worked with a subsidiary of Devco in the rearing of salmon on a farming type of basis. He made very important progress. In my last conversation with that man, he said that if he could get someone to help him a little Financially, he was quite prepared to risk all his savings in the establishment of a fish aquaculture program to rear salmon. That information has not been available to other people.
Therefore, in the province of New Brunswick, there was eventually evidence that, in fact, salmon could be reared in a farming type of set-up. I commend the government for eventually extending a grant to a company to do some experimentation in fish rearing after it was proven that it could be done. This proved to be successful and it illustrated the fact that, beyond question, it was profitable if properly conducted. The man to whom I referred was joined by three other people whom I know. They were all assured by departmental officials that this program would receive support for five years from the department. After that time, they would be on their own. Almost all the support these people needed was in the supply of fish from the fisheries department and its fish hatchery structures. This year they were advised that they will not get an adequate supply of fish next year. Therefore, that support has been withdrawn.
As I have mentioned in the fisheries committee, at least two people have made a final commitment to donate $500,000 each. If they have a season in which they do not have fish to sell, their very existence will be threatened. Their bank credits will probably be withdrawn, but other payments to financiers, particularly governments, will continue.
There has been a breach of faith, and I appeal to the minister. These people probably need 120,000 fish in total. Let us provide them with the fish which are being reared in Atlantic Canada. Their demand is not such that it will seriously affect the amount of fish which would ordinarily be put out for the sports or for professional fishermen.
I compliment the hon. member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais) for very strongly advocating more research. This is a case where it is proven that research can be done. However,
Fisheries
now we find that, on the one hand, we have some people within the public service structure who do not wish to extend research for public use, and, on the other hand, people who would like to see research extended and put to practical use. The whipsawing that is going on within the department is apparently what is depriving these people of the fish they need.
I say to the minister through Your Honour that it is time that he took this in hand and that the word of responsible officials was kept so that these people will be serviced as they were promised. I ask Your Honour whether you, as a responsible man, would commit yourself to $500,000 of ultimate expenditure on a whim or a chance. Your Honour would not, but these men did. Now the supplies are not there. I appeal to the minister to supply them with the fish which had been assured to them by the promise of support.
Today we have been discussing the quality of fish at length, and I would like to speak a little further concerning the matter. Licensing bears some influence on the matter. A couple of herring seiners decided that they could land better fish if they owned a third boat between them. They spent something approaching $400,000, and surely over $300,000, to buy a boat and equip it with refrigeration equipment so that if they were fishing a distance from shore they could put the fish in the new carrier and properly convey it home, refrigerated and in top quality. What happened then? They obtained a licence for the boat into which they had invested so much money, a licence to use the boat near home. From that distance, they could have brought the fish to the processors in a scow in good quality. However, when they wanted a licence to fish in distant herring regions, they could not get one. As far as I know, they never did.
Are we talking about quality? I say to Your Honour that officials of the fisheries department who denied that licence were talking out of both sides of their mouths. That refrigerated boat was badly needed in the fishing industry. However, it is useless and it is virtually restricted to shore use.
Again, by virtue of licensing regulations and restrictions, the size of the boat is restricted. There is no way that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will grant a man the right to build a boat which is a little bigger so that it will have the same capacity after refrigeration equipment is installed. How, in the name of all that is reasonable, can one get quality if a man is not allowed to build a boat which is a little bigger to refrigerate the fish he catches offshore? Let us become reasonable and rational in this licensing and regulatory structure.
I think the point blank statement which has been made in respect of the processing industry requires some questioning because, to a very large degree, fishing is a seasonal operation. There are times when fishermen will catch a lot of fish. I think it was the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate who again pointed out that we are wasting fish because the processing capability is not there. Processors establish boat quotas and fish are dumped overboard, either at the port or offshore before they get to port, because the quota of the processor in Gander-Twillingate has been exceeded. This is not unusual in the herring industry or in other industries where the catching

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
capability exceeds the processing capability. Because that industry is seasonal, the processing industry must be larger than that which can be kept occupied for 12 months of the year. It must be able to accept the peaks and valleys of delivery. Fishing in the ocean is perhaps not as uncertain as fishing in a stream. However, it is not certain enough that we can say to the processing industry that it has too much fish, while fishermen are saying to hon. members of the House that they cannot sell their fish because there is not sufficient processing capability. We cannot have it both coming and going. We must accept some realities.
It was my privilege to spend a week viewing some of the aspects of fisheries on the west coast. It was also my privilege to have been born in Carleton County, New Brunswick, and to have lived beside a fish hatchery for many years of my life. The fish hatchery was built in 1927. I was in and out of it, very regularly, for the next 20 years. I guess I could not have managed it, but pretty nearly. I learned a lot: from grinding liver to feeding fish, and picking fish to stripping fish. I want to ask the minister and the government, through Your Honour, how the government of Canada could support five fish hatcheries and one holding facility in the province of New Brunswick from 1927 until about ten years ago, but now it cannot. Can the minister tell me how, in the thirties, we could strip, set and hatch 20 million eggs in those five hatcheries, and today, we can only put 250,000 eggs in a hatchery which formerly hatched up to five million eggs a year? While this is happening on the Atlantic coast, we are spending $150 million in a five-year program in British Columbia. I do not begrudge British Columbia one cent as I know it needs the funds. However, I say to Your Honour that a minister who would be party to the expenditure of that sum of money in British Columbia, opening up plans for a second phase of the same program in British Columbia, has a duty and a responsibility to operate those five hatcheries in New Brunswick which we could operate in the thirties. We could operate those hatcheries in the 1930s when we did not have enough to pay six months' interest on today's budget. The budget of Canada at that time might not have been much bigger than the minister's own budget. Relatively speaking it was small. We cannot operate those hatcheries there now. We had the facilities. We had the staff. We had the expertise. But it has gone. That is why we cannot supply fish to these people.
I see the minister shaking his head. I tell him not to shake his head. His officials knew full well what these men were doing because they were in contact with the aquaculture people. If I am not mistaken two years ago-and I might be out a year-his department did not set the eggs it had, and offered to sell them. One year ago the department did not have enough eggs and refused to buy any. That is my understanding. Salmon eggs were offered to the minister's department. These eggs were not bought. They were sold. There are not enough eggs set now to give the support promised to the aquaculture people. We do not have a salmon enhancement
program nor do we have any surveillance of the salmon that are now in the sea. We need both of those.
The importance of salmon to the tourist industry is extremely significant to Atlantic Canada. The importance of salmon commercially and the importance of salmon for the tourist industry is extremely significant to British Columbia. Let us get some balance here. Over-the-side sales are something which may on occasion be necessary. I will not condemn them completely. But when that fish product comes from behind the Iron Curtain into markets into which our fishermen and our processors sell the rest of the catch at lower prices, our processors cannot pay a better price than they do. That is why they cannot be competitive with sales of mackerel and other fish because they are dumped into our potential markets after we have subsidized the foreign fleet by issuing an additional quota. Certainly they can pay more for the fish. But there has to be an adjustment of over-the-side sales, if any, to recognize the competition in the same markets with our fishermen and with our own processors into which the over-the-side sale is eventually marketed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Remi Bujold (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ATLANTIC FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to take part in the debate on this opposition motion on a very important matter. It goes without saying that this motion condemning the failure of the government to forecast or avert the current problems in the fishing industry concerns me deeply, as it does our government, because I could go as far as to say, Mr. Speaker, that I represent one of the great fishing constituencies in Quebec. And when I read this opposition motion condemning the failure of the government to forecast or avert the crisis facing the major fishing companies in Canada, I must say that I can't help smiling because of the naivety of the members opposite and their strange conception of the facts.
I was listening this morning to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) when he attempted to show to the Canadian people and the two opposition parties in his reply that since his appointment as minister, he is one of those in the Canadian government who has shown most concern for the fishermen, their families and the economy of their region since confederation. He pointed out that, on his appointment to this department in 1974, he looked fully into all these problems, that he had to stand up to the major companies to protect our small fishermen, that our friends opposite have strongly protested against the measures proposed by the minister to protect one particular category of fishermen in Canada, and that he is now being blamed for not having forecast that crisis. However, I believe. Mr. Speaker, that he had indeed forecast it and that he was determined to do something to avert it, but that our friends opposite would not have allowed him to do so. During those years, if the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans had been allowed to try to get involved in the processing industry on an
December 4, 1981

equal footing with our major companies, we would probably not be facing such problems.
During the short time when they were in power, the same people who are now accusing us of doing nothing managed to grant these major companies certain privileges and rights that the minister had withdrawn under the previous government, so that these major companies once again had the advantage over inshore fishermen of the Gaspe peninsula, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. And they are now blaming the government for its failure to prevent the current difficulties. If the opposition had really wanted to protect the interests of ordinary people, of fishermen, if it had co-operated, the minister would probably have succeeded, as he has done in all the areas where he has taken action, to better avert the crisis and to adjust government policies to meet the problems experienced in certain regions.
On reading, further on in the motion, that the government is being asked to give the fishing industry the same active support it gave some multinationals in this country, I feel our hon. friends have completely overlooked what the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of Employment and Immigration did jointly with their community development projects in Newfoundland. I shall come back to that later. But I mention it in passing just to point out to you that this motion, which is meant to prove that the government has done nothing, is absolutely harebrained and unfounded in fact.
Mr. Speaker, of course the big companies that hire thousands and thousands of workers are extremely important. Even I have some of their plants in the riding I represent here in this House, especially in the Magdalen Islands; their plants process the fish there. In that particular region, we have not felt the impact the other provinces have, perhaps because we have better administrators locally or because someone having foreseen a drop in prices and demand, this season's operations were planned accordingly. Looking at another aspect of the problem, we have to recognize that some multinationals are very important and beneficial for our economy; still, we must also keep in mind the countless small inshore fishermen on whom both small and medium-sized businesses depend for their fish. Naturally, when a big multinational has problems and shuts down, the whole economy goes down with it. However, if in another area where there are several small businesses in operation you have a couple of them doing bad, you could still have two or three others which would be going fine because they supply markets located in other areas or other countries.
These small businesses which very often are operated on a family basis or by a co-operative or a syndicate of businessmen living in the same area, are very much aware of the needs and interests of the whole community. And that is why it is tremendously important, Mr. Speaker, that we pay attention to these small companies which we are trying to set up in business in Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island
Fisheries
and the other Atlantic provinces, because they deal, as I mentioned a while ago, with limited numbers of fishermen in their effort to provide their respective small communities with the amenities of life which are sought by all concerned.
And that is why since 1974 the Minister of Fisheries in the Canadian government-except during that short nine-month period which fortunately did not last any longer, because during that short period, as I said earlier, it was the small fishermen who had to bear the brunt of some of the policies of the then government-this Minister of Fisheries has been able to implement extremely worthwhile and conclusive policies so that small Canadian fishermen have rediscovered the challenge and the incentive of returning to their occupation and now realize that their trade or their work was the same as all others in Canada rather than a third rate trade as it had been in the past unfortunately. It was our government and our Minister of Fisheries who managed over the last seven years to inspire confidence in Canada's fishing industry and in small fishermen so that at last they were able to look upon that very important vocation as a source of rewarding work to support their families and supply food to their fellow citizens.
But how is it that our government was able to give those people an opportunity for progress on a labour market similar to all others? Many programs have been established in Canada. There was the fishing boat construction program, among others, a very important program created by this department under which fishermen could apply for direct grants to build their own boats. The same goes for the construction of wharves. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer specifically to a very important program which has proved to be beneficial to all the residents of the Gaspe Peninsula, northwestern Quebec and the north shore of Quebec over the past year; it was set up in co-operation with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which generously offered enough funds to improve the fishing facilities in our areas again to enable fishermen to indulge in a more congenial occupation and carry on their fishing activities safely.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion transferred $10 million to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to complete those harbour facilities. I recall that about a year ago I urged the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) to secure such funds because, under the standard criteria of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and considering the volume of catches in our regions, we could not set aside enough money to complete those facilities when we were adversely affected by bad weather and physical considerations which were preventing us, with the money we did have, from building facilities large enough to allow protection from the existing hazards. In my constituency of Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine alone, Mr. Speaker, we are going to spend $2 million this year only to build wharves. In Bonaventure, on the

December 4, 1981
Fisheries
mainland, we are going to build two wharves for a total of $500,000 coming from DREE's first envelope of $10 million, and in the Magdalen Islands, we will be in a position to allocate, for the building of wharves, $1.5 million transferred from another DREE program jointly with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, and I will revert to this matter later if time permits.
Another important program, Mr. Speaker, that has enabled those fishermen to achieve profitability is the one promoting quality. My colleague from Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais) said earlier that last week a most important symposium on quality was held in Matane. Again, this government has made tremendous efforts to try and improve the quality of our fish. It goes without saying that with depleting stocks, fishermen must be made aware that the higher the quality, the higher the prices and the lesser the need to catch more fish. Under this program, we experimented with new plastic bins and we also tried to improve the cooling capacity of the fishing boats, these measures have vastly improved the quality of the fish.
Unfortunately, for this program the federal government did not receive from one sector all the co-operation it could have. I am talking of course of the Quebec government which, unfortunately does not seem to pay all the attention it should to the fishermen of the province. As has become increasingly obvious in the last few weeks, Mr. Speaker, the government in power in Quebec seems to be acting over the heads of people and putting political ideology above the interests of the people it was elected to govern. At a time when the government of Canada takes extraordinary measures to try and improve the quality of our fish and of the fishing facilities, that government increases unashamedly the price for bait, for ice, which fall
under provincial responsibility, and also for fishing gear. So we hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government of Quebec will put ideologies aside and will, this time, work in the interests of the people.
Before closing off, Mr. Speaker, as I see my time is running out, I would simply like to say that the program I was just talking about, and which is applied in Newfoundland in the area of community development projects, allows fishermen who are out of work, for the reasons we already know, to work the required number of weeks to be eligible for unemployment insurance. In the riding of Bonaventure itself, we will set up this year an important $275,000 program and we will also use substantial funds from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in order to provide the materials required and create jobs for these fishermen and especially to improve port facilities which otherwise could not be improved. Contrary to what this opposition motion suggests, I believe this government and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans are intent on protecting Canadian fishermen and providing them with the means necessary, as I indicated before, for a decent life and an adequate salary, like all their fellow Canadians.
